chapters.title: Chapter 1801 Arrogance
paragraphs: Quinlan held the old king's stare across the frozen basement, Iris still gathered against his side, and neither man had moved since the words 'my duty as king' left Alexios's mouth.

The frost held with them. It sat over the casks and the stone in a pale crust, the two lantern flames stayed drowned at their blue points, and beneath it all the sealed pillar kept its silence, forgotten by the very audience it had tried courting.
"You know," Quinlan said at last, "we've spent most of a year trying to kill each other. And in all that time, I felt respect toward you."

Quinlan's voice stayed level and conversational, which, against the pressure in the room, only made it heavier. "You hunted me with badly lacking information, yet you, proud king of humanity, still played every board to win."
Alexios's eyes narrowed.

"But that was when you didn't know what you were looking at. Now we're not talking about a primordial you have little information on, but one of your numerous corrupt vassals. Today, instead of a proud king, all I see is an arrogant man desperately clinging to power."
"..." Alexios remained silent for a long moment, then he laughed.
It came out dry and low and entirely unafraid, rolling around the freezing cellar.

"Arrogance." He turned the word over and shook his head slowly. "Far be it from me. I'm just a dying old man who wants to leave this world knowing his people are in a better place than where I found them."
He said it without a drop of self-pity, in the same tone he might use to report troop numbers, a man stating his deadline.
The winter eased.
Warmth crept back across the stone, the lantern flames climbed up out of their blue and filled the cellar with moving yellow light, and the mass went out of the dark.
Quinlan tilted his head. "Then talk."

"Think past the blood for one moment." Alexios flexed his sword hand open and closed, working feeling back into the fingers. "Say I stand aside. Say I let the Primordial Villain roam my kingdom meting out personal justice on whichever noble house he judges filthy. Whatever control the crown still holds dies alongside them, and every house with the means starts preparing for the day you decide it's time to 'judge them.' And you..."
He looked Quinlan right in the eyes.

"You become the wrathful tyrant. Oh, the commoners will adore you. A monster who butchers nobles, justified or not, is a folk hero by dinnertime. But powerful men will fear you, and what powerful men fear, they scheme against, and they won't scheme with armies. Not against you who just eats them all up."

His voice dropped lower. "You heard the same testimony I did tonight. Somebody seems to have rented the Covenant's name for one night of cruelty, because nobody audits the Covenant and nobody avenges its victims. Make yourself the continent's dreaded executioner, and your name will be rented a hundred times over. Every lord who wants a rival's house burned will burn it himself and whisper 'the villain's justice' over the ashes."
Against Quinlan's side, Iris went very still, her stare dropping to the chain doubled around her fist, split knuckles whitening over the iron.
A rented name...
In another world, where things played out differently, she could've been hunting him instead of the Covenant.
"Let them hate me, or falsely accuse me." Quinlan waved it off. "They'll fall in line soon enough, or the world will leave them behind."

"Leave them behind..." Alexios repeated the words the way he examined captured maps, from several angles, hunting the trap. "Tell me, Quinlan. When you imagine the world that comes after all of this, what does it look like?"
"I'm not giving you a political speech in a basement at night."
"Indulge a dying man."

"Hah..." Quinlan exhaled through his nose, and a corner of his mouth admitted defeat. "Fine. One thing. The one thing this continent keeps teaching me no matter which corner of it I dig up. Power that gets handed down long enough stops being earned, and anything that stops being earned rots. When a man receives everything from birth, land, title, armies, without ever having to achieve a single thing in his life..."
He glanced at the frozen undead.
"...you get the kind of sick men who buy a child and let terrible things be done to them without blinking."
Silence answered him for a while.
Alexios stood with the lantern light moving on his face, and the pause ran one beat too long, then several more.
Quinlan had aimed those words at nobles in general, but watching the old king's expression, he realized they'd struck his house perfectly as well.

Alexios Valorian was a dying man with a crown that would pass the way crowns always passed, to children born holding one. Both princes were seen as pushovers, lacking the old king's charisma, intellect, strength - everything. They would not be able to fill the shoes he left behind, not one bit.

The Princesses weren't much better either. One was wed to Duskmere Dukedom for political leverage, one belonged to the Goddess's church far more than to her father. The other had jumped through a portal and chosen the villain's family over her own palace.
His own children were the one battlefield the old king was clearly going to lose.
Quinlan could have pressed the wound. Instead, he let him have the silence. Kings were entitled to a few seconds of their own.

"You're right," Alexios said at last. "You are more right than you know. I've sat above that rot for almost a thousand years. I've watched houses I knighted myself thicken into things their founders would have put to the sword."

His chin lifted. "You've diagnosed the disease correctly, but it's your medicine that kills the patient. Tear the pillars down with nothing built to replace them, and it won't be dukes starving in the rubble, it will be the millions of small people who plant and haul and pay taxes to whoever owns the road they walk on. Order is a poor, ugly, corrupt thing, and it is still gentler than its absence."
He exhaled tiredly. "I don't have the years left to rebuild what you would raze in a weekend."
"So what do you propose?" Quinlan asked coldly.

Alexios squared himself. "A royal warrant. The crown opens the Ravenclaw investigation formally. My archives, their ledgers, every record they believe is buried, all of it under law and in the open. And if the trail truly ends where you believe it ends..."

However, Quinlan wasn't in agreement. "I'm sorry, old friend, but I can't trust your men to investigate properly. These are the kind of people who'd call the nation just and prosperous when the lands fester with criminal syndicates powerful enough to rival ducal houses."
"Are you two done?"
Iris's voice cut through the cellar, scraped raw by screaming at a skull for a long time.
She had pulled out of Quinlan's hold, and neither man had caught the moment she did it.

"Kingdoms, tyrants, the future of the continent." Her hands tightened into trembling fists. "You've been posturing in a freezer carving up my revenge like it's loot. My family. My brother. My revenge. Neither of you gets to decide what happens to the scum who did this. Warrant or massacre, I don't give a shit what paper it's wrapped in."
She looked them both in the eye, one after the other, for a long passing second.
"They're mine and mine alone."
Nobody spoke for a moment, then Quinlan's tension depleted from one second to the next, replaced by a big grin.
"This old fucker certainly knows how to rile me up. My apologies. I didn't mean to belittle you, Iris."
"You're one to talk..." Alexios grumbled, but Iris didn't hear it.
Her gaze remained on Quinlan, their eyes latched onto each other's, until Iris spoke again. "Quinlan... You've done so much for me I can't even put it into words-"

She wasn't allowed to finish, for Quinlan interrupted, his amusement gone. "You're not about to apologize to me, are you? It's your revenge, your justice, no matter how emotionally invested I might be. I merely hope to be there to see the end of it."

"..." It was Iris's turn to turn silent for a long second, mulling over his words. Then, a brilliantly unhinged, bewitchingly gorgeous, murderous smile greeted his words. "That... is my hope as well. Together..."

"Together," Quinlan nodded, feeling an irresistible urge to hug this amazing woman. But Iris was already a step ahead, stepping into his embrace and looking up. "Thank you... for everything. Without you... I'd..."
This time, Quinlan didn't chitchat, merely returning the hug with full force.
Iris allowed herself a few seconds of it, fierce and wordless, her forehead pressed into his chest. Then she reached her limit and moved to pull back.
She didn't move an inch.
"...Let go."
"No." Quinlan's chin settled on top of her head. "The moment isn't over."
"It's over. It's been over." Her palms pushed against his chest, the same palms that had cracked a frost monolith tonight. "You clingy bastard... Go hug the slit-eyed slut."
"Khm..." Alexios coughed into his palm, and Quinlan's head turned toward the king, unimpressed.
"Do you need a cough medicine, old man?"
"What I need is for you to release her before she reaches for that chain."
Quinlan's arms loosened with zero remorse, and Iris tore herself free, planted a full step of distance between them, and glared at Quinlan with dangerous eyes.
But she couldn't hold it any longer than a few seconds, and looked away.
Alexios then turned to face Iris fully.

chapters.title: Chapter 1802 The Master Plan
paragraphs: "You refused my offer, so let me ask you instead. What do you desire of the crown?" His tone carried no charity in it anywhere; he addressed her exactly as he had addressed the primordial.

"I refused because I don't need any of what you offered," Iris spoke, composure clawed back into place. "Your record, though... The one that dissolved my family in a single paragraph and never mentioned a child."
The flatness came apart on the last words. "Damian Ravenclaw. I want you to write him in."
"It will be the first name entered into the record when I return to the capital," Alexios told her.

Iris held his gaze for a breath longer, then gave the king a short nod and pulled herself up onto the nearest intact cask. She was done talking. Whatever the two men decided next, she'd made her claim, and the exhaustion of the whole day was finally collecting its dues.

"Which brings us back to the same wall," Quinlan picked the thread back up. "Your investigators aren't trustworthy enough, and according to you, my way will make me every killer's favorite scapegoat. That, old friend, is what I believe to be called an impasse."
"..." Alexios didn't answer right away.
The lantern light moved on his face while he weighed his options, and when he finally spoke, his voice had dropped into a lower register, the one he used when the theater was over.
"It's time I show you my cards."
He turned toward the sealed pillar without really seeing it, his thumb working over the pommel of his sword.

"Long before the world heard your wretched name, Ravenshade was the strongest duchy of the realm. Their armies nearly rivaled the crown's standing forces, and holding the border made them heroes to the commoners. Their slave markets refilled their coffers after every border war, and the dwarven slaves they took kept them in weapons and armor no other duchy could field. A few hundred years ago, they stood on the brink of declaring independence, and they would not have gone alone. If one declared war and the crown didn't immediately bulldoze them back to submission, the rest would've followed within days..."
"That's why you married the worst harpy of them all," Quinlan nodded in understanding.

"I married the duke's sister and made her my queen. A short bit later, I wed Calienne, my oldest princess, to Duskmere, Ravenshade's greatest supporter. Elisabeth was then chosen by the Goddess, further helping the crown consolidate its power. Marriage by marriage, pact by pact, the realm was dragged back into balance."

The old king's mouth thinned. "It held for centuries. But those marriages... Every child I have carries Ravenshade blood through Morgana, which means the next monarch of Vraven will be half Ravenshade no matter what I do. Tharion's house has been waiting on that arithmetic ever since. All they needed was for me to die as soon as possible, and for the right kind of heir to reach the throne."
"The right kind."
"Weak. Isolated. Grateful for guidance." Alexios let each word fall like a stone into a well. "And not long ago, Tharion and I struck a deal."
"You did not..." Quinlan's gaze darkened.
"In exchange for Ravenshade's full support of the crown in whatever decisions I make, I promised to name Felicity my heir."
Open disgust took over Quinlan's face. He made no effort at all to hide it.
"Felicity." He repeated the name as if he had to wipe it clean of the sentence it arrived in. "The most easily influenceable child. That's who you sold to Tharion as his future puppet."
From her cask, Iris's red eyes moved between the two men, too drained to interject and too invested to look away.

"It was one piece of a larger design to wrestle power back from the dukes," Alexios responded, unbothered by the disgusted words aimed at him. "When the deal was made, Tharion thought I only had a few months left to live at most. Upon my death, instead of one of my older sons who would at least know they're being manipulated and resist, he'd get an impressionable teenage girl to puppeteer to his heart's content, becoming the true king."
"Ah..." Quinlan's disgust left as if it never existed, replaced by an ominous glint in his eyes. "The longevity drug from the Fujimori..."
"They didn't know about it," Alexios smiled, his own eyes shining with even more sadistic cruelty. "I would've kept taking the concoction until everything was ready."

The old king then chuckled darkly, and his voice took on a tone Quinlan didn't recognize from the old man. He was mocking, quoting. "'Your Majesty, the Princess has been with the Villain for too long... I fear he'll corrupt her! We need to expend more resources on saving her!'"
Quinlan's villainous laughter responded. "He feared I'd snatch the position he wanted for himself..."
Alexios's silence was all the confirmation he needed.

Then the old man sighed, losing his ominous air. "I won't bore you with the details, since they stopped mattering the day a certain all-important bastard graced my kingdom, but the long and short of it is that the dukedoms would have spent the coming decades weakening one another for me, until I struck at the right time."

"...I'll admit that it's really impressive, but why are you telling me this exactly?" Quinlan asked, confused. "If you're fishing for an apology for the wrecked master plan, you might as well give up."
"You and apologizing?" The king shook his head. "I wouldn't dare dream of it."
"I just apologized to Iris," Quinlan shrugged.
"Yes. The only issue is that I'm not a beautiful woman," Alexios responded.
Before Quinlan could respond, the old man spoke up again. "Do you remember the offer I made you through Felicity's pendant?"
The memory arrived on its own, in the old king's voice, tinny through the enchanted metal back when Quinlan had still worn Devil's mask.

'The hand of my third daughter, Princess Felicity Valorian. A noble title of Count, seated in the Central Lands so no duke stands above you. A full pardon for every crime committed in the name of Devil and also while wearing the mask of Black. All of this, in exchange for your service to the royal court as its mage.'
Quinlan's eyes widened by a fraction, then slowly narrowed again as the pieces rearranged themselves into a picture he hadn't been meant to see for another couple decades.

A count answering to no duke. A court mage bound to the crown. Felicity's hand. Every clause of that offer had been a leash braided for the most ominous stray the old man could find, long before anyone knew what was actually wearing the mask.

"You're a much better schemer than I ever gave you credit for, old friend," Quinlan shook his head. "But the answer hasn't changed. I refused your daughter's hand then, and I refuse it now. I didn't claw my way up all the way here just to let politics force me into engagements. Especially not to children. The mere thought creeps me the fuck out."
Alexios laughed, low and genuine. He'd expected exactly that answer, and it showed.

"Believe me, I wouldn't want Felicity marrying a scumbag of your caliber either." The humor burned down and off his face like a spent lantern wick. "That's why I'm no longer asking you to marry her. But you are the one man alive I can trust with her safety once I'm gone."
For a moment, nobody in the cellar had anything to say to Alexios's words.
From her cask, Iris watched Quinlan, and a quiet scoff escaped her.
"I just told him to back off..." she murmured under her breath, meant for nobody's ears but her own. "Yet here he is, striking deals..."

There was no spite in it. The words came out soft, carrying a warmth she'd never authorized, and she looked away before her lips could finish what they'd started. A second later, her eyes widened as she realized she'd been about to smile.

Quinlan studied him, then shrugged. "Why are we even circling this? If Ravenshade turns out guilty, the house dies with the answer and your deal turns to dust on its own. If they're innocent, I subjugate the lot, and we get a duchy of very loyal, very obedient minions. Either way, Tharion never collects. Just don't make good on the promise. Simple."
"'We get a duchy?' Do you even hear yourself?" A vein twitched on Alexios's forehead before he declared, "But there's an issue with your proposed plan. I don't want to take my promise back."
"Is this about that nonsense duty of yours again?" Quinlan sighed, but to his surprise, Alexios shook his head.
"I've seen enough. I've seen who my daughter became at your side, and I've made my decision as a king and as a father both. I want Felicity to succeed me."

"So prove it to me." Alexios's hand left the sword hilt entirely, open at his side. "Prove that when you mete out justice, you can do it not as a wild beast, but as a man my people can trust. Prove it with Ravenshade, for every eye in the kingdom to see. Do that, and I will spend whatever time I have left helping you take this continent..."
The old king held the primordial's stare.
"...and become its 'ruler.'"
He gave the word the exact same weight the dead blade had given it in the soul realm, and there was no chance in the world that it was a coincidence.
Quinlan's lips slowly moved upward. "You old bastard..."

"They didn't know about it," Alexios smiled, his own eyes shining with even more sadistic cruelty.
"I would've kept taking the concoction until everything was ready."
The old king then chuckled darkly, and his voice took on a tone Quinlan didn't recognize from the old man.
He was mocking, quoting.
"'Your Majesty, the Princess has been with the Villain for too long...
I fear he'll corrupt her!
We need to expend more resources on saving her!'"
Quinlan's villainous laughter responded.
"He feared I'd snatch the position he wanted for himself..."
Alexios's silence was all the confirmation he needed.
Then the old man sighed, losing his ominous air.

"I won't bore you with the details, since they stopped mattering the day a certain all-important bastard graced my kingdom, but the long and short of it is that the dukedoms would have spent the coming decades weakening one another for me, until I struck at the right time."
"...I'll admit that it's really impressive, but why are you telling me this exactly?" Quinlan asked, confused.
"If you're fishing for an apology for the wrecked master plan, you might as well give up."
"You and apologizing?" The king shook his head.
"I wouldn't dare dream of it."
"I just apologized to Iris," Quinlan shrugged.
"Yes.
The only issue is that I'm not a beautiful woman," Alexios responded.
Before Quinlan could respond, the old man spoke up again.
"Do you remember the offer I made you through Felicity's pendant?"
The memory arrived on its own, in the old king's voice, tinny through the enchanted metal back when Quinlan had still worn Devil's mask.
'The hand of my third daughter, Princess Felicity Valorian.
A noble title of Count, seated in the Central Lands so no duke stands above you.
A full pardon for every crime committed in the name of Devil and also while wearing the mask of Black.
All of this, in exchange for your service to the royal court as its mage.'
Quinlan's eyes widened by a fraction, then slowly narrowed again as the pieces rearranged themselves into a picture he hadn't been meant to see for another couple decades.
A count answering to no duke.
A court mage bound to the crown.
Felicity's hand.
Every clause of that offer had been a leash braided for the most ominous stray the old man could find, long before anyone knew what was actually wearing the mask.
"You're a much better schemer than I ever gave you credit for, old friend," Quinlan shook his head.
"But the answer hasn't changed.
I refused your daughter's hand then, and I refuse it now.
I didn't claw my way up all the way here just to let politics force me into engagements.
Especially not to children.
The mere thought creeps me the fuck out."
Alexios laughed, low and genuine.
He'd expected exactly that answer, and it showed.
"Believe me, I wouldn't want Felicity marrying a scumbag of your caliber either." The humor burned down and off his face like a spent lantern wick.
"That's why I'm no longer asking you to marry her.
But you are the one man alive I can trust with her safety once I'm gone."
For a moment, nobody in the cellar had anything to say to Alexios's words.
From her cask, Iris watched Quinlan, and a quiet scoff escaped her.
"I just told him to back off..." she murmured under her breath, meant for nobody's ears but her own.
"Yet here he is, striking deals..."
There was no spite in it.
The words came out soft, carrying a warmth she'd never authorized, and she looked away before her lips could finish what they'd started.
A second later, her eyes widened as she realized she'd been about to smile.
Quinlan studied him, then shrugged.
"Why are we even circling this?
If Ravenshade turns out guilty, the house dies with the answer and your deal turns to dust on its own.
If they're innocent, I subjugate the lot, and we get a duchy of very loyal, very obedient minions.
Either way, Tharion never collects.
Just don't make good on the promise.
Simple."
"'We get a duchy?' Do you even hear yourself?" A vein twitched on Alexios's forehead before he declared, "But there's an issue with your proposed plan.
I don't want to take my promise back."
"Is this about that nonsense duty of yours again?" Quinlan sighed, but to his surprise, Alexios shook his head.
"I've seen enough.
I've seen who my daughter became at your side, and I've made my decision as a king and as a father both.
I want Felicity to succeed me."
"So prove it to me." Alexios's hand left the sword hilt entirely, open at his side.
"Prove that when you mete out justice, you can do it not as a wild beast, but as a man my people can trust.
Prove it with Ravenshade, for every eye in the kingdom to see.
Do that, and I will spend whatever time I have left helping you take this continent..."
The old king held the primordial's stare.
"...and become its 'ruler.'"
He gave the word the exact same weight the dead blade had given it in the soul realm, and there was no chance in the world that it was a coincidence.
Quinlan's lips slowly moved upward.
"You old bastard..."

chapters.title: Chapter 1803 Alexios's Promise
paragraphs: Quinlan let the word 'ruler' lie where the old king had dropped it, and for a while the only sound in the basement was thaw-water ticking off the casks as the last of his frost let go of the stone.
Then his grin shifted into a lighter gear.
"So. The rest of your life," he said. "That's what's on the table."
"It is." Alexios's thumb worked over the pommel of his sword, the grave weight of his own offer still sitting on him. "However little of it remains."
"Hmm." Quinlan began a slow, aimless stroll along the cask row. "What if I become the ruler before you die?"
The king's brow creased. "...Then I'd die having fulfilled my promise?"

"Sure, sure. But say it happens fast. Like, so fast you're still in peak form." Quinlan turned, and his voice came out weightless with innocence. "Would you help me take on the outside world as well?"
"The outside world," Alexios repeated.

"The Heavenly Restriction, the so-called 'domain,' comes down, and we gain access to all that uncharted horizon out there." Quinlan shrugged. "It'd be a shame to stop at only taking the domain down, no?"
The confusion drained off the old king's face, and suspicion pooled in its place.
He had spent his whole reign across negotiation tables from the finest liars aristocracy could breed, and every instinct trained at those tables was ringing at once.
Worse, much worse, those instincts had been calibrated for mere human nobles.
The thing smiling at him right now was Quinlan Elysiar, the man who took a mile the moment you offered him an inch and felt zero shame about any of it afterward.
"What are you scheming?"
"Nothing at all." Quinlan placed a hand over his heart. "No ill intentions. I swear it on all that is holy."
"I have heard bullshit from every duke in this kingdom," Alexios said flatly. "But never bigger than the utter nonsense you're spouting right now."
"You wound me, old friend."

"And yet." The king exhaled through his nose, and the suspicion folded itself away, filed under problems too vague to fight. "Fine. Whatever game this is, humoring it costs a dead man nothing. I'll spend the rest of my life helping you, shameless bastard. Outside world included, if I'm still strong enough to fight."
From her cask in the corner, Iris's boot swung in a slow arc. She said nothing, but the look she was aiming at Alexios held open pity.
"Excellent." Quinlan clapped once. "Speaking of which, how long is 'the rest of your life' these days?"
"...A few weeks of useful strength. A season, perhaps." He reported his own death the way he reported supply lines.

"Mm. Then here's what I don't get." Quinlan leaned his shoulder against a support beam. "The Fujimori are, for all intents and purposes, subjugated. Their estates, their cauldrons, their alchemists are ours. Why don't we simply have them keep brewing your youth soup? Problem solved, countdown cancelled."

"You believe I didn't think of that?" The laugh came out of Alexios dry as old paper. "One alchemist alive is said to be good enough to brew it, and the elders wrote a compact into her blood: should they be defeated, she dies on the spot. And if that's not enough of a lock, should any power try to compel the recipe... force, contract, hostage, anything... she dies before the first herb touches water."
The old king shook his head. "Or so I've been told. I'll confirm whether their threats were truthful, but I fully expect them to be."
"Ah." Quinlan waved the entire Fujimori clan out of the air with one hand. "Forget it, then. Them and their contingencies. I'm done with that."
Alexios stared at him.
"That thread is the only thing between me and a grave," he said. "You just waved it off like a fly at dinner. What a magnificent creature you are."
But then Quinlan clicked his tongue. "Old friend, why would I waste my breath on their soup..."
The innocence came off his face whole, dropped like a prop he was done holding, and what surfaced underneath was utter, demonic cruelty, the kind of expression the world had coined his title for.

The grin stretched a few teeth too wide, his eyes lit with an enjoyment that had nothing warm in it, and both lantern flames leaned gently away from him, as though they'd been asked to leave the room.
"...when I have something so much better?"
Every battlefield instinct Alexios owned fired at once, and his boot found a step backward before his pride could veto it.
Quinlan took a step forward.
Iris pulled one knee up onto the cask, settled her chin on it, and did absolutely nothing to warn anybody.
A pocket ring flashed. Between Quinlan's raised fingers, catching the lantern light, sat a single pearl-white pill.
"This little thing right here... stops your aging."
"What?!" Alexios's eyes flew wide, and his second step back was entirely voluntary. Quinlan's second step forward was faster.
Behind Alexios's eyes, the architecture of the last few seconds assembled itself one door at a time.
What if I become a ruler before you die.
Would you help me take on the outside world.
The rest of my life, outside world included, if I'm still strong enough to fight.
He had meant weeks.
He had built his entire surrender on the arithmetic of a dying man.
And the wretched scumbag in front of him was holding the arithmetic's repeal between two fingers.
Cold sweat broke across the King of Vraven's back.

"You fished for it," he breathed. "You made me swear the oath before you showed me the hook. You bottomless, black-hearted, primordial son of a..." His voice climbed with every word, and so did his retreat, one step, then another, boots scraping over old stone. "I take it back. I take all of it back!"
"A king's sworn word? In front of a witness?" Quinlan kept coming, unhurried, rolling the pearl across his knuckles. "Iris. Did he or did he not swear?"
Iris raised one lazy hand without lifting her chin off her knee. "...He did."
"You stay out of this!"
"Don't tell me what to do."

"Where are you even running, old friend?" Quinlan's head tilted as he advanced. "To your grave? Truly? And Felicity... you'd leave her behind, would you? With me as her guardian?" The grin sharpened another degree. "Is that the master plan?"
"She could do far worse than..."

"Did you know," Quinlan said pleasantly, "that I once let her go off on an adventure with zero surveillance? Her, her best friend Feng, Lyra, and Iris. Gone. The strongest of them wasn't even level fifty at the time."
Alexios stopped moving. His shoulders locked. "You did what."

"You royals pamper your children, and pampered brats grow soft." Quinlan pressed a hand to his own chest. "I follow Black Fang's school of child-rearing. Throw them into a monster-infested forest, and whoever crawls back out comes out amazing."
A fond nod. "Just take a look at my Vex. Literal perfection."
The memory arrived in Alexios's skull uninvited: white hair, red pentagram eyes bright with delight, and underneath it all that giggle, the one that never quite obeyed the rest of her face.
A psychotic, obsessed, murderous witch.
A shudder rolled through the strongest living human on the continent, crown to boots.
"That woman is supposed to be your success story?!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1804 Horrifying Reality
paragraphs: "A peerless existence, isn't she?"
He'd sent Rosie after them, of course, and received detailed reports for the entire trip. But that information... The king did not receive it.
"That is not the word I..." Alexios gave up halfway through the sentence. He wasn't one to badmouth other men's wives.
But he did not take another step backward.
Because the math had changed, and Alexios Valorian had never once refused to run new numbers just because he hated them.

Dying on schedule meant leaving Felicity to a guardian who called 'that' parenting. It meant leaving his life's work, the political plays, the succession, all of it half-built in hands he could no longer correct.
Set against all of that stood one disgusting, scheming, pearl-colored insult in a primordial's hand.
It was the best option among the terrible ones. That, too, was math.
Alexios straightened his spine, crossed the ground he had spent the last minute surrendering, and held his open hand out to Quinlan. "I'll take it."
Quinlan, beaming like a fiend, placed the pill in the royal palm with full ceremony.
Alexios looked at it. Then he fixed Quinlan with a long, flat, wry stare and let it say everything his dignity wouldn't.
He raised the pill to his mouth.
"By the way," Quinlan said conversationally, "it has a name. [Blessed Seed]."
The pearl stopped a finger's width from the king's lips.
"...What."
"Mm. It's made from my bodily fluids. My primordial essence."
The cellar went very, very quiet. Somewhere behind the casks, thaw-water ticked on and on against the stone.
Alexios's arm lowered with geological slowness. He looked at the pill, then at Quinlan, then back at the pill, and the color quietly drained out of him.
"Essence," he said.
Quinlan spread his hands, warm with pride. "All my girls take it. Triple experience gain, stopped aging, and I also theorize it moisturizes their skin, though that might just be my bias."
The king's mind worked through that. Then it arrived somewhere far worse, and his head snapped up in naked horror.
"Felicity."
"Hey." Quinlan looked genuinely offended. "I'm not a freak. Of course not. She's a child."
"Not a freak?" Alexios repeated tonelessly. "You were feeding it to me."
"You're a dying old fucker. Completely different situation."
Alexios's hands turned into trembling fists, only a moment from getting into the brawl of his life.
"So?" Quinlan gestured at the pearl sitting in the royal palm, supremely unbothered. "What will it be?"
"..." Alexios stared at the pill. His breath left him slowly. Then a thought crossed his face, and he turned, very slowly, toward the cask in the corner. Toward Iris.
Both of her middle fingers were up before his head finished the turn.
She said nothing. The fingers stayed up for the entire time it took him to look away.
Alexios, wisely, filed the entire subject under matters no king should investigate, and turned back to the pill.
The war that followed played out in the open on his face.
Swallowing the villain's... he refused to finish the thought, even privately. It was beyond disgusting.
It was, without competition, the most degrading proposition ever placed before the Vravenian crown, and that was saying everything considering who his vassals were.
And on the other side of the scale sat everything else.

Staying alive. Watching Felicity grow into whoever she was becoming instead of guessing at it. Seeing the warrant through with his own eyes, the rot dug out of his kingdom root by root, instead of bequeathing the shovel to children who had never held one.
Then, without permission, a third thing arrived.
His heart rate picked up.
A single hard beat out of rhythm, then another, and the feeling it dragged in behind it took him a moment to even recognize, it had been away so long.
Adventure.
The barrier coming down. The maps ending, and then the maps being wrong, and then no maps at all.
Whatever waited beyond Iskaris that no living soul had seen.
And his own status screen, that fossil, that tombstone, the level that had sat frozen at its cap for centuries... it would move again. It would climb.
His breath went deeper. His shoulders came back and down, and the grey, beaten stillness that had sat on him since the soul realm peeled away layer by layer.

The change was stark enough that Iris's boot stopped swinging mid-arc. The King of Vraven looked younger than he had a minute ago, and younger again by the time the breath finished, life pouring back into his tired eyes from somewhere that had been sealed far longer than this cellar.

He had never been a frail old man, but there was a world of difference between a strong man enduring his last season and one with somewhere to be. The room watched him cross from one to the other in the span of three heartbeats.
Alexios closed his fist around the pearl, looked up at Quinlan with his decision made, and opened his mouth.

A thread of wind slipped between his fingers and stole the pill clean out of them, and by the time the king's eyes finished widening, it had already sailed across the cellar into Quinlan's waiting palm.
The demonic air was gone. All of it, at once, swept out of the cellar between one heartbeat and the next, and what remained was just Quinlan, standing there with the pearl in his open hand.
"No," he said.
Alexios blinked at him. "...No?"
"I have too much respect for you to make you take this." The pill vanished back into his pocket ring.
Across the cellar, iron creaked.
Iris's fist had closed around her chain without consulting her, and inside her skull the tirade was already at full sprint.
Respect. RESPECT?!

He'd branded her skin with his demon tattoo. He'd wired his voice directly into her head through enslaving her. And if she had ever reached for that pill, he would have watched her swallow it with the biggest, happiest grin of his miserable eternal life, and not one syllable about respect would have survived the moment.
'I'm not angry. Why the fuck would I be angry?' Iris informed herself. Then her eyes narrowed. 'I want to beat the ever living shit out of him.'
The chain settled against the cask. She aimed her glare at the sealed pillar to demonstrate how little she cared, and the pillar wisely kept its silence.
"...Then what," Alexios asked at last, with tremendous care, "was all of that?" His gesture took in the length of the cellar, the whole hunt, every step of the retreat and the advance and the horror.

"A test to see if you were as much of a badass as I thought," Quinlan said, then grinned. "You are. Any man who'd rather die and leave behind his family than swallow his pride deserves nothing from me."
The king closed his eyes and pressed two fingers against the bridge of his nose. "I have an overwhelming urge to strangle you."
"It's okay, you'll get over it," Quinlan waved off the only man he could ever call his friend in this life. "Felicity having a dad instead of a grave to cry over depends on it."
Then the teasing left Quinlan's voice between one sentence and the next.
"Let me try something else before you swallow my cum pill."

Alexios closed his fist around the pearl, looked up at Quinlan with his decision made, and opened his mouth.

A thread of wind slipped between his fingers and stole the pill clean out of them, and by the time the king's eyes finished widening, it had already sailed across the cellar into Quinlan's waiting palm.
The demonic air was gone.
All of it, at once, swept out of the cellar between one heartbeat and the next, and what remained was just Quinlan, standing there with the pearl in his open hand.
"No," he said.
Alexios blinked at him.
"I have too much respect for you to make you take this." The pill vanished back into his pocket ring.
Across the cellar, iron creaked.
Iris's fist had closed around her chain without consulting her, and inside her skull the tirade was already at full sprint.
Respect.
RESPECT?!
He'd branded her skin with his demon tattoo.
He'd wired his voice directly into her head through enslaving her.

And if she had ever reached for that pill, he would have watched her swallow it with the biggest, happiest grin of his miserable eternal life, and not one syllable about respect would have survived the moment.
'I'm not angry.
Why the fuck would I be angry?' Iris informed herself.
Then her eyes narrowed. 'I want to beat the ever living shit out of him.'
The chain settled against the cask.
She aimed her glare at the sealed pillar to demonstrate how little she cared, and the pillar wisely kept its silence.
"...Then what," Alexios asked at last, with tremendous care, "was all of that?" His gesture took in the length of the cellar, the whole hunt, every step of the retreat and the advance and the horror.
"A test to see if you were as much of a badass as I thought," Quinlan said, then grinned.
"You are.
Any man who'd rather die and leave behind his family than swallow his pride deserves nothing from me."
The king closed his eyes and pressed two fingers against the bridge of his nose.
"I have an overwhelming urge to strangle you."
"It's okay, you'll get over it," Quinlan waved off the only man he could ever call his friend in this life.
"Felicity having a dad instead of a grave to cry over depends on it."
Then the teasing left Quinlan's voice between one sentence and the next.
"Let me try something else before you swallow my cum pill."

chapters.title: Chapter 1805 Dropping In
paragraphs: Alexios stood in the thawing basement, watching the primordial who had just confiscated his own miracle pill, and waited for the words 'let me try something else' to grow an explanation.
They didn't.
"Try what?" the king demanded. "Try what, exactly?"
"Why don't you trust me for once, old friend?"
Alexios couldn't help but blink. Did this creature truly utter those words just now?

Whatever he was about to say, Quinlan was no longer listening. His gaze had already gone somewhere past the mansion, past the night itself, and a faint crimson sheen rolled across his eyes while he hummed to himself.
Through [Overlord's Eyes], a cozy little scene arrived from far away: a warm common room, a teacup in a familiar, delicate hand, and two women laughing at whatever story his alchemist was telling.
"Perfect. They're still at it."
Quinlan flicked two fingers, and a [Warp Gate] unfolded.
"Iris. Would you accompany me for a short trip? Been a while since we spent time together."
"...I'm guarding the corpse." Iris grunted, arms crossed.
Quinlan tilted his head toward the gate. "Come. You'll enjoy this."
"I won't."
"Please?"
"..." She shoved off the pillar, muttering something about clingy bastards and their field trips.
The gate soon swallowed them all.
The common room of the inn was down to its last lamp and its best company. Aurora had both hands in the air, sculpting the climax of some story, and Lucille was laughing into her knuckles beside her.
A young woman with brown hair nursed a lukewarm teacup, pretending, poorly, not to smile.
Behind the counter, a broad man with a tired, honest face dried the day's last mugs while a round-cheeked woman stacked them beside him.
The air behind the two laughing women warped.

Neither the Essenceweaver nor the Bloodmonger sensed a thing. One heartbeat the space at their backs held nothing but lamplight, and the next it held a primordial, and two arms landed on two shoulders at once.
"Evening, ladies."
Aurora's yelp nearly took her out of her chair. Lucille's came out as half a shriek and half his name, and then both women were on their feet and rounding on him.
"Quin! You sneak~!" Lucille giggled.
"Why did you not give us a heads up...? Use your abilities..." Aurora huffed.

Whatever else they had for him died in transit. He gathered them in by the waist, one to each arm, pulled them flush against him, and kissed Lucille first, long enough that her fists gave up on his chest, then Aurora, long enough that she forgot she'd been mid-lecture.
When he finally let them breathe, neither made any move to leave his arms, and Aurora's glare had all the fury of a lit candle.
"Baby, you never visit, and now, tonight, of all the..." Lucille accused, glowing.
"Got some business with Aurora," Quinlan smirked.
"Oh, so it was all just a coincidence again..." It was the caramel-haired beauty's turn to pout with deadly efficiency.
The rest of the common room, meanwhile, was losing its mind.
A mug hit the floorboards.
Cela had backed into the shelves with both hands pressed over her mouth, working her way up to a proper scream that never arrived, because her eyes finished before her lungs could start.
She knew that face. Half the continent knew it, but she had seen it with her own two eyes, once, a lifetime and one relocation ago.
Robert made no sound at all.
The innkeeper stood exactly where recognition had found him, white as morning bread, towel dangling forgotten from one hand. The wolf was back, and this time it hadn't even used the door.

"Breathe, Cela," Mavena was already up and moving, planting herself in front of the round-cheeked woman and catching both her hands. "It's fine. That's..." A pause worth a whole biography. "...He's not an enemy."
"I know who he is," Cela whispered, without blinking once.

Behind them, the warped air delivered its afterthoughts: a black-haired swordswoman who stepped out with her arms already crossed, and an old soldier in a travel hood who emerged with all the dignity a man can salvage while climbing out of a hole in the world into a village taproom.
Cela made a very small sound and sat down on a crate, just as Quinlan loosened his hold on his two women, and his attention traveled to the counter.
"Robert." His voice was warm. "It's been a long time. How have you been?"
Then his eyes traveled to the woman he didn't know by sight, and grinned. "I see fortune hasn't been terrible to you..."
For a long moment the innkeeper didn't answer, because somewhere in his head a vow was dying.
He'd sworn it to himself in a shabby lounge what felt like a lifetime ago but was less than a year ago: whatever woman fate granted him next would never, ever stand in the same room as this man.
He'd built the vow a new town, a new inn, a new life. And the man had stepped out of the air itself, ten feet from her, without using a door for the vow to guard.

Robert set down the towel, came around the counter on legs that had opinions about it, and placed himself between the primordial and his wife's crate. Terrified, bloodless, and standing there anyway, he surrendered to etiquette.
"...Cela. My wife." A pause, then, through gravel: "Cela, this is..."
"Lord Quinlan," she breathed.
Robert's introduction died in his mouth.

His wife had come off her crate, smoothing her apron with both hands, cheeks glowing, and the words left her in one unstoppable ribbon. "I was there. At the Square, at the old stronghold, the day you took it from the Wraithclaws. My boy was on my shoulders, he saw you walking on the sky before I did, I didn't believe him until I looked up myself, and you had the... the head, on your saber, and..."
She caught herself mid-babble, curtsied to the lord, wobbled, and finished faintly: "I'm grateful for everything."
The taproom took a respectful moment to honor that sentence.

"Ah, the Wraithclaws. That brings back memories..." Quinlan inclined his head to Cela with perfect courtesy, as though she had delivered a proper court address. "Best audience a conqueror ever could ask for. I hope you'll find the life you hoped for in Miri Town."
Cela's smile turned brilliant. "I have. Life... it's never been better, my lord."

Beside her, Robert produced a sound that wanted very badly to be a growl and arrived as something closer to a hiccup. Of all the women in all the towns on the continent, he had married the one who told the story of the Square speech at every third dinner.
Then, mid-glow, reality caught up with her.

Cela's eyes traveled back up to the lord, and widened. Then they traveled to the woman tucked under his arm, the overly pretty, sweet-smiling visitor who had sat in this taproom a hundred evenings with tea and gossip and pastry crumbs, and they widened a great deal further.
"W-w-w-wait." Her finger rose, trembling, and aimed past Quinlan. "Who... who are you?"
Lucille's smile turned apologetic. She stayed exactly where she was, on the arm of the most dangerous being alive, and gave a tiny, guilty shrug.
"Lucille," she said gently. "It was always Lucille. Quinlan Elysiar's lover."
Cela sat back down on her crate without checking whether it was still there.
Mavena's mother. The quiet beauty from 'somewhere far, a wanderer' who complimented the stew and helped fold napkins when the evenings ran long. She had folded NAPKINS.
Cela never pried, despite some things not adding up. But...
Her head turned, very slowly, toward her husband. Robert studied the ceiling.
The alias had been Lucille's idea from the very first visit.

If Miri Town ever learned that its innkeeper's family stood one old marriage away from the Primordial Villain, the mundane life Robert and Mavena wanted would be over by sunrise: the inn a pilgrimage site, Mavena a celebrity, every regular replaced by gawkers.

So the Bloodmonger came as nobody, in a plain dress and a plainer name, and let her family stay ordinary. It was also why, tonight, Quinlan had stepped out of thin air inside the inn rather than let a single soul watch him walk its streets to their door.
Cela's gaze dragged, with visible dread, to the platinum-haired guest. "...You?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1806 Finally Meeting Again
paragraphs: "Aurora. His other lover." A beat, and a playful glance slid toward Quinlan. "Well. One of many."
"Many," Cela repeated faintly.
"You should have seen us at the Square, you know~" Aurora went on, warming to the subject with scientific enjoyment.
"Yeah, yeah!" Lucille giggled, eyes shining.
"Huh?" Cela gasped.
Aurora had a sly smirk as she explained, "We walked in right behind him. Ten masks, perfectly synchronized. We were very proud of that walk."
Cela's eyes went wide like saucers, searching the most vivid memory of her life and finding, at its very edges, a smear of masked figures she had never once looked at directly.
The procession had held eleven people, and her memory had kept exactly one.
"I... may have been looking elsewhere," she admitted to her apron.
Lucille and Aurora traded a look of deep, sisterly understanding. "We understand," they said in unison.
Robert, meanwhile, was busy sizing up Quinlan with immense worry evident on his face, still standing between the villain and his wife.
"Don't worry, my friend." Quinlan showed him an open palm. "My hands are already full."
Lucille, on his arm, beamed up at him in a way that made the statement a criminal understatement.
Quinlan crossed to the counter and offered Robert his hand. "You look good, Robert. This new life seems to suit you."

Robert stared at the offered hand like a summons from the tax office. Then he took it, and shook it, firm and brief, one honest grip between the man who had lost Lucille and the monster who had taken her, and if his knuckles were white through the whole exchange, nobody present was rude enough to mention it.

By the wall, Alexios Valorian stood watching with interest as the anomaly he kept hunting all across the continent was currently shaking hands with an innkeeper. One more page of tonight's running ledger quietly rewrote itself.
"Mavena."
Quinlan turned last to the young woman still standing guard over Cela's crate, and the room's temperature changed in a way that had nothing to do with frost.

Up close, the brown hair had her mother's caramel in it, and the green in her eyes was hers outright, but the look in them belonged to nobody but her. A knot sat on her face: wariness wound around anger wound around a hurt that had been waiting months for somewhere to go.

The man she remembered had been huge and frightening and human. He had filled the doorway of their shabby inn in Braedon, back when she was young enough to listen at doors and cry at what she heard. This one felt as if he filled the doorway of the world.

Stories had reached Miri Town the way they reached everywhere, each one taller than the last, kingdoms and monsters and armies of the dead, and every story wore the face that was currently smiling at her like a favorite uncle. The Primordial Villain, her mother's man, the man who had walked into her family and taken half of it away.
"You've grown into a wonderful young woman," he said.
"That happens, I guess..." Her voice came out steadier than she'd feared and sharper than she'd planned. "It's been some time."
"It has. I owed you a visit a lot sooner. I'm sorry I took so long," Quinlan bowed his head, looking truly apologetic about his lack of visits.
"..." Mavena kept eyeing him, tense. Then finally she exhaled. "Why are you apologizing? You're not my dad. I liked how you never visited. Why do it now?"

"Ouch. You definitely inherited your mother's bite," Quinlan chuckled while Lucille pinched his skin. He then pulled out the chair across from Mavena's, uninvited, and sat. "So. How's Miri Town treating you?"
Mavena returned to her seat slowly, because she was a grown adult who would not throw a hissy fit.

"Fine. Good." She turned the teacup once on its saucer. "The inn does twice what the old one did, especially now that you've allowed some people from New Whisperfield to visit. The roads are safe. Everyone's fed." She hated how much it sounded like praise. "Your governor... she's very effective."
"She's a treasure, isn't she."
"Mm."
"Friends?"
"Some."
"A boyfriend?"
The teacup clicked against the saucer.
"That's none of your business."

"Ooh, there is one?" Lucille had drifted in behind Quinlan's shoulder, hands clasped, glowing like a lantern. "Sweetheart, you never said! Who? Is it the fletcher's boy? Tell me it's not the fletcher's boy."
"Mother."
"Because you can do so much better than..."
"Mother...!!! Not in front of this scumb- your boyfriend, husband, or whatever."
Quinlan laughed, low and genuinely delighted. He reached across the table and ruffled Mavena's hair before she could duck, one big warm hand mussing it as if she were still six years old.

"I'm not twelve!" She batted it off and dragged her hair back into order, face burning. The hand had been warm, easy, utterly unafraid of her anger. Some traitorous corner of her had catalogued it as kind. That was the worst part.

She looked at her mother instead, looking for the ally that word was supposed to summon, and found Lucille draped against the monster's back, chin resting on his shoulder, wearing a smile that belonged on a girl half her age.

Her mother. The quiet woman who had folded linens and stirred stew and gone grey around the edges in a shabby Braedon taproom for Mavena's entire childhood, boring the way bread is boring, safe the way bread is safe. Hanging off the arm of the most dangerous thing on two legs and giggling.

Mavena's knot pulled tighter, and she was still deciding whether it was fury or grief or seasickness when Quinlan's head tilted a fraction, the way a hound's does at a sound the room hasn't heard yet.
His grin arrived before his explanation, which was to say, no explanation arrived at all.
"Everyone. Let's hide." He rose, soundless for a man his size, eyes bright with holiday.
"What?" said four people at once.

"Footsteps are approaching." He was already herding, one arm scooping Iris out of the chair she'd just sat down in, earning himself some almighty frowns, the other waving the king of Vraven toward the kitchen doorway like a stagehand clearing a set. Aurora giggled and followed after, while Cela and Robert hid behind the counter.
The room emptied of its monsters in four seconds flat, and mother and daughter were left blinking at each other across the table.
Then the door banged open without a knock.

The young man who filled it was built like a hay wagon and confident the way only eight beers can make a man. His shirt was good quality and worn open one button too far, and his eyes found Mavena with smug delight, as if his trap had already sprung.

"Knew the light'd be on." He let the door swing shut behind him and came on in, uninvited, past the sign that said closed. "Saw your da head up hours ago. Come on, Mavena. One drink. You keep saying no and I keep not believing you, so one of us has to be wrong, eh?"
"Get out, Tobin." Mavena didn't stand. "We're closed, you're drunk, and I've said no eleven times. The number doesn't reset at midnight."

"Aw, don't be like that." He reached the table. His hand dropped onto her shoulder, big and warm and entitled, and squeezed. "You're the prettiest thing in this town and you know it. Girl like you, it's time..."
He noticed Lucille.

The change in him was instant and gross. He straightened, chest out, grin widening to include the second woman at the table, the slim caramel-haired beauty with the teacup, and his eyes did a slow, frank tour of her that would have earned him an instant death sentence if Quinlan wasn't in a good mood.

"Well now." He looked between them, delighted with his own luck. "Who's your friend? You've been holding out on me." A wet chuckle. "You know what, forget the drink. I'm a generous man. I'll take you both dancing, how's that? Plenty of me to go around."
"That," Mavena said, flat and resigned, already watching the cart roll toward the cliff, "is my... friend."
Tobin barked a laugh. "Your friend. Right. And I'm the Primordial Villain." He gave Lucille a wink. "Sister, maybe. What's your name, gorgeous?"

Not in front of this scumb- your boyfriend, husband, or whatever."
Quinlan laughed, low and genuinely delighted.
He reached across the table and ruffled Mavena's hair before she could duck, one big warm hand mussing it as if she were still six years old.
"I'm not twelve!" She batted it off and dragged her hair back into order, face burning.
The hand had been warm, easy, utterly unafraid of her anger.
Some traitorous corner of her had catalogued it as kind.
That was the worst part.

She looked at her mother instead, looking for the ally that word was supposed to summon, and found Lucille draped against the monster's back, chin resting on his shoulder, wearing a smile that belonged on a girl half her age.
Her mother.

The quiet woman who had folded linens and stirred stew and gone grey around the edges in a shabby Braedon taproom for Mavena's entire childhood, boring the way bread is boring, safe the way bread is safe.
Hanging off the arm of the most dangerous thing on two legs and giggling.

Mavena's knot pulled tighter, and she was still deciding whether it was fury or grief or seasickness when Quinlan's head tilted a fraction, the way a hound's does at a sound the room hasn't heard yet.
His grin arrived before his explanation, which was to say, no explanation arrived at all.
"Everyone.
Let's hide." He rose, soundless for a man his size, eyes bright with holiday.
"What?" said four people at once.

"Footsteps are approaching." He was already herding, one arm scooping Iris out of the chair she'd just sat down in, earning himself some almighty frowns, the other waving the king of Vraven toward the kitchen doorway like a stagehand clearing a set.
Aurora giggled and followed after, while Cela and Robert hid behind the counter.
The room emptied of its monsters in four seconds flat, and mother and daughter were left blinking at each other across the table.
Then the door banged open without a knock.
The young man who filled it was built like a hay wagon and confident the way only eight beers can make a man.
His shirt was good quality and worn open one button too far, and his eyes found Mavena with smug delight, as if his trap had already sprung.
"Knew the light'd be on." He let the door swing shut behind him and came on in, uninvited, past the sign that said closed.
"Saw your da head up hours ago.
Come on, Mavena.
One drink.
You keep saying no and I keep not believing you, so one of us has to be wrong, eh?"
"Get out, Tobin." Mavena didn't stand.
"We're closed, you're drunk, and I've said no eleven times.
The number doesn't reset at midnight."
"Aw, don't be like that." He reached the table.
His hand dropped onto her shoulder, big and warm and entitled, and squeezed.
"You're the prettiest thing in this town and you know it.
Girl like you, it's time..."
He noticed Lucille.
The change in him was instant and gross.

He straightened, chest out, grin widening to include the second woman at the table, the slim caramel-haired beauty with the teacup, and his eyes did a slow, frank tour of her that would have earned him an instant death sentence if Quinlan wasn't in a good mood.
"Well now." He looked between them, delighted with his own luck.
"Who's your friend?
You've been holding out on me." A wet chuckle.
"You know what, forget the drink.
I'm a generous man.
I'll take you both dancing, how's that?
Plenty of me to go around."
"That," Mavena said, flat and resigned, already watching the cart roll toward the cliff, "is my... friend."
Tobin barked a laugh.
"Your friend.
Right.
And I'm the Primordial Villain." He gave Lucille a wink.
"Sister, maybe.
What's your name, gorgeous?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1807 Menace
paragraphs: Tobin barked a laugh. "Your friend. Right. And I'm the Primordial Villain." He gave Lucille a wink. "Sister, maybe. What's your name, gorgeous?"
Lucille set her teacup down on its saucer without a sound.
"I'd suggest you remove your hand from her," she said pleasantly.
"Or what?" And to the great misfortune of everyone who shared his blood, Tobin's hand stayed exactly where it was, and his grin came back around to Mavena. "She always this..."
Lucille moved.
Mavena would spend a long time afterwards trying to reconstruct the order of it.

Her mother's hand closed over the wrist on her shoulder. Then the wrist was no longer on her shoulder, and Tobin was bent over the table, cheek pressed to the wood, arm folded up behind his back at an angle arms were not issued with. None of it had made any noise except the soft clink of the sugar bowl.
"GH... AGH! LET, agh, LET GO..."
"Shhh. You'll wake the street." Lucille wasn't holding him down so much as resting her hand on the arrangement, the way you'd keep a page from turning in a breeze.
Her voice stayed exactly where it had been all evening, warm and light and maternal. "A woman tells you no eleven times and you barge into her home nonetheless... Isn't that a terrible crime?"
"I didn't, AH, I didn't know, I swear I didn't know..."
"Know what? That forcing yourself upon others is bad?" A gentle tut.
Then the weight on his arm was gone. Tobin ran. Or tried to.
He made it two whole steps, long enough to taste escape, before a hand closed around the back of his collar and the whole slab of him stopped mid-stride, boots still walking the air.
Lucille turned him around, gently, almost politely, so he could see it coming.

Her fist crossed the distance with a sound like a barrel lid slamming, wet at the center where his nose gave up its original shape, and Tobin left her grip sideways, took a table's corner on the way down, and spread himself over the floorboards. A tooth skittered away under a chair and came to rest against the wall, where it stayed.
He was asleep before the blood reached his lip.
Lucille looked down at him and shook the impact off her knuckles once, and when she spoke, the warmth was gone from her voice.

"Instead of doing what I truly want, I'll hand you to Jasmine's people. They'll decide your punishment." She straightened her sleeve. "But you'll never get to even think about hurting my Mavena again."
Silence owned the taproom.
Behind the counter, Robert rose into view by degrees, hands braced on the wood as though the floor had tilted, and Mavena hadn't moved at all.
They had both known, in the abstract way you know the ocean is deep, that Lucille carried a class and stats now, that she fought monsters at the villain's side.

But the slim wrists with flour under their nails had kneaded dough, hung laundry, shooed cats off the pantry shelf, and they had just caught, folded, and switched off a man twice her weight without her breath changing. There was nowhere in either of their heads to put it.
"...Goddess above," Cela whispered beside him.

The kitchen door chose that moment to fail entirely as a sound barrier. From behind it came a deep chuckle, followed by a thud that might have been a king's forehead meeting a shelf in the dark, followed by Iris's agitated voice hissing at Quinlan to put her down.
Mavena noticed none of them.
"Mom." Her voice came out small, and it hadn't been small in years. "Since when can you DO that?"
And Lucille did the thing she had done on every visit.

Mavena watched it happen without knowing what she was watching: her mother's shoulders rounding by a degree, her hands finding her apron even though she wasn't wearing one, her whole self folding down into something smaller and softer and easier to sit across a teacup from.
The humble mother, reassembled between one breath and the next.
"Oh, that was nothing, sweetheart," Lucille said, light as flour.
"Don't do that."
Quinlan's voice arrived from the kitchen doorway, with weight instead of volume, and every head in the room turned. The amusement was gone from his face, replaced by a fondness that had iron in it.
"You're an almighty warrior who happens to be a loving, caring mother. Why must you hide a side of yourself?"
"Quin..." Lucille spoke with immense worry and anxiety in her tone. <Can't you see? They're afraid of me now... That's why I never showed off before...>
<They're afraid because they don't understand. You never allowed them to.>
<You can't say that for sure!> Lucille protested.
<That's true,> Quinlan relented. <She's your daughter. I won't say more. Sorry for butting in.>
The Bloodmonger bit her lip. <No, that's not what I meant... Quin...>
Before she could say more, Mavena was out of her chair and in front of Quinlan, and the knot that had been pulling tighter all evening had slipped loose without her permission.
"Can you tell me more about my mother?! I want to hear... From your point of view, not hers. She keeps downplaying everything..." She sent her mother a strongly disapproving look. "So annoying!"
Quinlan observed Mavena for a moment, then turned toward his lover, waiting.
"..." Lucille's fists clenched white at her sides.
"No, I'm sorry. I can't." Quinlan shook his head at Mavena, gentle about it. "Those stories belong to your mother. If she wants them to stay buried, then buried they-"
"O-okay. Okay!"
The words burst out of Lucille before he could finish.
For months she had folded the warrior away with the linens, dreading the day her daughter would see the monster before the mother.
And now that the day had come, her daughter was leaning over the table and asking for more of her, asking for the exact half she'd spent every visit hiding.
Her fists loosened, finger by finger. The hope that crept onto her face was so raw it hurt to look at.
"Quin, please... Tell my daughter whatever you think is best."
"Alright," he nodded, smiling, and took Lucille's hand in his and squeezed.
Then, he faced Mavena.
"Your mother," he said, "is one of the most badass existences to have ever graced this world. What you saw tonight was her being polite."
"But..." His grin spread, proud and vicious. "I'm afraid mere words will never do her justice."
He raised his free hand, palm up.

Water rose out of the air above it, spinning itself into a figure no taller than a wine bottle: a slim woman in translucent detail, long hair, a large axe in one small liquid fist. The figure rolled its shoulders exactly the way Lucille rolled hers.
"Your mother struggled a lot to acclimate to combat, mostly because of her class's quirks. For months, she kept our healer busier than the rest of us combined."
"..." Lucille's cheeks went pink at that, memories resurfacing of how many times Sera told her off for being a reckless battle maniac.
"But little by little, she transformed herself. And now..." Quinlan continued, "She's menace itself."
Threads of magma lit around the water figure, hissing.
Mavena completely forgot she was supposed to be angry.
She was leaning in before she knew she'd moved, elbows on the table, chin dropping into her hands, and her eyes caught the magma light and kept it.
Wide, bright, mesmerized, the eyes of the little girl who used to beg for one more story before bed, aimed at the tiny, fearless figure standing calm in the middle of the fire.
Her mother.
That was her mother.

chapters.title: Chapter 1808 The Lorien Apothecary
paragraphs: Her mother.
That was her mother.
The threads of magma found Lucille's axe, winding up the haft and sinking into the blade until the whole edge burned molten orange, and the glow of it reached every face in the common room.
Then the rest of the water rose.

It came up in columns around the figure and built as it climbed: a troll five times her height with fists like boulders, a second one at its shoulder, a serpent thick as a barrel coiling around the whole arrangement, horned brutes filling the gaps, until a full warband of liquid monsters stood in silent ranks around one small woman.

"Quin!!" Lucille's voice came out smaller than it had been all evening, an adorable little squeal, her fingers finding his sleeve. "This is too much... An entire warband of monsters against just me? It looks like bragging..."
"No." Aurora propped her chin on her laced fingers, amber eyes gleaming. "It's perfect."

The first troll's club came down, and the little Lucille walked into the swing rather than away from it. The blazing axe rose to meet the club, went through it, through the arm behind it, through the shoulder behind that, and half the troll burst into steam that made Cela yelp.

She never stopped walking. The serpent struck at her back, and she split it along its whole length without turning. A horned pair rushed her from both sides and died on a single looping figure-eight of molten light. Every stroke rolled into the next, seamless, unhurried, and wherever that edge traveled, water became fog.

Mavena had abandoned her teacup somewhere around the first troll. She was leaning halfway across the table with her lips parted and magma light swimming in her eyes, and every bit of carefully maintained wariness had burned off her face along with the steam.
Her mother was amazing. The thought arrived uninvited, and she let it stay, because the little warrior on the villain's palm made looking away impossible.

"Most fighters, even those with higher levels and centuries more training, would take a group like this apart with careful strategy," Quinlan narrated. "But your mother walks straight through the middle. And the whole time..."
The tiny figure stood tall, axe raised, surrounded by dissolving enemies.
"...she smiles. Isn't your mother far too beautiful?"
"Q-Quinlan Elysiar!!!" Lucille's mortified squeak came, far too embarrassed.
"She is..." Mavena whispered under her breath.
"!!" Lucille's cheeks turned tomato red.

The last troll collapsed into spray around her final swing. The little figure straightened amid the ruin, then snapped her axe out to one side in a single flat swish, and the water clinging to the blade left it in one clean fan of droplets, the way blood leaves steel.
On his palm she stood alone in the thinning fog, small and bright under the inn's lamps, chest heaving, and the glow of her axe dimmed and cooled before she came apart into mist, and was gone.
Nobody in the common room made a sound.
"Mom."
Lucille turned. Mavena had lowered the hand from her mouth.
"Will you show me? Sometime." She swallowed. "The real thing. Not... " she gestured at Quinlan's empty palm, "...the puppet show."

Lucille froze. The half of herself she had hidden away for so long, so sure her daughter would flinch from it, and Mavena was reaching for it with both hands. The dread went out of her like a held breath, and her whole face lit with something too large to hold still.
"Any time you want..."
Robert, at the counter, elected to begin drying the same mug again.
Cela had both hands pressed over her heart.
Aurora, eyes soft, turned to Quinlan. "So there's something for me to do?"
"Right," he nodded. "Time for business."
Quinlan rested a hand on Lucille's head. "Aurora and I have somewhere to be. Why don't you bond with your daughter without hiding yourself?" Lucille barely heard him, her eyes still on Mavena.
But she replied nonetheless, whispering, "O-okay... Love you so much..."
"Love you too. Now then, my beloved alchemist." He flicked his fingers and the [Warp Gate] appeared.
"It's time to cook."

The [Warp Gate] opened onto an empty, sleeping street, directly in front of the Lorien apothecary: a tall, narrow building with a freshly painted sign and light burning stubbornly in the back workroom, exactly as Aurora had predicted.
"Cauldron hours," she confirmed fondly, and knocked on the recently built home's entrance.
Naomi, Aurora's mom, proposed that they relocate here from Quinlan's home, saying Miri Town needed proper alchemists.
But everyone understood that she mostly desired to give her daughter proper space to build her own life without her parents always being just around the corner.
The door opened on Gideon Lorien, monocle already in place at midnight, sleeves rolled for work. He found Aurora in the lamplight and blinked.
His brow furrowed with paternal bookkeeping. "Back already? You said you'd be helping Jasmine, then going to the inn with Lucille. Did the schedule..."

The darkness behind her chose that moment to resolve into people: the Primordial Villain, a hooded old soldier built like a fortress, and a black-haired swordswoman radiating the desire to be elsewhere.
"We need your help, Dad." Aurora was grinning the way she usually did over unstable compounds. "Tonight. Will you and Mom be my assistants?"
For a moment, Gideon's monocle was in genuine danger. "Assistants? To you?" He looked her up and down as though checking her for fever. "Young lady, you are far too green-"
"Stop barring the entry, Gideon." Naomi Lorien appeared behind her husband, took him by the elbow, and relocated him from the doorway.
Her eyes went straight to Quinlan, and her smile arrived whole. "Quinlan. Thank you for always taking such good care of our daughter."
"No thanks needed." Quinlan's answer came without a beat of hesitation. "It's my honor to protect the girl I love."

Gideon, still mid-outrage, nodded along to that as though it were the single uncontested fact of the evening. Naomi positively beamed. And Aurora, who handled explosive reagents without flinching, went quietly pink between her parents.
"Quin... Not in front of my parents..." she mumbled.
Naomi chuckled for a long moment, then her gaze traveled past Aurora and brightened all over again. "Iris! What a pleasant surprise. Where did you leave your friend?"
"..." Iris raised an eyebrow. "Friend?"
"Ayame, that gorgeous samurai friend of yours." Naomi said it as though it explained everything. "Whenever I see you two together, I get to imagine what having two daughters would've been like."
"???" Iris was struck right in the soul with existential damage.
Naomi turned a long, scrutinizing look on her husband. "We messed up, Gideon."
"The shop would not have survived two," he answered with conviction.
"Hey!" Aurora stomped.

Meanwhile, Iris's mouth opened. Nothing came out. Her, and that slit-eyed cunt? Friends? The sentence tried to assemble itself several different ways behind her red eyes and failed every time, so she closed her mouth, turned on her heel, and started walking into the night.
"Where are you going?" Quinlan called after her.
"Far."
"Come on..."
"No."

While the bickering unspooled behind them, Naomi's attention settled on the last guest, the hooded soldier who had stood in perfect, disciplined silence through all of it. "And who might you be, mister?"
Alexios remained silent, hood and the night's dark covering his face.
"You know him, Mom..." Aurora whispered, already feeling conflicted and worried.
"Do I, now." Naomi mused and began sorting aloud. "You can't be Blackjack. You're far too composed. A soldier from the Vraven Kingdom? No... too much spine. Hmm..."
Beside her, Gideon had gone very still. He leaned in for a second, much longer look, and the name came out flat and certain.
"Alexios Valorian."

Naomi's smile closed like a shop shutter. The King of Vraven, on her doorstep. The same crown that had dragged the two of them from their homes in Braedon, branded them bandit financiers, and buried them in a cell so deep that their own daughter couldn't learn whether they were still breathing.
"...Why are you here?" The warmth was gone from her voice, all of it. "This land isn't part of your wretched nation."
Alexios held her stare in silence.
Technically it was, as Quinlan's cities were in the northern part of Greenvale. Close to Ravenshade and the other two nations, just deep in the forests, far enough from everything to not be found.

However, instead of arguing, he inclined his head to her and to Gideon both, unhurried and deep. "I apologize for bothering you this late at night." He turned back toward the dark. "Thank you for being kind to Felicity."
Alexios did not apologize for capturing them, for he felt fully justified in that. They committed a crime by hiring thugs to invade his outpost.
But that mattered little now.
"Mom." Aurora caught her mother's hand. "I know, and I'm sorry for bringing him here, but..."
"But?" Naomi's eyes were narrowed into slits.
"Tonight, in your workroom, we might make alchemical history. The kind that gets cited for centuries. And he's needed for it."
Naomi held her daughter's gaze a beat longer, then her shoulders dropped and she stepped out of the doorway.
"Inside, all of you, before the street wakes up."

The workroom smelled of a hundred herbs and one long argument with entropy. Copper stills lined one wall, cauldrons in three sizes sat over banked burners, and Naomi took up station at the center bench, tying her apron strings tight.
"Well then." Her eyes, keen and pleased despite everything, found Quinlan. "History, was it? Talk."
Quinlan stepped into the lamplight. "I need a brew that has never been brewed. The recipe doesn't exist, and it might not be possible at all. I just have a hunch."
