The dread went out of her like a held breath, and her whole face lit with something too large to hold still.
"Any time you want..."
Robert, at the counter, elected to begin drying the same mug again.
Cela had both hands pressed over her heart.
Aurora, eyes soft, turned to Quinlan.
"So there's something for me to do?"
"Right," he nodded.
"Time for business."
Quinlan rested a hand on Lucille's head.
"Aurora and I have somewhere to be.
Why don't you bond with your daughter without hiding yourself?" Lucille barely heard him, her eyes still on Mavena.
But she replied nonetheless, whispering, "O-okay...
Love you so much..."
"Love you too.
Now then, my beloved alchemist." He flicked his fingers and the [Warp Gate] appeared.
"It's time to cook."

The [Warp Gate] opened onto an empty, sleeping street, directly in front of the Lorien apothecary: a tall, narrow building with a freshly painted sign and light burning stubbornly in the back workroom, exactly as Aurora had predicted.
"Cauldron hours," she confirmed fondly, and knocked on the recently built home's entrance.
Naomi, Aurora's mom, proposed that they relocate here from Quinlan's home, saying Miri Town needed proper alchemists.
But everyone understood that she mostly desired to give her daughter proper space to build her own life without her parents always being just around the corner.
The door opened on Gideon Lorien, monocle already in place at midnight, sleeves rolled for work.
He found Aurora in the lamplight and blinked.
His brow furrowed with paternal bookkeeping.
"Back already?
You said you'd be helping Jasmine, then going to the inn with Lucille.
Did the schedule..."

The darkness behind her chose that moment to resolve into people: the Primordial Villain, a hooded old soldier built like a fortress, and a black-haired swordswoman radiating the desire to be elsewhere.
"We need your help, Dad." Aurora was grinning the way she usually did over unstable compounds.
"Tonight.
Will you and Mom be my assistants?"
For a moment, Gideon's monocle was in genuine danger.
"Assistants?
To you?" He looked her up and down as though checking her for fever.
"Young lady, you are far too green-"
"Stop barring the entry, Gideon." Naomi Lorien appeared behind her husband, took him by the elbow, and relocated him from the doorway.
Her eyes went straight to Quinlan, and her smile arrived whole.
"Quinlan.
Thank you for always taking such good care of our daughter."
"No thanks needed." Quinlan's answer came without a beat of hesitation.
"It's my honor to protect the girl I love."
Gideon, still mid-outrage, nodded along to that as though it were the single uncontested fact of the evening.
Naomi positively beamed.
And Aurora, who handled explosive reagents without flinching, went quietly pink between her parents.
"Quin...
Not in front of my parents..." she mumbled.
Naomi chuckled for a long moment, then her gaze traveled past Aurora and brightened all over again.
"Iris!
What a pleasant surprise.
Where did you leave your friend?"
"..." Iris raised an eyebrow.
"Friend?"
"Ayame, that gorgeous samurai friend of yours." Naomi said it as though it explained everything.
"Whenever I see you two together, I get to imagine what having two daughters would've been like."
"???" Iris was struck right in the soul with existential damage.
Naomi turned a long, scrutinizing look on her husband.
"We messed up, Gideon."
"The shop would not have survived two," he answered with conviction.
"Hey!" Aurora stomped.
Meanwhile, Iris's mouth opened.
Nothing came out.
Her, and that slit-eyed cunt?
Friends?
The sentence tried to assemble itself several different ways behind her red eyes and failed every time, so she closed her mouth, turned on her heel, and started walking into the night.
"Where are you going?" Quinlan called after her.
"Far."
"Come on..."
"No."
While the bickering unspooled behind them, Naomi's attention settled on the last guest, the hooded soldier who had stood in perfect, disciplined silence through all of it.
"And who might you be, mister?"
Alexios remained silent, hood and the night's dark covering his face.
"You know him, Mom..." Aurora whispered, already feeling conflicted and worried.
"Do I, now." Naomi mused and began sorting aloud.
"You can't be Blackjack.
You're far too composed.
A soldier from the Vraven Kingdom?
No... too much spine.
Hmm..."
Beside her, Gideon had gone very still.
He leaned in for a second, much longer look, and the name came out flat and certain.
"Alexios Valorian."
Naomi's smile closed like a shop shutter.
The King of Vraven, on her doorstep.

The same crown that had dragged the two of them from their homes in Braedon, branded them bandit financiers, and buried them in a cell so deep that their own daughter couldn't learn whether they were still breathing.
"...Why are you here?" The warmth was gone from her voice, all of it.
"This land isn't part of your wretched nation."
Alexios held her stare in silence.
Technically it was, as Quinlan's cities were in the northern part of Greenvale.
Close to Ravenshade and the other two nations, just deep in the forests, far enough from everything to not be found.
However, instead of arguing, he inclined his head to her and to Gideon both, unhurried and deep.
"I apologize for bothering you this late at night." He turned back toward the dark.
"Thank you for being kind to Felicity."
Alexios did not apologize for capturing them, for he felt fully justified in that.
They committed a crime by hiring thugs to invade his outpost.
But that mattered little now.
"Mom." Aurora caught her mother's hand.
"I know, and I'm sorry for bringing him here, but..."
"But?" Naomi's eyes were narrowed into slits.
"Tonight, in your workroom, we might make alchemical history.
The kind that gets cited for centuries.
And he's needed for it."
Naomi held her daughter's gaze a beat longer, then her shoulders dropped and she stepped out of the doorway.
"Inside, all of you, before the street wakes up."
The workroom smelled of a hundred herbs and one long argument with entropy.
Copper stills lined one wall, cauldrons in three sizes sat over banked burners, and Naomi took up station at the center bench, tying her apron strings tight.
"Well then." Her eyes, keen and pleased despite everything, found Quinlan.
"History, was it?
Talk."
Quinlan stepped into the lamplight.
"I need a brew that has never been brewed.
The recipe doesn't exist, and it might not be possible at all.
I just have a hunch."

chapters.title: Chapter 1809 Melting Iceberg
paragraphs: Quinlan stepped into the lamplight. "I need a brew that has never been brewed. The recipe doesn't exist, and it might not be possible at all. I just have a hunch."
"A hunch, you say," Gideon spoke up, adjusting his monocle. He was already as invested as can be.
"What's the base?" Naomi asked.
Quinlan raised his hand. Wind gathered at his fingertip, thinned to an edge no eye could follow, and opened a clean line across his own palm.
Blood welled up, catching the lamplight.

It was a shade of crimson that had no business in a living body, deep and dark, somehow heavier than the light falling on it. Every alchemical instinct in the room leaned toward it at once, the way compass needles lean north.
"My blood."
Nobody spoke. Somewhere on the bench, a burner hissed softly under a cauldron.
Gideon's voice had gone reverent and clipped at once. "A brew from primordial blood. Purpose?"
A pocket ring flashed, and between Quinlan's raised fingers, catching the lamplight, sat a single pearl-white pill.
"To replace this little thing."
Both parents' eyes lit up in the same instant. Gideon crossed half the workroom in three steps, monocle first. Naomi didn't move at all, but her eyes had gone bright enough to read by.
"[Blessed Seed Pill]," Gideon breathed. "Aurora's concentrate."
Naomi's stillness finally broke. "The unaging pill," she said, and reverence sat plain in it. "Aurora's masterwork."
"The very pill she has never once needed for herself, of course," Gideon added with scholarly precision, "given her standing access to the source material in its fresh, unrefined-"
"DAD!"
Aurora had achieved a shade of red no reagent on the shelves could reproduce.
"He means we're proud of you, sweetheart," Naomi translated.

Quinlan rolled the pearl once across his knuckles, then closed his fist, and it vanished back into the ring. "I need what it does, without the [Blessed Seed] being its ingredient, replaced by my blood. Or whatever else you theorize could make it work. All that matters is that it has to hold a dying man's age where it stands."
Behind the king's eyes, the whole night reassembled itself one door at a time.

The refusal of the pill. Try something else. The midnight gate, the zero answers, the town, the inn, the theater of it all, and at the end of the corridor, this: a workroom, three alchemists, and the man he spent months hunting opening his own veins to keep him alive.
"You..." the king said quietly. "Will you really go that far?"
"Felicity would be sad." Quinlan grinned.
"You don't want to watch your only friend die," Aurora corrected, smiling softly at her lover. "Why make such a weak excuse?"

"Nonsense, I care for Felicity's happiness." Quinlan denied instantly, prompting his platinum-haired lover to smile even brighter. "And he promised to help me conquer Iskaris and what's beyond. I'm protecting my investment."
"Mhm," Aurora nodded along. "Sure."
Naomi Lorien, however, entered professional mode while looking at the blood dripping from his hand. She asked the only question that mattered.
"How much can you give?"
"How much do you need?"
The answer took the three Loriens half a notebook, one shouted argument about reduction ratios, and two ruined test batches to produce, and when it finally came, Naomi delivered it.
"All of it. Every drop your body can spare without dying, distilled to essence. And if the essence collapses in the heat, we start over, so best assume this won't just be an hour-long ordeal."
"Alright," said Quinlan.
He settled onto a stool beside the largest cauldron, held his arm over the copper, and gave.
The first problem announced itself within minutes: his own body fought him. His high Vitality tried to seal the shallow cut, so he cut again, and again, wind parting flesh every few minutes.
For a while he kept up his usual commentary, rating Aurora's stirring form together with Gideon while asking how Iris felt about giving him a shoulder massage.
"Would that help?" The response greatly surprised Quinlan. But he wasn't called an opportunistic scumbag for nothing.
"It'd mean the world to me."
"..." Iris studied his face for a long second, her mouth a flat line. Then she stepped up behind him and, with amateur motions, squeezed.
"What a pleasant surprise..." Quinlan muttered, leaning back against her.

But within an hour of constant bloodletting, the commentary grew shorter. Then it stopped altogether, and the workroom belonged to the hiss of burners, the scratch of Aurora's pen, and the slow ring of blood on copper.
The color left him by degrees.
His lips went grey ahead of his face, a tremor moved into his forearm and had to be pinned in place by will alone, and sweat beaded at his temples in a room not nearly warm enough to explain it.
Aurora's pen had stopped. "Quin, please speak up when you need a break. This is not the time to be cool."
"I understand." The grin made it about halfway up his face. "But it's okay."
"[Awaken]."
Two of his Elite souls stepped out of ghostly pale flame, healers in life, robes and unhurried calm intact in death.

They took station on either side of his stool without being told a thing, and soft light sank into his shoulders and chest, coaxing his body to keep pace with the cauldron's appetite. It helped, though nothing about it came close to painless.
Neither soul asked Iris to move. They settled in around her hands as though their orders had included her from the start, and she understood, without a single word said out loud, that they had.

The ease of it bothered her. She was reading him through his summons now, through nothing but the way two dead healers chose to stand, and it had taken her no effort at all. Since when? Since when did she understand this bastard better than she understood most living people?
She found no answer she liked, so she kept kneading, amateur grip and all.

On the benches, the three alchemists had stopped being three separate people. Aurora called temperatures and timing windows without looking up, Gideon's hands were already moving before her sentences ended, and Naomi folded the reductions together in figure-eight strokes that never broke rhythm. Vials passed between them blind and never collided.
The man under Iris's hands had broken armies and cowed kings, but none of that power was worth anything on this stool.

This was a fight with no enemy to hit, a battle of sitting still while his strength drained out of him drop by drop. Hour after hour, grinning through grey lips, for the sake of one old man's tomorrow.
Iris watched him do it, and for a rare, unguarded moment, her expression was unrecognizable.
And by the door, the King of Vraven stood witness to the strangest sight of his reign.
There the creature sat. The monster he had hunted across a continent, holding his own wounds open, emptying himself into a cauldron so that one old man could stay on his feet long enough to matter.
The tightness that had been climbing the king's throat for hours finally demanded motion, and Alexios pushed off the wall.
"Villain." It came out rough.
"What, you got bored?"
"...No. I'll initiate the Ravenclaw investigation. Open your gate and let me repay a fraction of this by working instead of watching. Whenever you need me back, just let me know."

Quinlan held his gaze for a moment. Then he nodded, and two fingers of his free hand flicked sideways. A [Warp Gate] unfolded against the workshop wall, its edges a touch less crisp than usual, and nobody was unkind enough to mention it.
Alexios squared his hood and stepped through.
"Iris. Why don't you go with him?"
"..." Her hands stopped on his shoulders. "What do you mean?"
"Have him name you a secret agent. Or whatever he thinks will work best." The grin he aimed at her was pale but entirely his own. "Have the investigation answer to you. Lead it yourself."
Iris didn't respond right away. She had gone very quiet.

He was placing the entire machinery of a kingdom underneath her revenge and stepping out of her way, exactly as she had demanded it in that freezing cellar. Hers, top to bottom, with nobody deciding a single thing over her head ever again.
She looked down at him for a long moment, the ridiculous man under her hands with bloodless lips and dead healers at his sides, still bleeding, still grinning like tonight was a holiday.
"What about the massage...?" Iris asked with a tone she didn't quite recognize.
"It was wonderful. Truly wonderful," Quinlan smiled. "Perhaps you can finish it another day?"
"...I've been at it for hours. How greedy can you be?"
"Well-"
Before he could reply, she leaned down and pressed a quick kiss to the top of his head.
For once, she was taller than he was. The Child of Reckoning seemed to have made good use of that.
"...Maybe this'll help you," she muttered, and was through the gate before anyone could see her face.
The gate winked shut behind them.
Quinlan sat very still. His free hand rose, slowly, to the exact spot. "I'll be damned... Iris..."
"The ice wall is melting~" Aurora giggled.
"Focus, you two." Naomi didn't look up from her stirring. "Young man, you still owe this copper a few more hours of you. Young lady, break time hasn't arrived yet."
"I know," the duo spoke together in perfect sync.
The night wore on. The cauldron drank, the burners hissed, and Quinlan's grin grew quieter by the hour, held up by stubbornness and soft necromantic light.
He was fine.
There was, however, one detail the plan had not accounted for.
How have you been finding the recent chapters? Are they boring?

Truth be told, I've been having a lot of struggle writing the war and ensuing chapters with all those factions present, so it feels really good to finally write some simpler chapters. They still take multiple hours to write, but not the insane amount those chapters required of me.
That said, I fully understand if they're not to your liking. If it's any consolation, the Alexios stuff will be dealt with very quickly.
Thank you for all the support.

chapters.title: Chapter 1810 Cooking with the Lorien Gang
paragraphs: Quinlan had planned for the pain. He had planned for the hours, for the cauldron's appetite, for the slow indignity of being emptied one drop at a time into Naomi's warm copper, and on every one of those counts the plan was holding.
What he had not planned for was the family living in his chest.

The Bloodfather bond never slept. Every kill his women made whispered through it, every flare of their gifts pulsed against his sternum, and the current ran both ways. For six hours now, the strongest signature in the whole network had been quietly, steadily draining, and across half a continent, on skin he had marked with his own blood, crimson sigils were beginning to burn.
Blossom arrived first.
<MASTER!!>
The shout hit the inside of his skull hard enough that both Elite healers paused mid-cast. <Blossom feels it! Master's emptying like a bathtub!>
<Yeah...> Quinlan chuckled. <I kind of am...>
<Hubby.> Vex's voice slid in underneath, low and sweet and completely wrong, the register she saved for moments when she was already holding her sword. <Give me a name.>
<Quin.> Ayame, crisp as a drawn blade. <You should be sleeping. Just what on earth are you up to even at this hour?>
<Did you try to kiss Iris or something?> Sera cut in. <Why are you bleeding out?>
As the rest of the gang made their opinions heard, Aurora winced.
"...Why are they both making those faces?" Gideon whispered, glancing between Aurora and Quinlan.
"Eyes on your reduction, dear," Naomi said.
Aurora set down her pen, pressed two fingers to her temple, and joined the channel with the audible patience of the family's only scientist. <Everyone, calm down. He's with me.>
<Aurora?!>
<He's donating blood. Voluntarily,> she continued. <For a brew.>
<Donating,> Ayame repeated, then her tone lost its edge. <For Alexios.>
<Yes.>
The samurai had a soft smile on her face, patting the mark on her belly tenderly. <Finally... You found a friend you're willing to go out of your way to help...>
<...> Quinlan remained silent where he sat.

It was no secret that his beloved samurai wanted him to bond with a person of his gender, instead of surrounding himself exclusively with women. She believed it wasn't good for his mental health, or something like that.
She'd been begging him to find Ignis and go out for drinks with him, or whatever mundane guy stuff they wanted, but that never materialized. Perhaps later.

Quinlan didn't really get why she was so hopeful he'd one day find a male friend, and he didn't agree one bit. Surrounding himself with gorgeous babes was literal perfection, the best way for a man to lead his life. He didn't miss having a perpetually grumbling, hairy creature in his life.

Yet here he was, doing this for Alexios, because he... respected that old fucker too much. If their situations were reversed, Quinlan would be disgusted to take that pill from another man. He would still do it, no doubt, but he wouldn't like it one bit. That's why he did what he did.
<Hehe~> Ayame's soft giggles sounded, far too happy for him for a reason Quinlan really didn't understand.
But if she was happy...
The third batch died a little past midnight.

Naomi saw it first. The reduction had been holding a deep, steady crimson through the whole fold, and then between one stroke of her paddle and the next it simply gave up, the color collapsing out of it like dye poured into a river, leaving thin red water and six hours of work dead in the copper.
"No. No, no, NO." She threw the paddle down. "The same wall! Everything holds until the final fold, and then it just... leaves. Like it was never a substance at all!"

"Because it isn't." Gideon was bent over the ruined batch, monocle nearly touching the surface. His voice had gone hollow and calm, the sound of his life's assumptions failing in real time. "Essence-density readings straight through the collapse. It doesn't degrade, it doesn't scorch, it doesn't separate. It's not behaving like matter, it's behaving like..."
"Like it's waiting for something," Aurora finished quietly.
The workroom went still around that sentence.

Quinlan sat on his stool with his opened arm over the cauldron's rim, and felt the truth of it before any of them finished saying it, a pull behind his sternum, faint and patient, in exactly the rhythm of his own heartbeat. He looked down into the fresh batch, at the blood he'd spent all night giving.
It was looking back.

Every drop of it, gallons of him spread across copper and glass and reduction flasks, was aimed at him the way a hound aims at a door. The hollow above his heart warmed in answer. Then the idea simply arrived.

His hands knew, suddenly and completely, what to do, the way they knew how to close around a saber. His blood had never been an ingredient. Outside his body it was still his, still family, still waiting on its patriarch, and no alchemist alive could give it the one thing it was waiting for.
An order.
"Oh," Quinlan said softly. "I'm an idiot."
Gideon adjusted his monocle. "In this house, we prefer to phrase it as 'the theory was incomplete.' What have you thought of?"

Quinlan rose from the stool. Both Elite healers reached for him, and Aurora's mouth was already opening around a protest, and he waved all three of them off with his good hand, crossing to the cauldron on legs that had earned the wobble in them.

"You've been trying to cook me like an herb." He spread his palm flat over the copper, and the surface of the batch rose toward it, a slow crimson swell, like a cat pushing up into a hand. "It won't hold a form for you, because it isn't yours to shape."
Naomi's eyes widened, excitement overtaking her tired features. "You're saying the final fold needs..."
"Me." He grinned, grey-lipped and delighted. "Well, maybe. I don't know for sure."
"Your intuition is rarely mistaken," Aurora offered. "It's like with smithing. You have zero clue about the technique of it, yet you somehow gain an insight into it." She pouted. "How unfair."

Quinlan merely chuckled, steadying himself against the bench edge. "Aurora, you can continue your utterly adorable pouts while we try this. The way you brew your primordial batches... same principle, except tonight the drop is conscious and charming."
"Modest, too," Aurora scoffed, but eyes were dancing and her pen was already moving. The plump alchemist was always having the time of her life when her lover was in the lab with her.
They rebuilt the brew from zero as the sky greyed toward morning.

Naomi drove the process, calling folds and temperatures in a voice that took no arguments. Gideon ran the stills with both hands and narrated essence readings under his breath, taking dictation from history.

Aurora sat closest to Quinlan, two fingers resting on his wrist, timing every addition to the beat of his heart. Quinlan stood over the cauldron through all of it, his will threaded down into his own blood, holding.
No spell name covered what he was doing, and no notification offered one. As the work taught him its shape, he understood it was more than any single power of his acting alone.
The Bloodfather class held the door open. It was what made his blood family instead of material, what gave his voice the standing to be obeyed, what named every drop in that cauldron his.
"Fold," Naomi called, without looking up from the copper. "Slow count."
"Holding," Quinlan answered through his teeth, and held.
But Bloodfather was a ledger of bonds, not a craftsman, and ledgers do not write.
The thing doing the writing, folding living essence toward a shape no recipe in the world had ever held, was the engine underneath everything else he was.

The Abyssal Genesis Physique, the same primordial appetite that had once caught a class and felt it lacking so it authored it anew, had recognized tonight's work the moment his palm crossed the copper.
He bled, and the physique wrote, the same quiet authorship that had shaped his class and stitched the marks into his women. Tonight, for the first time, it was writing outside his body.

He simply spoke to the essence as he would speak to any of his own, and it obeyed the way family obeys, because it was asked by the right voice. Where Naomi folded, he held the fold. Where the heat should have collapsed it, he told it to endure, and it endured.
Endurance, it turned out, was the cheap half of the work.
Around him the workroom kept its own rhythm, a burner hissing steady under the copper, Naomi's paddle knocking the rim on every turn, Gideon whispering numbers to his notebook.
As the reduction deepened, the essence began to drift under his grip.

Unlike the earlier batches it held together, obedient, and still it refused to set, turning slowly under his will like a thing waiting for the rest of its instructions. It knew whose it was now. That question had been settled the moment his will touched it. All it still waited for was the answer to the only question that matters to a gift.
Who is it for?
Quinlan exhaled, closed his eyes, and gave it Alexios.

Not the crown, nor the warrant, nor the convenient ally with a kingdom's machinery bolted to his name. The class had no appetite for politics. So he held the man himself at the center of his mind: the old monster who had hunted him across a continent. The man who trusted his enemy with his daughter's life. The king who worked himself to the bone for centuries straight, for a nation that did not deserve a fraction of his effort.
And with the target held, the Bloodfather class began taking his answers, one by one, weighing each of them like coin.
He accepted the word for what Alexios was to him: an ally he cared about, more than the asset and the investment he'd claimed to Aurora with a straight face.
The first male he actually cared about in his whole reincarnated lifetime.

chapters.title: Chapter 1811 Friend
paragraphs: The first male he actually cared about in his whole reincarnated lifetime.
He accepted that he did not want to watch the old man die.
Somewhere far away, in the world where his body lived, Naomi called another fold, and Aurora's fingers tightened on his wrist as his pulse stumbled.
And he accepted the last one, the one underneath all the others. He wanted the badass geezer to keep his dignity.

To never choke down another man's seed pill for the privilege of breathing, not while Quinlan had a drop of blood left to offer instead. To be standing, spine straight, when the Heavenly Restriction came down, and to be there beyond the edge of every map after it, that fossil of a status screen climbing again.
He wanted to see. A level 75 Alexios Valorian.
A level 100 Alexios Valorian.
An Alexios Valorian who fought demons and gods alike, whatever entity stood in his path. Quinlan knew the old fucker would make it possible, just like his girls would.
The essence stopped turning and aimed.
None of this would ever be said out loud, naturally, not even to Ayame.
And when the final reduction came, the class showed him the last requirement, and its price, in the same breath.
The lattice across his chest and back lit up through his shirt.

The Crimson Reservoir, the family's shared vessel, stirred at the hollow above his heart and began to pour. It ran down the inside of his arm in a thread of deep red light and into the cauldron, and the brew drank it the way dry earth drinks rain.

He could have stopped it. He understood, with the same authored certainty as everything else tonight, that he could refuse, and that the batch would die like the other three, because this was the half no alchemist could supply. The blood was the body of the gift. The Reservoir was its life. And an oath, it turned out, was not made of words at all.
Quinlan let it pour.
The understanding kept unrolling as the vessel drained, and it was not gentle about its terms. This door opened for family, for oath, for a man its holder would bleed for.

The Reservoir would fill again at his women's pace, not his, and until it did, the family would fight without the reserve their kills had built. And unlike the normal Bloodfather ritual, this was not a thing he could repeat whenever he felt like it.
"Reduction's holding!" Gideon's voice cracked on it. "The essence is binding to the... Naomi, the density, look at the density...!"
"I see it. Final fold." Naomi's paddle moved in one long, unbroken figure-eight, her whole weight behind the calm of it. "Aurora. Cap the heat. Now."
"Capped."

The cauldron's contents pulled inward from the copper walls, contracting like a closing hand, smaller, denser, brighter. The light in the workroom bent toward it with the same wrongness that had once made lantern flames lean away from Quinlan in a freezing cellar.
The thread from his chest thinned, thinned further, and finally parted, and the lattice under his shirt went dark and quiet, a spent hearth.
What remained above the empty copper did not fall.

A single bead of deep, impossible crimson floated where the brew had been, no larger than the pearl it was built to replace, and it sat in the air like it weighed more than the cauldron beneath it. It trembled, faintly and constantly, like a nocked arrow the instant before the loose.
Naomi set down her paddle, walked to the nearest bench, and sat, all at once, like her strings had been cut.
"Forty years of alchemy," she informed the ceiling.

Gideon approached with a crystal flask and the reverence of a man about to bottle a saint. The flask's mouth rose under the bead, and the bead drifted aside without appearing to move at all. He tried again, slower. It drifted again, calm and effortless, three times in a row, until the scholar turned around wearing an expression of pure scientific heartbreak.
"It refuses containment. Why would it refuse containment?!"

"Because it isn't finished." Quinlan was grinning at the little crimson star through a face gone paper-white. He could feel it at the edge of his will, familiar as his own hand, straining in one direction only, steady as a compass needle, and the night's last piece of knowledge unrolled in him along with it, in the physique's wordless handwriting.
A flask was an insult. A courier was an insult. A gift like this was given, palm to chest, by the man giving it, and his arm, tonight, was very long.
"Naomi. How attached are you to your roof?"
"...What does my roof have to do with anything?" Her gaze went from him, to the trembling bead, to the beams overhead, and she came up off the bench. "Young man. Don't you dare-"
"Sorry. I can't hold it any longer."
Quinlan gathered everything that was left in him.

The Abyssal Genesis Physique rose to meet the call, dark script flooding up his forearms and throat, every line of the lattice burning through his shirt at once, the whole failing engine of his body agreeing, one last time tonight, to be spent. He looked at the little red star he had paid for, and gave it the only instruction it had ever been waiting for.
'Go.'
The bead went through the roof.
It left a crack of parting air, a perfect circle of missing tiles raining splinters across the benches, and dawn pouring down through the hole into a workroom full of drifting dust.
Naomi's shriek and Gideon's awed, broken laugh arrived together, and Aurora got her shoulder under Quinlan just as his knees handed in their resignation.
Above Miri Town, the first morning light acquired a companion.

A seam of red light crossed the rooftops and was gone, out over Lumi Forest, still holding its night mist, over rivers and roads and border stones, streaking through the dawn faster than any bird had ever flown it.

A farmer dropped his pail and pointed. A watchman on a border wall opened his mouth to shout, and by the time sound came out, the sky was empty again. It flew straight and unwavering, because it knew where it was going the way blood knows its way home.
The King of Vraven had not slept either.

Dawn found Alexios Valorian at the great desk of the royal study, buried to the forearms in sealed orders, while across the room Iris sat with her boots up on a table worth a village, working through a stack of records she had refused to let anyone summarize for her.
The instincts arrived first.

Every battlefield sense the old king owned fired at once, the same full-body alarm that had once walked him backward across a freezing cellar, and he was on his feet with his hand on his sword before his mind caught up.
The tall windows flushed red, dawn drowned in a deeper color, and then it was through the glass without breaking it and into his chest before the blade cleared an inch.
Warmth.
Ferocious and total, flooding out from his sternum into every limb at once, and with it came the strangest sensation of Alexios Valorian's very long life.

The slow falling in his marrow, the one he had carried so long he had stopped calling it falling, stopped. The ground arrived under a man who had forgotten he was still dropping, and his next breath went all the way down, and the one after that went deeper.

He knew the signature. Of course he knew it. He had hunted it across a continent, mapped its habits, cursed its owner's name a million times, and now it had crossed a kingdom at dawn to hunt him back, and it had caught him.
Alexios gripped the edge of the desk and laughed once, rough and low, at nothing his dignity was prepared to explain.
"You just couldn't have handed it over like a normal person, could you?" he managed, to the empty morning air. "You absolute showoff..."
Iris hadn't moved from her chair. She watched the last of the red light soak out of the air around the king, then turned back to her records.
"Now you get to deal with him forever. Dying would've been mercy."

Alexios straightened, and his shoulders came back and down. Outside the tall windows, dawn was spreading over his capital, and for the first time in a very long while, its king was not counting his mornings.
With the morning sun's arrival, and as the Ravenshade investigation began taking shape, it was time for Quinlan to visit the elven capital!

chapters.title: Chapter 1812 Embarrassed Daughter
paragraphs: Morning finished rising over Miri Town, and the workroom finally surrendered.

Sunlight fell through the hole in Naomi's roof in one honest golden column, dust still turning lazily inside it, and beneath that accidental skylight, an alchemist family was coming apart at the seams.

Naomi sat on her bench with her apron strings undone and her hands open in her lap, too spent to pretend otherwise. Gideon had sunk into the room's only armchair, notebook against his chest like a sleeping infant.

Aurora was the best off, thanks to her being higher level than her parents, but she still leaned against the center bench with her platinum hair escaping its tie one strand at a time, and even her posture, usually the straightest in any room, had filed for a leave of absence.
Quinlan stood among them, his vitality already returning, skin going from pale parchment to healthy.
He inclined his head to Naomi and Gideon both.
"Thanks, you two." His voice was quieter than the room was used to hearing from him. "You didn't owe me any of this."
Gideon's monocle came off. He polished it on his sleeve, set it back, looked at Quinlan, and took it off again, as though the words might parse better through cleaner glass.

"Thanks... us?" The third adjustment failed as thoroughly as the first two. "Young man, do you have any grasp of what we witnessed tonight? Essence that answers speech! A reduction bound by will! Alchemists will be arguing about this night centuries after our names are dust, and we were here for it! It's us who should be grateful for being present at this moment!"
"What my husband is trying to say," Naomi cut in, "is that there's no need for gratitude between family."
Her smile was soft. It was also, in a way that had nothing to do with her tired shoulders and everything to do with the glint underneath, dangerous.
"But if you insist on repaying us..." The glint sharpened. "I want grandchildren. Big, healthy ones. One girl and one boy, minimum."
"MOM!"
"Grandpa Gideon does have a ring to it," Gideon mused from the armchair.
"DAD!"
Quinlan smirked, entirely unbothered. "I'm afraid that desire of yours will have to wait a while."
"Aww." Naomi pouted. A full pout, lips and all, and she knew exactly how effective it was.
"Stop pouting! Why are you pouting?! You're a middle-aged woman, act like one!" Aurora had pushed off the bench, pointing at her own parent like she was flagging a safety violation.
"Excuse me, young lady? I'm not middle-aged."
"..." Aurora didn't mean to say something too rude, so she instead turned delusion into a weapon. "Then stop demanding grandkids!"
"No."
What a cute family.

Aurora achieved a new shade of red, seized Quinlan by the arm, and began hauling all two meters of him toward the door with the strength of pure mortification. "We're leaving. Mom's gone crazy, she needs time alone to calm down."
"Really? She looks pretty normal to me," Quinlan noted, letting himself be hauled.
"My daughter is just flustered," Naomi told him warmly, waving from her bench. "Isn't she adorable?"
"Yeah," Quinlan smiled over his shoulder. "She is. You have great genes."
"Right?"
"Mom, take your meds!" Aurora shouted, and slammed the door on her parents' laughter.
The morning street had opinions about what came through that door.
The apothecary stood on one of Miri Town's waking lanes, and the lane was busy enough that recognition arrived within three heartbeats.
"The lord! The lord is here!"
"By the walls, it's him..."
"Someone get Tomas, he'll never believe..."
Unlike Lucille, whose family's quiet life had needed a plain dress and a plainer name, the Loriens had never asked for anonymity.
Half the town had watched their apothecary go up board by board, and everyone knew whose parents had moved in, the same way everyone knew their daughter stood beside the lord himself.
It was no secret, so Quinlan spared the gathering crowd exactly none of his attention.
Aurora had stopped at the top of the steps, arms crossed, fuming at the cobblestones.

Strands of platinum stuck out where the night had pulled them loose, her amber eyes were bright with leftover embarrassment, and the morning light was being frankly unfair about the whole arrangement. Flustered, rumpled, and utterly sexy.
"They're too much," she muttered. "Dad's a fanatic. And Mom... Mom is Mom. There's no fixing either of them."
Quinlan stepped in close.
She noticed the shadow fall over her and looked up, and whatever she found in his face made her take half a step back against the railing. "W-what? What is it?"
"My gorgeous alchemist," he said, "is way too cute. I wanted to see from up close."
The red came back all at once, ears included, and she began observing her feet furiously. "You lost too much blood tonight. You need rest, your brain is clearly..."
He reached out and caught her chin, tilting her face up to his, and her protest died somewhere on the way out. The pout arrived instantly.
"You always play the straight woman for everyone. Dependable, smart, calm and collected." His thumb traced the line of her jaw. "Let me enjoy this view for once."
"Not fair..." she murmured, quieter, making no attempt whatsoever to reclaim her chin.
"I'll have to visit your parents more often with you."
"Don't you dare, they'll only get worse, Mom will start knitting baby clothes just to pressure me-"
He leaned down and kissed her.

"No! Quin...! Bad Quin... I'm not done..." She melted almost instantly, complaint and all, her hands closing on the front of his shirt as though she'd merely been waiting for a better argument. Two big hands slid down to her round butt, and Aurora left the ground in one practiced hop, legs wrapping around his waist, night-long exhaustion apparently negotiable after all.

And just like that, in front of a street's worth of audience, Quinlan turned, carried his woman down the apothecary steps, and walked into the [Warp Gate] that unfolded ahead of him, her lips never once leaving his.
The gate winked shut, and Miri Town's morning was left to fend for itself.

Jealous men stared at the empty air. So did no small number of jealous women. Teenagers of both kinds went variously red, and a baker's boy dropped an entire tray without noticing. Several small children asked questions that several parents suddenly found fascinating reasons not to hear.
Another legendary sighting of the town's lord went down in Miri Town's history that day.
The [Warp Gate] delivered Quinlan into the morning air of his own garden, and Aurora neither noticed nor cared.

She was busy. Her fingers had buried themselves in his hair somewhere between one town and the next, her thighs stayed locked around his waist, and the kiss had long since stopped being a farewell to Miri Town.

The family's dependable buffer and scientist, the calm and collected voice of reason who had spent the entire night holding three alchemists and one bleeding primordial together, was currently making small, impatient sounds against her man's mouth, pressing closer with every one of them, a night's worth of worry demanding payment all at once.
"Mmh... Quin..."

chapters.title: Chapter 1813 Father-Daughter Partners in Crime
paragraphs: "Mmh... Quin..."

Quinlan paid, gladly. His hands roamed the generous mounds he was holding her up by, and whenever her breath ran out she pulled back a finger's width, amber eyes hazy, only to dive right back in before air could talk her into behaving. Whoever needed the rest here had clearly stopped being him.
The garden, meanwhile, went about its morning around them.
Rosie's tree ruled the grounds, wide enough to shade half the estate, morning light pooling pale and gentle through its canopy.

On one of its low, broad branches sat two of the most important women of the elven world, and neither had survived the night with her dignity intact. Myrasyn's braids had surrendered hours ago, loose strands framing a face soft with exhaustion and shining with joy.
Beside her, Isveth's immaculate shrine maiden dress was creased in ways no devout of the faith would ever willingly permit.
Neither had slept, neither was presentable, and neither had ever looked happier.
They sat like village girls on a fence, legs swinging over open air, and between them, enthroned sideways across both women's thighs, sat Rosie, currently receiving pats from four hands at once.

"...and when the Holy Mother raised her hand, the whole forest bowed at once," Isveth was murmuring, her fingers combing slow and reverent through the little girl's hair. "Every branch, every root, every leaf..."
"And then? And then?!"
"Then, little one, she planted the very first seed..."

"Haah..." Myrasyn sighed from somewhere far past bliss, chin dipping, her hand never once breaking its patting rhythm. The queen of the elves looked like she had found the meaning of her reign on a tree branch.

Below them, among the roots, lay the casualties. Five elven handmaidens were scattered across the moss in various states of surrender, one still clutching a half-braided flower crown, all soundly asleep. Rosie had outlasted every last one of them. The queen and her maiden had simply refused to fall, running on devotion alone.
Then, mid-pat, Rosie's eyes found her papa across the garden.
Quinlan's eyes found his daughter back over a shoulder of platinum hair, his lips otherwise occupied.
A silent conference was held.

Her papa was exactly where he wanted to be. So was she, pampered from both sides by warm, dedicated, wonderful ladies who smelled like flowers and never ran out of stories. Neither position could be improved upon, and greetings would keep.
Rosie sent him a tiny smile and turned back to Isveth's story. Quinlan's eyes crinkled in answer, and he returned his full attention to his plump lover.
Perfect partners in crime.
"Pah..." When the kiss finally ended, it ended the way expensive things break: slowly, and with protest.

"No... Come back..." Aurora chased his mouth twice before accepting that air had won, and even then she stayed wrapped around him, flushed and unwilling to dismount, so Quinlan simply carried her toward the smell of fresh bread.
The breakfast table stood on the terrace at the garden's edge looking directly toward Rosie's tree, a comfortable arrangement of cushioned chairs around more food than three women could ever finish.
Seraphiel lounged with a teacup, smiling like she'd enjoyed the morning's entertainment immensely.
Kaelira sat straight-backed beside her with a diplomatic amount of attention aimed at her plate.
And across from them, in full Church regalia at a villain's breakfast table, Elisabeth Valorian was being refilled by a maid for the third time despite having announced her imminent departure twice.

"Morning, ladies." Quinlan dropped into the widest chair and arranged Aurora sideways across his thigh, where she curled up against his chest with zero scientific dignity remaining and no visible intention of recovering any.
"Morning, Quin~" Seraphiel's grin was radiant. "I see you managed to work our alchemist up 'a bit'..."
"G-good morning," Kaelira managed, ears already pink. "And to you too, Aurora..."
"H-hey..." the platinum-haired beauty managed, still nestled against Quin.
"Wait, is 'Daddy's Little Girl' Aurora returning to us?" Sera asked, eyes twinkling.

Aurora, for the longest time, preferred to be treated exactly as such. It was Rosie's arrival and consequent screeching of 'Daddy!!' that made Aurora's schtick harder to justify in her head, thus she stopped doing so.
"No..." Aurora whispered. "This is... 'I Love Quin Too Much' Aurora..."

Elisabeth set down her cup with a click that said she had been rehearsing. "'Morning'? That is all you have to say? You materialized out of thin air already devouring that poor woman like a... a..." Her hand described a scandalized circle. "There are children on these grounds! Does shame simply not exist for you?"

"Rosie was born knowing more stuff than we'll ever manage to fit into our heads because Geims pass down information between generations. So there's no need to be ashamed, she knows perfectly well what's up even if she might pretend otherwise," Quinlan confirmed pleasantly, reaching for the tea with one hand.
"T-that's a weak excuse, Villain..."
"Just call me Quinlan."
"No."
"Whatever makes you happy, Elisabeth."
"I didn't permit you to call me by my first name."
"Okay, Elisabeth."
While a certain hypocrite was busy fuming, Quinlan's other hand had already disappeared beneath the table.
Aurora's breath hitched against his collarbone.

His fingers had found the hem of her dress and slipped under it without ceremony, tracing slow, idle lines up the inside of her thigh, and the family's voice of reason responded by biting her lip and shifting her hips a quarter turn to make the road easier. Needy mode, it appeared, had not been dismissed.

The soaked fabric between her legs lost the negotiation to a single hooked finger, and then he was touching her properly, fingertips gliding through slick, drenched folds that had been waiting for him since the apothecary steps.
He took his sweet time with her, spreading her in slow strokes, circling the exact spot that made her knee bump the table's underside.
When two fingers finally sank into her to the knuckle, the sound she made against his neck could almost have passed for a yawn.
Almost.
Two elven noses wrinkled in perfect unison.
Seraphiel's teacup paused halfway to her lips. Her nostrils flared once, delicately, and the radiant grin evolved into pure delight as she leaned back to enjoy the show properly.

Beside her, Kaelira caught the same information on the same breeze, went rigid, and turned red enough to clash violently with her own hair, eyes boring a hole into her breakfast as though the bread might rescue her.

"Shame," Elisabeth continued, fully armored in her own righteousness and blind as a newborn kitten, "is what separates civilized society from beasts. The Goddess teaches that the flesh makes demands, and the righteous refuse them."

On the villain's lap, Aurora was refusing nothing. Her hips had begun to move in tiny, secret rolls, riding his fingers with motions she sincerely believed were invisible, and her grip on the front of his shirt had gone white-knuckled.
"Mm. Go on." Quinlan sipped his tea and set his fingers to the same unhurried rhythm as his sips. "I hope to one day become a paragon of virtue."
"A futile dream," Elisabeth decreed without pause.
Seraphiel, meanwhile, had appointed herself a new duty.

chapters.title: Chapter 1814 Paragon of Virtue
paragraphs: Seraphiel, meanwhile, had appointed herself a new duty. With one of her man's hands devoted to his tea and the other, by all appearances, resting innocently on his lover's hip, someone clearly had to keep him fed, so she buttered a slice of bread, leaned across, and held it up to his mouth.
"Say aah~"
Quinlan bit into it without so much as glancing away from the sermon, and chewed like he was being handsomely rewarded for his crimes.

"Still, would you please tell my hopeless lover more, Eli?" Seraphiel propped her chin on her palm, eyes dancing between Elisabeth's sermon and Aurora's slowly unraveling posture. "He desperately needs your guidance. Spare no detail~"
"Don't call me that," came the instant scoff, followed by a satisfied smirk. "But at least someone at this table respects doctrine."
It took everything the cheeky elf had to keep her laughter back.
Kaelira made a strangled sound into her plate. "This can't be real..."
"As I was saying." The Arch Priestess straightened, warming to her audience. "Temptation withers before discipline. Proper conduct begins at the table. A shared meal is a sacred..."
"Ahn!" Aurora shuddered, gripped Quinlan's wrist with both hands, and pressed it closer.
"...a sacred act of communion," Elisabeth pressed on, granting the feverish interruption a charitable pause.
Emily drifted by and, without a flicker of expression on the head maid's face, replaced the napkin beside Aurora's untouched plate with a fresh, considerably larger one.
"Say, Aurora dear~" Seraphiel's voice turned silken. "You're our scholar. Surely alchemy knows a cure for fevers like yours?"

Aurora's eyes cracked open just enough to aim a dying glare across the table. "It's not good... anhnn... to drink potions... for every illness... mmnnmm... some are best left... to run..." Under the table, two fingers curled against the exact spot with slow, merciless precision. "...t-their course. Hnn. Naturally."
"Fascinating," Quinlan said, and accepted a honey-glazed morsel straight from Seraphiel's fingers.
Kaelira stood so fast her chair squealed against the terrace stones. "I have work. At the forge. The runes won't-"
"Breakfast isn't over, Kaeli~" Seraphiel's hand landed on the smith's shoulder and guided her back down without negotiation. "It's rude to leave before all participants finish, isn't it, Eli?"
"Yes, that is exactly right." The Arch Priestess nodded. "I'm happy at least one member of this household seems to know how to act civilized."
"I try my best~"

Then, having secured her prisoner, Seraphiel slid the pastry basket in front of Kaelira. "Here, Kaeli. Our man is starving and both his hands are occupied. I'll make him a sandwich, can you meanwhile..."

"O-okay..." Kaelira murmured, shy. The tomboy elf observed the basket, ears twitching. Was she really about to feed her boyfriend? Excitement swelled in her chest as she picked out a pastry, turned to Quinlan with all the stiffness of approaching a live monster, and held it out at maximum arm's length. "H-here. Eat."
Quinlan leaned in slowly, eyes on hers the whole way, and then struck like a shark, one enormous bite claiming the entire thing to within a hair of her fingertips.
"Hyah!?" Kaelira's yelp sent a bird off the terrace railing. She snatched her hand back, counted all five fingers, and her face flamed. "Y-you...! You beast! Eat like a person!"
"That's exactly what I've been saying," Elisabeth nodded along sagely.
"No promises," he said, catching a stray flake with his tongue.

"..." The adorable smith sat there fuming, redder by the second and failing completely to look displeased, and after a few moments of furious silence she picked out the next one and raised it to bite range, braced for teeth this time.
Under the table, matters were leaving diplomacy behind.
The soft, wet rhythm of his fingers was climbing dangerously close to audible, so Aurora coughed, twice, with impeccable timing.

Her thighs trembled around his wrist, and every muscle in her lower body wound itself tighter around the pressure building where his fingers worked. She had stopped following the sermon entirely. She was mouthing numbers against his neck, actually counting primes, the best defense her scientist brain could improvise, and losing track somewhere after eleven.

Elisabeth's gaze snagged on the platinum-haired woman trembling against the villain's chest, and her sermon faltered into a frown of honest concern. "Her fever is worsening by the minute. Have you people truly done nothing for the poor thing?"
"There's nothing to be done," Quinlan said gravely. "It comes and goes in waves."
"It's chronic~" Seraphiel added, sparkling.
"I'm fine," Aurora announced to his collarbone, in a voice two octaves above her usual register.

That did it. Elisabeth set down her cup, rose from her chair, and rounded the table at a brisk stride, patience with heathen medicine finally spent. "Enough. You've all clearly given up on this poor woman. The Goddess mends what herbs and excuses cannot."
Aurora's eyes flew open. "No. W-wait. That's really not..."
The Arch Priestess laid her blessed palm flat against Aurora's forehead with all the tenderness of her office. "O Goddess, grant your suffering daughter relief."
Golden warmth flooded down through Aurora's body, gentle, holy, and aimed with divine precision at muscles already wound past their limit.
Relief was granted.

Aurora came undone on the Primordial Villain's fingers with an Arch Priestess's hand upon her brow, thighs locking around his wrist, back arching off his chest, wave after long wave rolling through her while she pressed her mouth shut against his shoulder and drenched the hand that had spent the entire breakfast earning it.
It went on for a small eternity.
Quinlan drank his tea through all of it, steady as bedrock, and did not stop until she had wrung out every last tremor against his palm.
Then the alchemist sagged, boneless, faintly glowing with residual blessing, and let out one long, shivering breath that fogged no glass but should have.
Elisabeth withdrew her hand and observed her patient with deep professional satisfaction. "There. See? The trembling has stopped."
"The Goddess is truly merciful," Quinlan said solemnly.
"Amen," Seraphiel managed from somewhere inside her teacup.
"...amen," Aurora whispered bashfully.

sentences.text: Seraphiel, meanwhile, had appointed herself a new duty.

With one of her man's hands devoted to his tea and the other, by all appearances, resting innocently on his lover's hip, someone clearly had to keep him fed, so she buttered a slice of bread, leaned across, and held it up to his mouth.
"Say aah~"
Quinlan bit into it without so much as glancing away from the sermon, and chewed like he was being handsomely rewarded for his crimes.
"Still, would you please tell my hopeless lover more, Eli?" Seraphiel propped her chin on her palm, eyes dancing between Elisabeth's sermon and Aurora's slowly unraveling posture.
"He desperately needs your guidance.
Spare no detail~"
"Don't call me that," came the instant scoff, followed by a satisfied smirk.
"But at least someone at this table respects doctrine."
It took everything the cheeky elf had to keep her laughter back.
Kaelira made a strangled sound into her plate.
"This can't be real..."
"As I was saying." The Arch Priestess straightened, warming to her audience.
"Temptation withers before discipline.
Proper conduct begins at the table.
A shared meal is a sacred..."
"Ahn!" Aurora shuddered, gripped Quinlan's wrist with both hands, and pressed it closer.
"...a sacred act of communion," Elisabeth pressed on, granting the feverish interruption a charitable pause.
Emily drifted by and, without a flicker of expression on the head maid's face, replaced the napkin beside Aurora's untouched plate with a fresh, considerably larger one.
"Say, Aurora dear~" Seraphiel's voice turned silken.
"You're our scholar.
Surely alchemy knows a cure for fevers like yours?"
Aurora's eyes cracked open just enough to aim a dying glare across the table.

"It's not good... anhnn... to drink potions... for every illness... mmnnmm... some are best left... to run..." Under the table, two fingers curled against the exact spot with slow, merciless precision.
"...t-their course.
Hnn.
Naturally."
"Fascinating," Quinlan said, and accepted a honey-glazed morsel straight from Seraphiel's fingers.
Kaelira stood so fast her chair squealed against the terrace stones.
"I have work.
At the forge.
The runes won't-"
"Breakfast isn't over, Kaeli~" Seraphiel's hand landed on the smith's shoulder and guided her back down without negotiation.
"It's rude to leave before all participants finish, isn't it, Eli?"
"Yes, that is exactly right." The Arch Priestess nodded.
"I'm happy at least one member of this household seems to know how to act civilized."
"I try my best~"
Then, having secured her prisoner, Seraphiel slid the pastry basket in front of Kaelira.
"Here, Kaeli.
Our man is starving and both his hands are occupied.
I'll make him a sandwich, can you meanwhile..."
"O-okay..." Kaelira murmured, shy.
The tomboy elf observed the basket, ears twitching.
Was she really about to feed her boyfriend?
Excitement swelled in her chest as she picked out a pastry, turned to Quinlan with all the stiffness of approaching a live monster, and held it out at maximum arm's length.
"H-here.
Eat."
Quinlan leaned in slowly, eyes on hers the whole way, and then struck like a shark, one enormous bite claiming the entire thing to within a hair of her fingertips.
"Hyah!?" Kaelira's yelp sent a bird off the terrace railing.
She snatched her hand back, counted all five fingers, and her face flamed.
"Y-you...!
You beast!
Eat like a person!"

Under the table, matters were leaving diplomacy behind.
The soft, wet rhythm of his fingers was climbing dangerously close to audible, so Aurora coughed, twice, with impeccable timing.
Her thighs trembled around his wrist, and every muscle in her lower body wound itself tighter around the pressure building where his fingers worked.
She had stopped following the sermon entirely.
She was mouthing numbers against his neck, actually counting primes, the best defense her scientist brain could improvise, and losing track somewhere after eleven.

chapters.title: Chapter 1815 Dispersing Ladies
paragraphs: The terrace was down to crumbs and casualties by the time Emily carried Aurora off to bed, the alchemist asleep before her head even found the maid's shoulder, still faintly glowing with residual blessing.
Elisabeth Valorian watched them go, set down her emptied cup, and announced her imminent departure for the fourth time that morning.
"Allow me." Quinlan's fingers flicked before the sentence finished landing, and a [Warp Gate] unfolded beside the table, opening onto sunlit stone in the human capital.
The Arch Priestess stared at it, then her eyes moved to Quinlan and narrowed into suspicious slits.
"You're way too accommodating all of a sudden..."
"You wanted to leave. As a devout follower of the Goddess, would I dare-"
"Don't you dare make such terribly ill-mannered jokes, Villain!"
Elisabeth scoffed and began moving toward the swirling doorway, accompanied by a lot of huffs and puffs.
"Can I visit you sometime, Eli~?" Seraphiel waved from her seat.
"Do not call me that." A pause, one step from the seam. "...I will consider it."
The gate winked shut on her exit, and the terrace felt briefly, strangely larger.

Quinlan leaned back and took stock of his morning. Ayame and Black Fang were nowhere to be found, which likely meant one sister had dragged the other somewhere private again, reluctance and all. He smiled into his tea and left that door firmly alone. Some things went better without him.
"Incoming," Seraphiel noted, chin tipping toward the garden path.

Lilith Ravenshade came up from the grounds with her sister at her shoulder and the Scarlet Lilies strung out behind them, Void riding Bronnya's back with her cheek pillowed on the tanker's shoulder, asleep or close enough to make no difference.
The enslaved Queen of Vraven, by the boundless mercy of her generous master, was permitted to spend time with her visiting sister.
"Villain." Lilith stopped at the terrace steps and inclined her head to Quinlan, courteous and precise. "Where is Black Fang? We have matters to discuss."
"Mm." Quinlan set down his cup. "You might want to visit the Vraven capital instead."
The pause stretched long enough for a bird to cross the whole garden.
"...Why," Lilith said, "would I want that?"
"Because Alexios is opening an investigation into the Ravenshade duchy." He said it the way other men discussed weather. "You could help them."
Void's eyes cracked open a slit. "He's sending us away..." she muttered into Bronnya's shoulder, dejected down to the syllables.
Lilith had gone very still. Beside her, Morgana's spine straightened by a degree that a less observant household might have missed.
"What investigation?" the elder Ravenshade demanded.
"What investigation?" Lilith echoed, flat and sharp in the same breath.
"I'll let Alexios fill you in on the details." Quinlan's smile gave back nothing at all.
"He's really sending us away..." Void confirmed to no one, and burrowed deeper into her mount.
Lilith held the villain's gaze for a moment longer, searching it for a game and finding only that pleasant, infuriating calm. Then she turned on her heel. "Lilies. We're leaving."
A new [Warp Gate] bloomed open at the garden's edge before she finished the sentence, the grey stone of the Vraven capital waiting beyond it.
She was three steps from it when Quinlan spoke again.
"Lilith Ravenshade."
There was no tea in his voice anymore. She stopped.
"I told you about this investigation as a courtesy, not so you could meddle with it."

He didn't elaborate, and he didn't need to. The warning arrived whole: whatever the crown's diggers found under her family's name, if she buried it, redirected it, or warned a single Ravenshade cousin of what was coming, there would be no conversation afterward. There would be no afterward at all.
Lilith scoffed without turning around.
"I became an adventurer for a reason. I won't shield scum." She resumed walking. "Family or not."
Scar raised one knuckle to the mouthline of her mask and produced a pointed, artificial little cough, her eyes traveling from Lilith to Morgana and back, slow as evidence being entered.
The message was clear.
'Are you sure you're not shielding scum, family or not? After all, you shielded your cunt of a sister.'
Lilith's middle finger came up at her former scout without her stride breaking once.
Scar's eyes danced.
Bronnya barked a laugh and hauled Void through the seam. Jallen offered the terrace a parting nod and followed. The Scarlet Lilies left like they did everything, fast and without ceremony.
Scar remained, watching the gate close.
"Master." Her voice had gone quiet. "Did you see?"
"See what? That your good friend of four centuries flipped you off?"
"...No, that's nothing overly shocking. She's the Orc Boss, after all."
"Ah, understandable. Then what?" Quinlan asked, instantly accepting the explanation.

"They walked into your portal without hesitation," she murmured, keeping her eyes on the empty air where it had been. "No one checked the far side or asked where it truly led. All that instinct they built to survive, and not one of them thought to doubt it." A pause. "They trust you."
She said the last part softly, the way she reported nothing else.
Quinlan looked at the spot too, and his smile changed shape, losing its performance. "...Yeah. You might be right."
Then he turned, and the warmth went right back into costume.
"Morgana."
The Queen of Vraven regarded him with a perfect poker face.

"Go with your sister. Help the investigation. Your knowledge of the duchy might expedite the process." He smiled, benevolent as a temple mural. "And spend some time with your sister while you're at it. You've earned that much."
'You shameless, scheming, silver-tongued fraud,' Morgana thought.

She knew exactly what she was being handed. He would be behind her eyes whenever it pleased him, watching the crown's investigators from a chair in his own garden or wherever he decided to stroll that day, and he had wrapped the leash in so much generosity that refusing it would make her the ungrateful one.
The most galling part, the part she cursed him for with real venom, was that the kindness wasn't even false, just free. It cost him nothing to be gracious, so he was, the way rain fell.
'May every gate you open deposit you in a latrine, you insufferable primordial con art-'
"Morgana dear," Seraphiel said pleasantly, buttering a fresh slice of bread, "kindly stop cursing our man inside your head."
"I was doing no such thing."
Her left eye twitched, once.

The Queen of Vraven said nothing further. Loudly. Then she walked through the reopened gate with her chin at an angle that dared anyone present to comment, and the villain's garden was two Ravenshades lighter.
"She's warming up to you," Seraphiel decided.
"Mm," Quinlan agreed. "Practically family."
<Baby~> Lucille's voice arrived on the family channel. <We're ready whenever you are. No rush. Whenever's convenient. It's really not a big deal.>
Quinlan's grin spread as he flicked the next gate open toward the inn. It was, by his count, the least convincing sentence his Bloodmonger had produced in her entire life.
She couldn't wait a single extra second, despite whatever nonsense her delicate lips spouted.
Lucille's request had gone out on the harem chat, also known as [Master's Link], not too long ago, and the channel had rendered its verdict instantly.

Serika had signed on before Lucille finished the second sentence. Blossom had answered at a frequency that made Lucille wince before she giggled joyously. Kitsara had received the words 'best behavior' before she managed to say anything at all, and was still sulking about the presumption on principle.
<I hadn't even said anything yet,> the fox had protested.
<Preemptive,> Lucille had replied, sweet and immovable.
Now the hunting party stood assembled on the lawn in full kit, polished to a shine no casual monster cull had ever warranted, because it mattered to Lucille, and therefore it mattered.
The gate's surface rippled, and Lucille stepped through with her axe on her back, her hammer at her hip, and her daughter's hand in hers.
