chapters.title: Chapter 1816 Time to Depart
paragraphs: Mavena made it two steps before the world caught up with her. The inn's bread-and-hearth air had swapped for open garden in a single stride, her stomach arrived a half-second behind the rest of her, and she stopped dead, knuckles whitening on the straps of her pack while her eyes tried to be everywhere at once.
"That's..." Her voice came out younger than she'd have liked. She cleared it and tried again, aiming for professional. "Portals are normal for you now. Okay. Noted."

The pack deserved its own introduction. It towered over her shoulders, expedition-grade, bedroll and coiled rope and two full rows of potion loops, provisions for a fortnight strapped to a hunt scheduled to end by lunch. She had packed it herself and refused all commentary at the inn, reportedly.
Lyra stepped forward and offered one hand for it, a silent, practical courtesy aimed at the girl.
Mavena stepped back and gripped the straps harder. "I'm the supporter." Her chin came up, daring the Juggernaut to argue. "Supporters carry the team's equipment. Mom told me so!"
Apparently someone decided being a pack mule was the most important mission of her life.
Lucille watched her daughter plant her feet in front of the Juggernaut who could bench the inn, and pride swelled through her chest, warm and fierce.

Months of hiding half of herself behind a plain dress, wondering what her girl would think if she ever saw the axe in action, and here Mavena stood instead, strapped into a ridiculous pack, demanding to be useful in her mother's world.
Lucille had imagined this going a hundred ways, but not one of them had felt this good.
"Mavena smells like warm bread," Blossom smiled, sniffing. "Blossom approves!"
"Uh... I'm glad...?" Mavena murmured, shy and confused.
"Alright, recruit." Serika cracked her knuckles, grin blazing. "Stay behind us, holler if you see anything move, and watch how your mom works. That last part's the whole trip, honestly."

Kitsara drifted closer, visibly wrestling with her entire personality. Her mouth opened. Lucille's eyebrow rose. The fox's mouth closed, reconsidered from the ground up, and finally produced, straining like she was lifting a wagon:
"What a... wonderfully practical bag."
"Thank you," Mavena said warily.
Quinlan flicked the next gate open onto pine forest and mountain air, the woods beyond already whispering with things that would deeply regret being nested near a trade road.
"Try to leave some of the valley standing," he offered.
"No promises, baby." Lucille kissed his cheek in passing.

"...Baby? I know he's younger, but... Ugh..." Mavena mouthed, scandalized to her bones, and was still processing it when Serika steered her through the gate by the top of her pack, the rest of the hunting party flowing after them into the trees.
The seam closed on Blossom's happy tail wag.
The garden had one departure left in it.

By Rosie's tree, the five handmaidens slept on in the moss where devotion had felled them, and Emily was already directing a detachment of maids among the roots with blankets, stepping around flower crowns with professional respect.
Rosie sat among the roots with her feet swinging, watching the maids work, and giggled.
"They tried very hard." She pointed at the nearest casualty, whose fingers were still tangled in a half-finished flower crown. "She was last."

Isveth knelt beside the dryad princess with Myrasyn a step behind, and bowed her head toward Quinlan across the garden. "Thank you for allowing us to stay the night with her, Holy Son. It was a true blessing." The thanks came out in the register she usually reserved for scripture.
Then Rosie looked toward the duo.
"Can Rosie come with you?"
Two sets of long elven ears went straight up.
Isveth leaned forward. "Can you? Your tree..."
"Rosie's roots go very, very far now." Rosie kicked her feet once, demonstrating their independence from any root system. "And Rosie has become very strong."

She flexed one small green arm. The bicep that appeared was purely theoretical, the arm wobbled with the effort, and the effect was devastating. "So the tree can't hold Rosie back anymore. She can go wherever she wants in the whole of Iskaris!" A factual pause. "She just can't call on her powers if she's too far away."
Then all three of them turned to Quinlan, and three sets of pleading eyes landed on the terrace like a diplomatic incident in the making.
Quinlan took a long sip of his tea.
"Why not." He tapped a finger against the rim. "You've been a well-mannered young lady recently. You've earned a vacation."
Rosie beamed. Myrasyn and Isveth beamed harder.

Then, with the unanimity of two people who had spent centuries making decisions at speed, both elves arrived at the same conclusion: if Rosie could not call upon the tree at range, she would need their help. Their protection. Their constant, devoted attention for every step of the journey.
Rosie could walk perfectly well without the tree. She had legs and balance and had been using both since before either of these women had learned her name. She did not correct them.
On the terrace, Seraphiel watched the whole performance over her teacup with sparkling eyes. Kaelira looked on with warm recognition; she knew craftsmanship when she saw it.
"Little one." Myrasyn knelt before Rosie, as formally as if protocol demanded it. "Would you allow me to carry you? Without your tree's support, the journey may tire you."
Rosie put a finger to her chin. She tilted her head to the left. Then to the right. Her brows drew together as though weighing a matter of considerable state importance.
"...Okay," she decided at last, generous beyond measure. "You may carry me."
Myrasyn's whole face lit up, ears and all, and the four-thousand-year-old monarch rose from her knees beaming so hard that her composure never stood a chance.

Small green hands settled on the queen's shoulders, little legs found their seats on either side of Myrasyn's neck, and Rosie took her throne with fingers sinking happily into lush blonde hair. The Queen of the Elves adjusted her passenger with the gravity of a coronation.
"Tomorrow," Isveth said, to no one and to everyone, "is my turn."
"The schedule has not been finalized," Myrasyn replied while refusing to meet the shrine maiden's gaze.
"Bottomless greed is what brought down Elvardia. Don't follow in its footsteps!" Isveth screeched, outraged.
Seraphiel arrived back from the house dressed for travel with luggage enough for a diplomatic mission, none of which, she explained, anyone was permitted to question.
Kaelira came last with a single neat pack and hovered half a step closer to Quinlan than usual, violet eyes fixed somewhere south of the horizon they were about to cross.

Quinlan looked over his traveling party. His daughter, mounted and smug about it. His first elf, smugger about the itinerary. His smith, quietly bracing to see her homeland again from the other side of a verdict. The elven queen and the elven faith's leader, both still wearing last night under their eyes.
"Well then." The day's last gate tore open, tall and wide, its far side breathing cool forest air into the garden. "Let's go claim a nation."

sentences.text: Mavena made it two steps before the world caught up with her.

The inn's bread-and-hearth air had swapped for open garden in a single stride, her stomach arrived a half-second behind the rest of her, and she stopped dead, knuckles whitening on the straps of her pack while her eyes tried to be everywhere at once.
"That's..." Her voice came out younger than she'd have liked.
She cleared it and tried again, aiming for professional.
"Portals are normal for you now.
Okay.
Noted."
The pack deserved its own introduction.
It towered over her shoulders, expedition-grade, bedroll and coiled rope and two full rows of potion loops, provisions for a fortnight strapped to a hunt scheduled to end by lunch.
She had packed it herself and refused all commentary at the inn, reportedly.
Lyra stepped forward and offered one hand for it, a silent, practical courtesy aimed at the girl.
Mavena stepped back and gripped the straps harder.
"I'm the supporter." Her chin came up, daring the Juggernaut to argue.
"Supporters carry the team's equipment.
Mom told me so!"
Apparently someone decided being a pack mule was the most important mission of her life.
Lucille watched her daughter plant her feet in front of the Juggernaut who could bench the inn, and pride swelled through her chest, warm and fierce.

Months of hiding half of herself behind a plain dress, wondering what her girl would think if she ever saw the axe in action, and here Mavena stood instead, strapped into a ridiculous pack, demanding to be useful in her mother's world.
Lucille had imagined this going a hundred ways, but not one of them had felt this good.
"Mavena smells like warm bread," Blossom smiled, sniffing.
"Blossom approves!"
I'm glad...?" Mavena murmured, shy and confused.
"Alright, recruit." Serika cracked her knuckles, grin blazing.
"Stay behind us, holler if you see anything move, and watch how your mom works.
That last part's the whole trip, honestly."
Kitsara drifted closer, visibly wrestling with her entire personality.
Her mouth opened.
Lucille's eyebrow rose.
The fox's mouth closed, reconsidered from the ground up, and finally produced, straining like she was lifting a wagon:
"What a... wonderfully practical bag."
"Thank you," Mavena said warily.
Quinlan flicked the next gate open onto pine forest and mountain air, the woods beyond already whispering with things that would deeply regret being nested near a trade road.
"Try to leave some of the valley standing," he offered.
"No promises, baby." Lucille kissed his cheek in passing.
"...Baby?
I know he's younger, but...

Ugh..." Mavena mouthed, scandalized to her bones, and was still processing it when Serika steered her through the gate by the top of her pack, the rest of the hunting party flowing after them into the trees.
The seam closed on Blossom's happy tail wag.
The garden had one departure left in it.

By Rosie's tree, the five handmaidens slept on in the moss where devotion had felled them, and Emily was already directing a detachment of maids among the roots with blankets, stepping around flower crowns with professional respect.
Rosie sat among the roots with her feet swinging, watching the maids work, and giggled.
"They tried very hard." She pointed at the nearest casualty, whose fingers were still tangled in a half-finished flower crown.
"She was last."
Isveth knelt beside the dryad princess with Myrasyn a step behind, and bowed her head toward Quinlan across the garden.
"Thank you for allowing us to stay the night with her, Holy Son.
It was a true blessing." The thanks came out in the register she usually reserved for scripture.
Then Rosie looked toward the duo.
"Can Rosie come with you?"
Two sets of long elven ears went straight up.
Isveth leaned forward.
"Can you?
Your tree..."
"Rosie's roots go very, very far now." Rosie kicked her feet once, demonstrating their independence from any root system.
"And Rosie has become very strong."
She flexed one small green arm.
The bicep that appeared was purely theoretical, the arm wobbled with the effort, and the effect was devastating.
"So the tree can't hold Rosie back anymore.
She can go wherever she wants in the whole of Iskaris!" A factual pause.
"She just can't call on her powers if she's too far away."
Then all three of them turned to Quinlan, and three sets of pleading eyes landed on the terrace like a diplomatic incident in the making.
Quinlan took a long sip of his tea.
"Why not." He tapped a finger against the rim.
"You've been a well-mannered young lady recently.
You've earned a vacation."
Rosie beamed.
Myrasyn and Isveth beamed harder.

Then, with the unanimity of two people who had spent centuries making decisions at speed, both elves arrived at the same conclusion: if Rosie could not call upon the tree at range, she would need their help.
Their protection.
Their constant, devoted attention for every step of the journey.
Rosie could walk perfectly well without the tree.
She had legs and balance and had been using both since before either of these women had learned her name.
She did not correct them.
On the terrace, Seraphiel watched the whole performance over her teacup with sparkling eyes.
Kaelira looked on with warm recognition; she knew craftsmanship when she saw it.
"Little one." Myrasyn knelt before Rosie, as formally as if protocol demanded it.
"Would you allow me to carry you?
Without your tree's support, the journey may tire you."
Rosie put a finger to her chin.
She tilted her head to the left.
Then to the right.
Her brows drew together as though weighing a matter of considerable state importance.
"...Okay," she decided at last, generous beyond measure.
"You may carry me."
Myrasyn's whole face lit up, ears and all, and the four-thousand-year-old monarch rose from her knees beaming so hard that her composure never stood a chance.
Small green hands settled on the queen's shoulders, little legs found their seats on either side of Myrasyn's neck, and Rosie took her throne with fingers sinking happily into lush blonde hair.
The Queen of the Elves adjusted her passenger with the gravity of a coronation.
"Tomorrow," Isveth said, to no one and to everyone, "is my turn."
"The schedule has not been finalized," Myrasyn replied while refusing to meet the shrine maiden's gaze.
"Bottomless greed is what brought down Elvardia.
Don't follow in its footsteps!" Isveth screeched, outraged.
Seraphiel arrived back from the house dressed for travel with luggage enough for a diplomatic mission, none of which, she explained, anyone was permitted to question.
Kaelira came last with a single neat pack and hovered half a step closer to Quinlan than usual, violet eyes fixed somewhere south of the horizon they were about to cross.
Quinlan looked over his traveling party.
His daughter, mounted and smug about it.
His first elf, smugger about the itinerary.
His smith, quietly bracing to see her homeland again from the other side of a verdict.
The elven queen and the elven faith's leader, both still wearing last night under their eyes.
"Well then." The day's last gate tore open, tall and wide, its far side breathing cool forest air into the garden.
"Let's go claim a nation."

chapters.title: Chapter 1817 Into Luminareth
paragraphs: The gate opened at the forest's edge, and Luminareth was already there.
The city had no walls and no skyline.
It had a forest so vast it filled the horizon, and every tree in it was alive with civilization.

Walkways of living wood connected trunk to trunk in a web that stretched for miles, buildings growing from the bark at every level, their walls half-timber and half-tree, windows catching morning light.

Bridges arced between canopy heights in curves no architect had drawn, because the wood had been asked, and the wood had agreed. At ground level, elves tended crops between the roots and berry-gatherers worked the understory with baskets on their backs. Above, spires of shaped heartwood rose through the canopy where the sunlight hit first.
The whole of it breathed with the patience of millennia.
Rosie leaned forward over Myrasyn's head, fingers tightening in blonde hair, and stared.
"Wow..." she breathed.
Seraphiel stepped through the gate behind him and stopped in her tracks, blue eyes wide and shining.
"Quin..." She seized his arm. "It's beautiful."
"...Yeah."
It truly was a breathtaking sight, the gem of elven civilization.

Seraphiel was tracking every bridge, every spire, every building growing from the bark, and her usual cheeky composure had been replaced by undisguised wonder. "I heard many tales, but they don't do it justice..."
Kaelira came through last, and went quiet.

Her violet eyes traced the grown architecture from root to crown with the stillness she brought to masterwork inspection, the kind of silence that meant she was learning faster than words could keep up.
"What marvelous architecture..."
But before the newcomers could keep gawking, two elven guards stepped from behind the nearest trunk in pale armor, planting themselves in the road.

Their eyes went to Quinlan first. A human male, two meters tall, radiating a signature that made trained soldiers reconsider career choices. Then to Seraphiel and Kaelira, elves traveling in his company, which raised different questions. Then to the two disheveled women leading the group, one carrying a small green child on her shoulders, and the questions stopped fitting into categories entirely.
"State your business," the taller guard said, hand settling near her blade. Her eyes kept drifting to Rosie.
"My business," Myrasyn said, through twenty hours of visible exhaustion, "is to enter my own capital."

The guard blinked. Her partner leaned in. They studied the woman in the wrinkled dress, the ruined braids, the general air of having recently lost a fight with a hedge, and searched for the Queen of the Elves in there somewhere.
"...Your Majesty?"
"Present and accounted for," Isveth confirmed beside her, in a shrine maiden dress that had creases in places creases should not exist.
"Head Maiden?!"
Both guards snapped to attention, hands to their chests in salute to Myrasyn, then to Isveth. The taller one was already turning to call for an escort.
"That won't be necessary." Myrasyn adjusted Rosie on her shoulders. "We'll walk."
"Your Majesty-"
"I'm sure of it, yes," the queen repeated, and started forward. "Thank you for your hard work."
The guards parted, ears perking as the praise reached them.
One glanced at Rosie, who offered a small wave. "Hello, pretty guard lady!"
"G-greetings, child..." The guard waved back before catching herself and snapping to attention, and her partner's mouth twitched.
The city received them with more than staring.

Elves filled the walkways at every level, and the first reactions were predictable enough: the queen's ruined braids drew double-takes, Rosie's green skin drew pointing, and the two-meter human drew the kind of cautious attention that large predators earned in public spaces.
But as the group moved deeper along the main thoroughfare, something else began.
A merchant sorting berries on the nearest walkway turned toward Quinlan with quiet reverence, one hand drifting to her chest, eyes going glassy.
Behind her, an older elf tending a window garden froze mid-planting, eyes gone distant, and forgot the trowel in her hand.

A pair of young elves on a bridge overhead leaned over the railing, and one pressed both hands to her mouth. The other grabbed her friend's arm and whispered something that made both of them bow their heads without deciding to.
But these actions weren't aimed at Myrasyn or Isveth. Not even Rosie, Quinlan realized.
An old elf on a root-bench dipped her head as he passed. A shopkeeper stepped from her doorway, froze, and slowly sank to one knee with her fist pressed over her heart.
He hadn't taken a single drop from the Requiem before walking through the gate.
He should appear as a large and overly handsome human, yes, he reasoned, but...
Why do they react like that to a human in casual clothes strolling through an elven capital?
They should be standing at attention, preparing for conflict. Yet the elves were responding to him like he'd carried the spring in with him.
"What's going on?"

Seraphiel noticed because Seraphiel always noticed when women reacted to her man. She hooked her arm through his, blue eyes bright with interest. "Quin~ We're on a business trip... You know that, right?"
"How can you blame me? I have done nothing."
"Their ears go low when you pass," Kaelira said from his other side, quiet and focused. "They're being pulled toward you."
"They all feel the same thing," Rosie observed from atop Myrasyn's shoulders, chin propped on the queen's crown. "Warm."
Quinlan turned toward Isveth and Myrasyn, who walked half a step ahead. Both had been watching the citizens' reactions, and when they glanced back, neither looked confused.
They looked proud.

"You've consumed several drops from the Requiem over recent days, Holy Son," Isveth said, and her voice dropped into the low, reverent register she kept for matters of the faith. "Their effects seem to linger..."
Myrasyn shifted Rosie's weight on her shoulders, and her smile went soft.

"When you take a drop, we feel the First Elf's screaming declaration of her love for you." The queen's gaze moved across the walkways, across the citizens who kept turning toward the human in their midst like flowers following a light they could not name. "Now it has become her soft, constant embrace. Quieter, but no less real."
Quinlan watched the merchant still pressing her hand to her chest, and the old elf who had gone back to her planting with wet cheeks, and let the information settle.
His mother. Still reaching for him through whatever she'd left in his bones.
'...Damn. To think she really cares this deep about me... I mean, I always knew, but...'
Seeing the extent of her motherly affection for her adoptive son was overbearing sometimes, but far be it from Quinlan to reject her love.
He said nothing, and they kept walking.
As they did, Myrasyn's exhaustion began losing ground to something else entirely. She pointed toward a cluster of spires rising through the canopy on the group's left.
"The High Arbors." Pride crept into her voice like sunlight through leaves. "Every trunk in that grove is said to have been planted before the first human kingdom drew its borders."
"Every one?" Seraphiel craned her neck.

"Every one." The queen pointed again, toward a bridge that arced between two enormous trunks in a curve that seemed to ignore weight entirely. "That bridge was grown in a single season, forty thousand years ago. It has never been repaired. The wood remembers the shape it was asked to hold."
"Forty thousand..." Kaelira whispered, and her hand twitched toward the nearest bark.

"The roots go deeper than any hole dwarves dig to hide," Isveth added, and the shrine maiden's pride was quieter than the queen's but no less present. "Every structure you see is still part of a living tree. The trees give form, and we give purpose. Neither one owns the other."
"So the whole city is alive?" Rosie bounced once on Myrasyn's shoulders. "Like Rosie's tree?"
"Your tree is far too unique for me to say yes, little one." Myrasyn smiled up at her passenger. "But these trees are the pride of my people."
Rosie considered this with appropriate gravity, then nodded. "Rosie approves. The trees are gorgeous and Rosie senses how happy they are!"

Myrasyn held her chin up through it all, composure stitched together by will alone, though the effect was slightly undercut by the dryad princess using her head as a viewing platform and the human beside her making elves weep by doing nothing more strenuous than existing.
A polished shopfront ended the performance.

chapters.title: Chapter 1818 Pure Terror
paragraphs: A polished shopfront ended the performance.
The queen caught her own reflection in the glass and stopped dead. The image staring back at her told a tale of pure terror.
Isveth walked into the same reflection a step later.
Silence.
"Myrasyn." Isveth's voice went very quiet. "How long have we been walking through the capital looking like this?"
"Since the gate."
"And you didn't think to check?"
"I thought I looked fine!" The queen's hiss could have cut glass. "You didn't say anything either!"
"I was looking at you all night! I got used to it!"
"So did I!"
They stared at each other, then at the window, then at the gathering crowd of elven citizens who had been watching their queen parade through the capital looking like she'd slept through a hurricane.
Then their eyes found Quinlan.
"Why did you say nothing...?" Myrasyn muttered, dissatisfied.
Quinlan shrugged in response. "You two look cute."
"C-cute?!" The duo shuddered in perfectly scandalized sync.
With strong blushes, both of them decided he was just messing with them.
What happened next was the fastest exercise of royal authority Quinlan had seen.
"You." Myrasyn pointed at the nearest shopkeeper. "Point us toward the closest salon."

Directions were provided at speed. Both elves were moving before the sentence finished, and the salon - grown into the side of an enormous trunk, all curved wood and soft light - never stood a chance.
Myrasyn swept through the door with Rosie still on her shoulders and Isveth at her flank, and the salon's quiet morning shattered on contact.

The lead stylist had been mid-sentence with a client when the Queen of the Elves materialized in her doorway looking like she'd been dragged through a forest backward, and the woman's hands simply stopped.
The comb she was holding clattered to the counter. Around her, every stylist in the room turned, recognized, and went pale in the same breath.
"Y-Your Majesty...?"
"Please tend to us," Myrasyn said.

Despite the queen making no demands, existing appointments had been abandoned with stammered apologies within seconds. Chairs had been vacated at speeds that suggested the occupants feared for their lives, and both the Queen of the Elves and Isveth were seated before adjacent mirrors.

The remaining stylists divided between them with the frantic coordination of soldiers redeploying under fire, several of them still visibly trembling as they reached for combs and pins and the finest oils on the shelf, the ones they saved for occasions that never actually came.
This occasion had come, and it had brought the dryad princess.
"Rosie too!!" Rosie announced from Myrasyn's lap.

The stylists looked at the tiny green girl, at each other, and at their queen, and after a nod from Myrasyn, two of them peeled off to attend to her with hands that shook from reverence as much as nerves.
Rosie took to the chair like she'd been waiting for this her entire life, which at her age was not especially long but had been packed with relevant opinions.
"Up," she instructed.
The stylist gathered a section of hair and lifted.
"No. More up."
Higher.
"Now make it go sideways but also down."

The stylist's hands stopped. She looked at her colleague, who offered nothing. She looked at the queen, who was mid-braid and could not save her. She looked back at the dryad princess, who waited, patient, certain her instructions had been perfectly clear.
"...Like a waterfall, Your Highness?"
"No. Like a tree."
"Which... part of a tree, Your Highness?"
"The pretty part."
The stylist's fingers slowed to careful, measured strokes, and Rosie supervised each one with an intensity that made the queen's lead stylist look relaxed by comparison.
"Softer."
"Yes, Your Highness."
"But also stronger."
"...Yes, Your Highness."
Seraphiel observed the proceedings with growing interest, then turned to Quinlan.
"It's for research," she declared.
"I didn't say anything."
"You were going to." She was already being seated. "Elven styling is a matter of scholarly curiosity. I'll be documenting the experience."
"Enjoy yourself, Sera."
"Hehe~"
Quinlan settled into a chair by the window with a view of the whole operation, and Kaelira sat beside him, straight-backed and quiet, her hands on her knees.
"You didn't want to join?" He nodded toward the mirrors.
"I asked Anna and Beatrice last night." She touched her hair. "The twins handled it. Does it look... is it bad?"
Quinlan reached over and ran his fingers through the bluish-purple strands. Kaelira's eyes went wide, but she didn't pull away, and her long ears twitched once.
"They did a fantastic job," he said.
Kaelira's smile was small and real. "...Glad you like it."
From his chair, Quinlan had a front-row seat to the finest display of elven professionalism he'd ever witnessed.

The lead stylist was rebuilding Myrasyn's braids from the roots up, fingers moving with extreme speed. She was good. He could tell because the queen's reflection was improving in real time, and because the stylist's long ears kept angling toward Myrasyn's face to check for approval.
"That braid work is nice," Quinlan said, to nobody in particular.
The stylist's ears perked straight up. So did Myrasyn's. So did both of Isveth's stylists'. So did the three attending Rosie.
Every elf in the room went to attention at the same moment, and Quinlan's inner voice sat up.
"The left section could use some more work, though."
Every ear wilted.
He looked at Kaelira. Her violet eyes were already tracking the phenomenon, because she missed nothing that moved with that kind of precision.
Not just queens and shrine maidens, then. Species-wide.
What happened next, he would later maintain, was science.

"Good. Very good." Every ear in the salon, save for members of the Elysiar gang, rose. "Hmm. Wait." They froze at the apex. "No, I had it right the first time, that's lovely." Ears crested, blushes bloomed across a dozen elven faces. "Although..." Down they came, trembling at the tips. "No. Perfect." Up.
The entire salon rose and fell to his tempo, and Quinlan conducted with deep, quiet joy. He had discovered that every elf was an instrument, and he was sitting in the middle of an orchestra.
"Quin... They're going to faint at this rate..." Kaelira said beside him.
"Eh? But I'm just offering my sincere opinion."
"..." A certain tomboy elf with perfect abs didn't buy his bullshit for some odd reason.
But after only three minutes of messing with the overly expressive elves, the novelty of it wore off and, while his victims reeled from the bullying, his gaze found something curious.

The salon shelves held the things elves crafted instead of metalwork: hair ornaments woven from preserved leaves, pins of shaped bark, necklaces strung with polished seedpods and flowers set in amber resin. The materials sat in trays along the counter, fine and delicate and distinctly not metal.
Quinlan picked up a half-finished piece and turned it in his fingers. "Can you work with these?"

Kaelira glanced at the tray. "Those are for decorative elven craft, placed there so those waiting can do something. But this kind of nature-craft is done by elven females and males you'd probably categorize as females knowing you..."
"Hey, I'm nice to everyone. Far be it from me to be rude to effeminate elven twinks."
"..." Kaelira sent him a look full of judgment. "Anyhow, that's not my thing."
"Fair enough." He set it down. "Apologies for the assumption. Sera's actually pretty good with this kind of thing, she made some beautiful pieces. Thought all elves were good at it..."
Kaelira's ears went rigid.
Her eyes snapped to the tray, to the materials, to the weaving tools beside them, and the decision was never in doubt.
"...I didn't say I was bad at it. Give me those."

She pulled the tray toward her with both hands, and within seconds the smith who had dismissed nature-craft as not real forging was bent over a workstation with the same intensity she brought to tempering battle-grade steel. Her fingers moved through leaves and resin with the precision she reserved for runes, brow furrowed, lips pressed, the rest of the room gone.
She held a leaf to the light, rotated it, set it aside. "Structurally unsound." She reached for another tray.

Quinlan watched her work and made no effort to hide how much he was enjoying the view.

And around Quinlan's neck, resting against his collarbone, sat a necklace of woven leaves and polished seedpods in clean geometric lines, crafted by a smith who had poured every ounce of her competitive pride into proving that her hands could master anything.
Kaelira walked beside him and said nothing about it. But her ears were pink, eyes stealing glances to check how he looked, and her chin was up.

sentences.text: A polished shopfront ended the performance.
The queen caught her own reflection in the glass and stopped dead.
The image staring back at her told a tale of pure terror.
Isveth walked into the same reflection a step later.
Silence.
"Myrasyn." Isveth's voice went very quiet.
"How long have we been walking through the capital looking like this?"
"Since the gate."
"And you didn't think to check?"
"I thought I looked fine!" The queen's hiss could have cut glass.
"You didn't say anything either!"
"I was looking at you all night!
I got used to it!"
"So did I!"
They stared at each other, then at the window, then at the gathering crowd of elven citizens who had been watching their queen parade through the capital looking like she'd slept through a hurricane.
Then their eyes found Quinlan.
"Why did you say nothing...?" Myrasyn muttered, dissatisfied.
Quinlan shrugged in response.
"You two look cute."
"C-cute?!" The duo shuddered in perfectly scandalized sync.
With strong blushes, both of them decided he was just messing with them.
What happened next was the fastest exercise of royal authority Quinlan had seen.
"You." Myrasyn pointed at the nearest shopkeeper.
"Point us toward the closest salon."
Directions were provided at speed.
Both elves were moving before the sentence finished, and the salon - grown into the side of an enormous trunk, all curved wood and soft light - never stood a chance.
Myrasyn swept through the door with Rosie still on her shoulders and Isveth at her flank, and the salon's quiet morning shattered on contact.

The lead stylist had been mid-sentence with a client when the Queen of the Elves materialized in her doorway looking like she'd been dragged through a forest backward, and the woman's hands simply stopped.
The comb she was holding clattered to the counter.
Around her, every stylist in the room turned, recognized, and went pale in the same breath.
"Y-Your Majesty...?"
"Please tend to us," Myrasyn said.
Despite the queen making no demands, existing appointments had been abandoned with stammered apologies within seconds.
Chairs had been vacated at speeds that suggested the occupants feared for their lives, and both the Queen of the Elves and Isveth were seated before adjacent mirrors.

The remaining stylists divided between them with the frantic coordination of soldiers redeploying under fire, several of them still visibly trembling as they reached for combs and pins and the finest oils on the shelf, the ones they saved for occasions that never actually came.
This occasion had come, and it had brought the dryad princess.
"Rosie too!!" Rosie announced from Myrasyn's lap.

The stylists looked at the tiny green girl, at each other, and at their queen, and after a nod from Myrasyn, two of them peeled off to attend to her with hands that shook from reverence as much as nerves.
Rosie took to the chair like she'd been waiting for this her entire life, which at her age was not especially long but had been packed with relevant opinions.
"Up," she instructed.
The stylist gathered a section of hair and lifted.
"No.
More up."
Higher.
"Now make it go sideways but also down."
The stylist's hands stopped.
She looked at her colleague, who offered nothing.
She looked at the queen, who was mid-braid and could not save her.
She looked back at the dryad princess, who waited, patient, certain her instructions had been perfectly clear.
"...Like a waterfall, Your Highness?"
"No.
Like a tree."
"Which... part of a tree, Your Highness?"
"The pretty part."
The stylist's fingers slowed to careful, measured strokes, and Rosie supervised each one with an intensity that made the queen's lead stylist look relaxed by comparison.
"Softer."
"Yes, Your Highness."
"But also stronger."
"...Yes, Your Highness."
Seraphiel observed the proceedings with growing interest, then turned to Quinlan.
"It's for research," she declared.
"I didn't say anything."
"You were going to." She was already being seated.
"Elven styling is a matter of scholarly curiosity.
I'll be documenting the experience."
"Enjoy yourself, Sera."
"Hehe~"
Quinlan settled into a chair by the window with a view of the whole operation, and Kaelira sat beside him, straight-backed and quiet, her hands on her knees.
"You didn't want to join?" He nodded toward the mirrors.
"I asked Anna and Beatrice last night." She touched her hair.
"The twins handled it.
Does it look... is it bad?"
Quinlan reached over and ran his fingers through the bluish-purple strands.
Kaelira's eyes went wide, but she didn't pull away, and her long ears twitched once.
"They did a fantastic job," he said.
Kaelira's smile was small and real.
"...Glad you like it."
From his chair, Quinlan had a front-row seat to the finest display of elven professionalism he'd ever witnessed.
The lead stylist was rebuilding Myrasyn's braids from the roots up, fingers moving with extreme speed.
She was good.
He could tell because the queen's reflection was improving in real time, and because the stylist's long ears kept angling toward Myrasyn's face to check for approval.
"That braid work is nice," Quinlan said, to nobody in particular.
The stylist's ears perked straight up.
So did Myrasyn's.
So did both of Isveth's stylists'.
So did the three attending Rosie.
Every elf in the room went to attention at the same moment, and Quinlan's inner voice sat up.
"The left section could use some more work, though."
Every ear wilted.
He looked at Kaelira.
Her violet eyes were already tracking the phenomenon, because she missed nothing that moved with that kind of precision.
Not just queens and shrine maidens, then.
Species-wide.
What happened next, he would later maintain, was science.
"Good.
Very good." Every ear in the salon, save for members of the Elysiar gang, rose.
"Hmm.
Wait." They froze at the apex.
"No, I had it right the first time, that's lovely." Ears crested, blushes bloomed across a dozen elven faces.
"Although..." Down they came, trembling at the tips.
"No.
Perfect." Up.
The entire salon rose and fell to his tempo, and Quinlan conducted with deep, quiet joy.
He had discovered that every elf was an instrument, and he was sitting in the middle of an orchestra.
"Quin...
They're going to faint at this rate..." Kaelira said beside him.
"Eh?
But I'm just offering my sincere opinion."
"..." A certain tomboy elf with perfect abs didn't buy his bullshit for some odd reason.

chapters.title: Chapter 1819 Royal Welcome
paragraphs: The palace of Luminareth had been grown, not built, and it wanted every visitor to understand the difference.

Myrasyn led them up the last living stair with her fresh crown of braids and her restored dignity, and the moment her foot touched the palace terrace, horns of shaped heartwood sang out across the canopy.
Two full columns of royal guards stood in polished pale armor along the approach, ears high, spears grounded in perfect unison.

"Announcing Her Majesty, Myrasyn, Queen of the Elves!" a herald called from the terrace steps. "And her honored guests! The Son of the First Elf, Beloved of the Requiem, Conqueror of the Continent, Quinlan Elysiar! The Granddaughter of the First Elf and Princess of the Eternal Tree, Rosie Elysiar! Lady Seraphiel and Lady Kaelira of the Holy Son's family! Head Maiden Isveth of the Faith!"

The herald had clearly been coached, and very recently: no elven registry on the continent contained half of those titles. They weren't even true, at least as far as conqueror of the continent went. Someone was piling on extra flair for their guest.

And Quinlan knew exactly where the flair had come from. On their way to the palace grounds, Myrasyn had hurriedly pulled a soldier aside without breaking stride, whispered something behind her hand, and sent the woman sprinting ahead like the fate of the realm depended on it.
Mystery solved.

Rosie, perched on the queen's shoulders with tiny flowers threaded through her curls, waved at the assembled guards, chin lifted, reviewing them like she owned every spear in the column. Several spears dipped out of formation before their owners caught themselves.

Beneath her passenger, Myrasyn was stealing a glance at him. Sideways, quick, gone again, a queen absolutely not checking whether her arrangements had landed, ears angled his way and betraying the entire operation.
Quinlan reached over and patted the Queen of the Elves on her fresh crown of braids, right between his daughter's dangling feet.

The terrace stopped breathing. A tray rattled somewhere among the maids, one guard's spear clattered on the ground, and down both columns, discipline fought raw jealousy to a standstill in a hundred elven hearts.
Their queen. Patted. Like a village girl.
"My mother's descendants truly know how to impress," he grinned.
"T-this much is merely proper hospitality," the queen replied, cheeks blooming, making no attempt whatsoever to escape the hand.
The herald visibly fought for her composure and won by a hair.
The welcome that followed involved more bowing staff than Quinlan could count, under a ceiling of woven canopy that filtered the morning into green-gold panes.

Refreshments arrived in the hands of maids who shook exactly as much as the salon stylists had. The Holy Son's effect on the citizenry had not weakened one bit after stepping through the palace grounds, and word of his walk through the capital had clearly beaten them to the palace.
Then a whole gang of stewards appeared at the queen's elbow with a stack of scrolls, and the morning's warmth died a bureaucratic death.
The Queen of the Elves looked at her palace, her canopy ceiling, her assembled staff, and accepted her fate.
"How long will all that important nation business take~?" Seraphiel asked sweetly.
Myrasyn looked at the cheeky elf. The cheeky elf looked back, all innocence.
The queen understood precisely what was being asked.
"...You will likely have a day of free time," she grumbled.
Two sets of elven ears perked at once. Kaelira's rose in a way she would have denied, and Seraphiel's practically vibrated.
"However." Myrasyn raised one royal finger. "You are guests of my crown, in my capital, and I refuse to let anything happen to any of you. You will have an escort."
She turned to the guard columns. "Elowen. Step forward."
A guard detached herself from the nearest column and crossed the terrace at parade pace. "Your Majesty."
"You will accompany the Holy Son's family today. Their safety, their comfort, and their satisfaction are your charge. Guard them with your life."
"With my life, Your Majesty." Elowen's fist pressed harder against her breastplate. She turned and bowed to Quinlan next, deep and precise. "Holy Son. It is the honor of my bloodline."
Quinlan merely nodded back, smiling lightly as he accepted the words.

"Then it's settled." Myrasyn began peeling Rosie off her shoulders like she was defusing a live bomb, misery already creeping back into her face. A whole day of the dryad princess, lost to policy making.
Rosie, dangling mid-transfer, made her decision.
"Rosie wants to come."
Everything stopped.
"...Come?" Myrasyn repeated. "Little one, it's just paperwork."

"Rosie wants to see how queens do it." The little girl's eyes were shining with purpose. "Rosie's roots hold a very large land now... Soon the entire continent. She should learn how ruling works, so she can do it properly and help her Daddy!"
Silence held for a heartbeat.

Then two of the most powerful women of the elven world lit up like sunrise. The queen's misery evaporated so fast it should have left a sound. Isveth's hands came together in front of her lips, and a slow, reverent breath left her.
"She wishes to learn governance," the Head Maiden whispered. "The Holy Granddaughter wishes to learn governance at our side."
"We will show you everything," Myrasyn promised, resettling Rosie on her shoulders with the reverence of a coronation. "The lawbook, the ledgers, the petitions..."
"Yaay!"

Quinlan watched his daughter get carried off toward a full day of elven bureaucracy, waving over the queen's crown braids at him, thrilled about spreadsheets, and elected not to warn her that she'd hate her life five minutes in.
Some lessons you had to forge yourself.
"Daddy!! Rosie will learn everything so Mommy Jasmine can ask her for guidance!"
"Good luck," he called back, and quickly made a solemn prayer for the girl inwardly.
The council doors of living wood swallowed queen, maiden, and princess whole.
Elowen had a plan.
She walked half a step ahead of her charges through the palace gardens with her spine straight and her purpose clear, laying it out with the crispness of a morning briefing.
"If you have a location you desire to witness, we shall go there. But if you don't, I have the perfect itinerary already assembled."

She began listing just like that: "The High Arbors first, while the light is eastern. Then the Weaverbloom district, the finest boutiques and craft-halls in the capital. The forest promenade at midday, and I have taken the liberty of arranging a canopy luncheon-"
"We're going to the royal smithy," Quinlan interrupted.
Elowen's itinerary died mid-sentence. Her stride, to her credit, only faltered for half a step. "The... forgive me, Holy Son. The royal smithy?"
"Mm."

"There is no royal smithy in Luminareth. Metalwork is a filthy..." Her eyes moved to Kaelira, caught themselves, and moved back. "The only royal smithy is the dwarven one. In the dwarven capital. Under the mountains."
"That's the one."
Elowen stopped walking entirely.

"Holy Son. The dwarven capital is a sovereign... Considering the current circumstances, they'll attack us on sight..." She started over. "The passage of an elven royal escort into dwarven territory requires diplomatic clearance, formal notice, a negotiated route, and by rights several months of..."
"Yeah. That's why we're not asking anyone for permission."

Sera patted the guard on the pauldron in passing, sympathetic, and kept strolling with her arm hooked through Quinlan's. Kaelira, meanwhile, had gone very still on his other side, violet eyes wide and shining.
The royal dwarven smithy. The forges she'd read about under a blanket as a girl, in books that were themselves contraband.
"Quin," she said, quiet and tight, the words clipped short to keep the eagerness from spilling over. "Don't joke about this. I thought we'd wait for Myrasyn to make the arrangements..."
"I'd never make a joke like that at your expense," he smiled, then added, "I've made my own arrangements." He raised the Soul Reaper, and the morning filled with pale fire.
"You prepared?!" Kaelira's eyes widened. He knew she'd want to visit and he did that for her...?
"[Awaken]."
They came out of the saber itself, moving as if they'd been standing there all along and the world had only now caught up.

Three dwarves in riven war-plate, their edges wrapped in ghostly pale flames, their eyes calm points of the same cold light. The one at their head wore a commander's mantle over his shattered cuirass, his beard bound in iron rings, a war-axe resting easy across his back.
Elowen's sword cleared its sheath before her mind caught up with her hand, and then stopped, because her mind had caught up with her hand.
"Master," the commander said. His voice came from somewhere deeper than his chest, gravel over old coals.
"As discussed, I want to see the royal smithy without being attacked."
"Yes, Master."
"This is an invasion," Elowen said faintly, to nobody. "I am escorting an invasion."
"Think of it as a field trip," Quinlan grinned, already following the dead toward the roots of the city.
The entrance lay beneath Luminareth's oldest quarter, down stairs that wound between roots thicker than towers, where the living wood gave way by degrees to worked stone.

The transition was gradual and then absolute: one turn wrapped in the warm smell of sap and green things, the next standing in cool mineral dark, elven curves surrendering to dwarven angles, the ceiling suddenly carved in interlocking geometric bands that repeated with fanatic precision.
The first ward-door stood where the deep road proper began: a slab of black stone the size of a house wall, its face carved with a single dwarven rune and brimmed with dormant power.
This was the kind of barrier that armies broke themselves against.
Thorgar walked to it and laid his dead hand flat against the rune.

chapters.title: Chapter 1820 Through the Secret Passages
paragraphs: The ward tasted his oath, found it good, and the black slab swung inward on silent hinges, a hundred tonnes moving like a garden gate.
"That should not have worked," Elowen said. Her voice had gone up half an octave since the palace. "The wards are keyed to the... Oh..."
The deep road ran wide and true, its floor grooved smooth by cart wheels, cold lamps of dwarven make still burning a patient blue along the walls.

Twice the wide way ended in purposeful ruin, whole junctions dropped with engineering precision, and twice Thorgar turned without pausing into narrower passages faced in royal seal-stone, patrol routes built for crown business alone, untouched.
"They dropped the trade roads..." Elowen whispered, running her eyes over the sheared rock. "They prepared for this. So how..."

"They prepared for everything within their reach," the dead general replied, the same flat verdict he'd once handed green recruits. "Every gate a living dwarf ever held a key to must've been re-keyed already. But the crown's own passages take the king's oath to re-key." A stretch of gravel silence. "They don't have one. Coronating a new ruler will take three days at the least."
The final battle lay only a couple dozen hours behind the mountain.

With its military crippled and its capital in chaos, manning every forgotten patrol route was beyond the dwarven nation's current strength. The few patrols that did wander near were never met: Quinlan read their footsteps through the stone with his earth magic from a truly unfair distance, and strolled his party down whichever fork stood empty.
The traps were the greater danger, and the dead were the answer to those too.
Ward-glyphs slept in the seal-stone, pressure-seams waited under a year of dust, listening-runes lay strung to wake a barracks at the wrong tread.
But the three who walked point had known where most were located, and the few hastily added defenses were read without failure.

Just like that, they passed under the roots of the elven nation and into the bones of the mountain that the dwarves had made their capital all those years ago, when the alliance was formed. The migration to the previously empty mountain had been the gesture of the dwarven king who ruled at the time, made toward his wife, the elf queen he loved.
Somewhere past the fourth door, the air changed. Warmer. Mineral. Smoke and hot metal.
Kaelira's breath went shallow.

Sound arrived next, distant and rhythmic through the stone, a heartbeat of hammers that grew with every step. Then light: a red-gold glow bleeding around the last turning of the road, the color of industry, the color of a working forge multiplied by hundreds.
"The royal smithy of Elvardia," Thorgar said. "Well, I suppose I should call it the smithy of the dwarven people now..."
After all, Myrasyn had already declared she considered the Elvardian Alliance null and void before the entire Elvardian army.
The hall was a cathedral built for fire.

It dropped three tiers into the mountain and climbed five in vaults overhead, and every level of it worked. Forge-hearths stood in ranked rows like organ pipes, chimney-shafts drawing their smoke up through channels cut in the living rock, water racing in stone troughs between anvil stations.

Hundreds of dwarves moved through the red-gold light with the unconscious choreography of people who had done this their whole lives, and the sound of it all, hammers, bellows, steam, and shouted measurements, filled the vaults like weather.
The sealed door in the hall's east wall had not opened in over a year.
It opened now.
"The east door...?" someone said from a middle tier, over the groan of hinges no one had duty to oil anymore. "That's the crown's door!"
Then the dead walked in, and the hall received its answer.

A hammer stopped mid-swing. Then a row of them. The silence spread outward across the hall the way frost spreads over glass, tier by tier, station by station, until the last bellows sighed out and the only sound left was the fires themselves.
"...General Thorgar?"

An old master near the east door said it. His beard was ash-grey and bound in the clasps of fifty years of rank, and the hammer in his hand sagged like it had suddenly remembered its own weight. "Thorgar Emberhold. They sang our defeat yesterday..."
"They sang true, Dain," Thorgar said.
Grief moved across the old master's face, silent and total.

Around him, the word spread in whispers: the general, the general's ghost, the pale fire. Somewhere on the second tier, a young smith made a sound like a swallowed sob. Every dwarf in the royal smithy knew that armor, and every dwarf in the royal smithy could see the cold flame wearing it.
Then Quinlan stepped through the door, and the temperature of the hall's fear changed.
There was no herald this time, and none was needed.
A human two meters tall, in the company of elves, walking out of a sealed door with the honored dead at his heel.

The description had crossed the mountain long before the final battle took place, carried by survivors of his sieges into dwarven forts: the Primordial Villain. The one the elves called Holy Son. The one who had ended a war, a kingship, and the world's old order in a single week.
Hammers came up across the hall the way a man grabs a railing when the floor tilts, hands finding the only solid thing they knew.
Masters stepped in front of apprentices. Apprentices, with the suicidal loyalty of the young, tried to step in front of their masters and were held.
And the dread came down on all of them.
He wasn't doing anything. That was the horror of it.
He was just standing there, looking up at the vaulted tiers with mild interest, and the pressure of his existence rolled off him anyway, filling the hall the way deep water fills lungs.

The forge-heat thinned around him like the fires themselves were paying attention. On the nearest tier, a journeyman's legs quit without permission and dropped him onto a bench. A pair of tongs slipped from someone's grip and rang against the stone, obscenely loud, and nobody so much as glanced at it.
Old Dain locked his knees and stayed upright by pure spite, and it cost him everything he had.
"Stand down." Thorgar's voice rolled across the silence, flat as a shield wall. "All of you. Stand down and hear me."
"You serve him," someone said from the tiers, half accusation, half prayer. "General, you... you of all dwarves..."

"The war is over. Dwarven hegemony is over." The dead commander's pale eyes swept the hall he'd once guarded. "We lost it, and not by any margin or stroke of fortune. We lost it the way a candle loses to winter, and I know, because I stood in the worst of it and it killed me."

His voice never rose and never fell. "The king who spent your sons and daughters sits frozen in his own failure and answers for it. That debt is his, and he pays it alone. Do not add your names to the list of people who drove the Villain to a cruel revenge like that. It's over. So let it be over and make the most of it."
The hall took that the way a body takes a blow it can't return.
"He came here without an army," Thorgar went on, quieter. "Take a breath, and understand what that means. If he wanted this mountain broken, you would not have heard a door open."

Elowen chose that moment to step through the door behind her charges, take up an escort position at the Holy Son's flank, and level upon the assembled population of the royal smithy a look of such crystalline elven condescension that several dwarves physically braced.

Here it was, the look said. The conqueror who was worshipped at elven altars, with elven ladies on his arms and an elven guard at his side, come down at last to their holiest hall. Every rumor they'd heard of his favor of their race over the dwarven one stood confirmed in a single tableau.
The smiths waited for it. The sneer, the decree, the boot.
Quinlan finished his survey of the vaults, the tiered forges, the chimney-shafts breathing up through the mountain's bones, and pointed at the great ranked hearths of the lowest tier.
"Twin-hearth stacks on a shared flue," he said. "How are you holding temper on the far hearths?"
Silence.

chapters.title: Chapter 1821 Silent Hall
paragraphs: "Twin-hearth stacks on a shared flue," he said. "How are you holding temper on the far hearths?"
Silence.
A different flavor of it this time: three hundred craftsmen simultaneously failing to process a sentence.

A dwarf came forward through it. She was built like the anvils she ruled, forearms as thick as the tongs racked behind her, iron-grey hair twisted back in a smith's knot and singed at the temples where a smith's hair always singed.

The masters made way for her without needing to look, which said everything about who she was, and she planted herself a spear's length from the most dangerous being on the continent with her chin out.
"Brokk," she said. "First Hammer of the royal smithy. If you've come with terms, Villain, say them plain and say them to me."
"I haven't come with terms. My elven lover is interested in your smithy, and frankly, so am I."
The First Hammer stared at him, then at Kaelira, who seemed completely checked out of the conversation, taking in the vast compound with mesmerized eyes.

"...Baffle-gates," she replied to his question slowly, feeling for the trap she was sure hid somewhere in the question. "Every third stack. The draw balances itself, if your gate-smith knows her work."
"Self-balancing." Quinlan's eyebrows went up, and he looked back at the hearth-row with honest appreciation. "The whole row breathes as one system. Wonderful."
"...Aye," Brokk said. "It is."

And she had no idea, none at all, what to do with the fact that the big bad evil, the one the dwarven high nobility swore would bring down their entire race should he win, had just praised their setup.
It became, against every instinct the royal smithy possessed, a tour.
Nobody declared it one. It simply happened, one question at a time, the way a frozen river breaks up: first a crack, then a groan, then the whole surface moving.

Quinlan asked about the water-troughs and got a grudging answer. He asked about the crucible steel and got a longer one. He asked about the quench-oil blends, and a master on the second tier, forgetting himself entirely, shouted down the answer, and then went white as his own beard when the hall turned to look at him.
The apprentices broke first, as the young always did.

Dread has a short shelf life at that age, and curiosity has none at all. They began accumulating along the rails of the upper tiers, in doorways, behind pillar and post, watching the impossible thing below: the conqueror walking their hall, asking about flux ratios.
Not every face on the rails thawed. On the second tier a young master named Vorn stood planted, arms locked over his chest, watching his colleagues forget themselves one answered question at a time.
The smith who'd raised him from his first nail had marched out with the army and hadn't marched back. Let the whole hall warm itself around the invader if it wanted. He intended to remember.

It was then Kaelira spoke up. She'd stopped before a squat, riveted machine crouched beside the third-tier forges, all pistons and countersunk gearing, and circled it twice with her brow furrowing deeper on each pass. "Quin. What is this?"
"You know that all my smithing knowledge comes from that old bastard and you, so..." He shrugged, shameless. "We're standing in a hall full of professionals. Let's ask one."

The nearest professional was a stocky master with copper wire braided through his beard, who had been eavesdropping from a respectful five paces and froze solid when the overly curious elf turned and looked at him expectantly.
"You build it?"

"I... aye. It's a drawing bench. Wire-work, for inlay." The master glanced at his colleagues for rescue and found none, and then a force older than his fear took over, because his hands were already moving to the crank. "Easier shown than said. Here. Watch the guide-screw..."

The hall watched the heretic elf and the Conqueror bend over the bench together, watched their own master forget who he was talking to somewhere around the third turn of the crank. And the last of the frost went out of the royal smithy without anyone marking the moment it left.
"You know smithing," Brokk said at one point. It landed as an accusation.

"Just a bit. My smithing partner is the real deal, though." He nodded at Kaelira, proudly grinning. "She does the real work. I just do finishing enchants, so I've picked up enough to know what I'm looking at. Enough to know this hall is the best thing this continent has to offer for smiths."
Brokk's mouth opened, reconsidered several responses, and settled on a grunt that failed to disguise itself as indifference. "Right on..."
Two rows later, Quinlan went quiet in the middle of somebody's answer about bloom furnaces.

He drifted off mid-sentence, crossed to the hearth-stack against the wall, and laid both palms flat on the stone. Then he simply stood there, silent, eyes closed, listening with his hands. The draw ran smooth under his palms, a warm even pull deep in the stack, until two feet in it snagged on something cold and wrong.
The row's noise died around him one gulp at a time.
The channel-master of that row had given half her life to the channels behind that stone, and soot had worked so deep into her knuckles it no longer washed out.

She watched the thing the high nobility swore would tear down every dwarven work standing lay his hands flat on her life's work, and the dread the hall had spent the last hour letting go of found her again, all at once.
"G-get your hands off my flue, Villain!" She stomped despite all her survival senses screaming at her. Her colleagues, Brokk included, looked like she'd just signed her death warrant.
"That flue's cracked." Quinlan's eyes stayed closed. "Third channel in, two spans up. It's bleeding your draw into the rock."
"H-huh?" The channel master's overwhelming sense of dread and panic turned into condescension from one moment to the next. "With all due respect, Villain, there's no crack in my channels."
"There is."
"There is not."
"Yes."
"No."
"Okay," Quinlan shrugged, moving on. "If you care so little, then it can't be helped."
"???" The channel-master looked ready to lunge at the man who sported the greatest audacity of them all.
Her? Not caring???
Heresy!
"Open it up!" she shouted, eyes narrowed.

Her assistants did just that, opening the inspection plate to humor him. The hall listened to the channel-master clamber up into the shaft, heard the scrape of her measuring hook against the stone, and then heard nothing at all for a long moment.
"...Lamps." Her voice came back down the shaft muffled and entirely changed. "Lamps and a mortar-lad. Now. NOW!"
The row detonated into activity, and Brokk stood in the middle of it without moving, looking at the creature who had just read a hairline fault through two feet of her mountain with his bare hands.
"How," the First Hammer demanded of the universe at large.
"Magic," Quinlan grinned as he took his palms off the stone and wandered on toward the next row.

Brokk watched him go, knowing there was more to it. She had numerous geomancer-types who could read the earth, but not one of them ever came close to this level. He displayed such an unnatural level of affinity for their element that every single dwarf took a collective breath, silence reigning supreme.

High in the shaft, the shouting for mortar had stopped. The channel-master had pushed the plate wide instead, and stared down at the Villain's back with open respect, the kind she'd given maybe three dwarves in her whole life.
Sera, for her part, had appointed herself exactly one duty, and it was hanging off Quinlan's left arm being luminously content.
His right hand, meanwhile, belonged to Kaelira between stations, reclaimed without looking each time she finished touching something.
The topic interested Sera not at all. The topics could have been discussed in gibberish and she'd have kept the same warm, content smile.

She watched her lover and best friend geek out, Kaelira coming out of her shy elf shell and blossoming into the overly enthusiastic master smith she was, while Quinlan went on a generational run of subverting expectations.
Elowen was having a harder day.
"Holy Son, please do not stand so close to the... Holy Son, that is an active forge. Holy Son, the soot, your clothing..." Her protests fell like arrows on armor.
Around her, dwarves kept doing the thing she found most disorienting of all: relaxing.

She had entered this hall as the haughtiest thing in it, and the hall was steadily forgetting to be terrified. Watching dwarven apprentices creep close enough to eavesdrop on her Holy Son's opinions about crucible steel was quietly unmaking assumptions she'd carried since childhood.
And through all of it, Kaelira burned.

She'd held herself together through the first tier on discipline alone, but the smithy kept happening to her. The gravity-fed coke hoppers. The water-troughs' triple gates. The anvils, entire dynasties of anvils, each one worn to a silk polish by ten generations of hands.
She moved from station to station with her fingers hovering just off every surface, asking questions in a voice that kept losing its calm, and the dwarves watched her.
Quinlan clocked it early, and said nothing, and kept watching.
They weren't glaring. That was the thing.
An elf stood in the royal smithy of the dwarves, in the holiest hall of the craft her people had been legally barred from for centuries, and the masters watching her didn't wear disgust.
They wore something closer to hunger. A knot of them had drifted in her wake for a full tier now, elbowing each other at the way she handled a set of tongs.
It was at the billet racks that she stopped them all cold.

"Lamps and a mortar-lad.
Now.
NOW!"
The row detonated into activity, and Brokk stood in the middle of it without moving, looking at the creature who had just read a hairline fault through two feet of her mountain with his bare hands.
"How," the First Hammer demanded of the universe at large.
"Magic," Quinlan grinned as he took his palms off the stone and wandered on toward the next row.
Brokk watched him go, knowing there was more to it.
She had numerous geomancer-types who could read the earth, but not one of them ever came close to this level.
He displayed such an unnatural level of affinity for their element that every single dwarf took a collective breath, silence reigning supreme.
High in the shaft, the shouting for mortar had stopped.
The channel-master had pushed the plate wide instead, and stared down at the Villain's back with open respect, the kind she'd given maybe three dwarves in her whole life.
Sera, for her part, had appointed herself exactly one duty, and it was hanging off Quinlan's left arm being luminously content.
His right hand, meanwhile, belonged to Kaelira between stations, reclaimed without looking each time she finished touching something.
The topic interested Sera not at all.
The topics could have been discussed in gibberish and she'd have kept the same warm, content smile.

She watched her lover and best friend geek out, Kaelira coming out of her shy elf shell and blossoming into the overly enthusiastic master smith she was, while Quinlan went on a generational run of subverting expectations.
Elowen was having a harder day.
"Holy Son, please do not stand so close to the...
Holy Son, that is an active forge.
Holy Son, the soot, your clothing..." Her protests fell like arrows on armor.
Around her, dwarves kept doing the thing she found most disorienting of all: relaxing.
She had entered this hall as the haughtiest thing in it, and the hall was steadily forgetting to be terrified.
Watching dwarven apprentices creep close enough to eavesdrop on her Holy Son's opinions about crucible steel was quietly unmaking assumptions she'd carried since childhood.
And through all of it, Kaelira burned.
She'd held herself together through the first tier on discipline alone, but the smithy kept happening to her.
The gravity-fed coke hoppers.
The water-troughs' triple gates.
The anvils, entire dynasties of anvils, each one worn to a silk polish by ten generations of hands.
She moved from station to station with her fingers hovering just off every surface, asking questions in a voice that kept losing its calm, and the dwarves watched her.
Quinlan clocked it early, and said nothing, and kept watching.
They weren't glaring.
That was the thing.
An elf stood in the royal smithy of the dwarves, in the holiest hall of the craft her people had been legally barred from for centuries, and the masters watching her didn't wear disgust.
They wore something closer to hunger.
A knot of them had drifted in her wake for a full tier now, elbowing each other at the way she handled a set of tongs.
It was at the billet racks that she stopped them all cold.

chapters.title: Chapter 1822 Truth of the Dwarven Smiths
paragraphs: She'd asked leave of the master whose work it was with a look and received a mute nod, and the watching knot waited for her to lift the folded billet and tilt it against the light, the way any smith on the continent would.
Instead, she brought it up beside her ear, closed her eyes, and flicked the edge with her fingernail.
*Tiiing...*

The dwarves traded glances over their beards. She flicked it again, lower down, head tilting, long elven ears angling toward the steel like it had started talking, and the muttering around her died into baffled silence.
"Sixty-four folds," she said, eyes still shut. "And every weld is clean. How, at this size?"

The master whose billet it was stared at her, then down at the tally-marks punched into the billet's end, sixty-four, by his own hand, and forgot entirely to be afraid of her. "Hydraulic hammer for the first thirty." He glanced at Brokk. Brokk did not rescue him. "...The rest by hand. Lass. The rest by hand."
"Would you show me the hammer?"
He showed her the hammer. Of course he showed her the hammer.
The hall, however, was no longer looking at hammers. An apprentice hanging over the third-tier rail went round-eyed and lost her running battle with protocol.
"You listened?! How?!"
Her master cuffed the back of her head on principle, growled about manners in front of guests, and then turned back to Kaelira and waited for the answer along with everyone else.

"Every weld line is a string," Kaelira said, most of her attention already on the hydraulic hammer. "Strike the edge and they all sound together. Clean welds ring in tune. A cold shut buzzes against the rest. You quiet yourself and count the voices." She glanced up, found some three hundred dwarves staring at her, and misread it completely. "...I couldn't hammer-test anything in a hidden forge. The neighbors would have reported the noise. Listening was the only test I could afford."C
Nobody said a word.

They tested steel by striking it, by breaking a corner off, by biting an edge in acid and reading the scar. Proud, loud, honest methods that had served the mountain since the first forge was lit, and not one dwarf in this hall or any other had ever thought to ask the steel quietly and let it answer. A dwarven forge hall had never once in its existence been quiet enough to try.
And even if they had...
'Is this a natural advantage of an elven smith?' they wondered.
Somewhere along the tier above, a hammer-butt knocked twice against an anvil's horn, and a second answered from the stock racks, the same low double-knock, there and gone.
Elowen's head came up. 'They dare?!' she seethed inwardly.

She knew that sound. Every royal guard who had ever stood a post at an alliance ceremony knew it: the smith's salute, the knock the mountain's masters gave a masterwork at its unveiling, the highest courtesy their craft possessed. Dwarven envoys used to boast that kings waited whole reigns to hear it twice.
And they were giving it to the heretic elf and her Holy Son. Casually. In passing. As if the Son of the First Elf were some... colleague, to be appraised and found impressive.

Her fists found her hips. This was all wrong. These creatures were supposed to be in terror of him, on their faces before him, not grading him on their sooty little anvils, and the sheer presumption of it made her want to draw her sword on principle.
But nobody consulted her. The tour rolled on.
Kaelira, for her part, had certainly heard the knocks. She'd filed them as more smithy noise and gone back to the steel.
It was Brokk who finally said it out loud.

The First Hammer had been watching the heretic elf orbit her hall for the better part of an hour, her expression fossilized. When Kaelira leaned over an anvil to study its face, Brokk's eye caught on the woven necklace lying against Quinlan's collarbone where he leaned beside her. Leaves, seedpods, resin. Forest trash, by every dwarven standard that mattered.
Arranged in interlocking geometric bands that repeated with fanatic precision.
"Whose work is that?" Brokk demanded.
"Mine," Kaelira said, straightening to her full height, braced by ancient habit for the verdict.
Brokk looked at the necklace for a long moment. Looked at Kaelira. Looked at the necklace.
"Good geometry," the First Hammer said. "Wasted on leaves."

It took Kaelira a visible second to understand she'd just been complimented and recruited in the same breath. The smile she fought down won anyway, and around the anvil several dwarven masters grinned into their beards at the sight.

"I don't understand you people," she said. The words came out before she could stop them. "Elvardian law states that elves who craft are criminals. I was sentenced to die in a conscript wave for owning a shabby forge, thanks to the law that only exists because you people wanted it." Her hands had closed at her sides. "So why are you looking at me like... like that? Why are you not disgusted?"

She parted her arms wide, and declared to the entire hall, "I'm an elf who loves smithing! I cherish it more than anything! My dream is to become the greatest smith ever, surpassing every single ancestor you have!"
"Hoho..." Multiple old dwarven eyes lit up with competitive fire upon hearing those sacrilegious words come from the elf's delicate lips.
But they were gazes of pure challenge.
Soon, however, the grins died. The hall's older silence came back, but changed, weighted now with a grievance much older than the war.
"We," Brokk said, and the word carried an ocean of contempt, "wrote nothing. Kings wrote it. Councilors wrote it."

She turned her head and spat, with great accuracy, into a slag channel. "You know what a smith is to the crown of the mountain, elf? A tradesman. A tool that feeds itself. There's never been a hammer at that council table, not in any meaningful capacity. Oh, some of them held a hammer once. Doesn't matter. A seat at that table turns a smith into a politician, and a politician counts.

"They count us like they count the anvils, and when they demanded your ban, they consulted us exactly as much as they consulted the anvils. Same with their war. It ran on our steel and it ran on our sons, and the first time the crown asked this hall what it thought of either was never."

"The ban was fear," old Dain said from his bench, quiet. "Their fear, never ours. You elves outlive us by thousands of years, and the crowns couldn't stomach what your hands might learn from ours in all that time. So they made sure your hands never got near."

"Aye..." another old smith nodded, grim. He looked at Kaelira, and his old eyes were wet and steady at once. "Girl, a smith would sooner ban kings. Half this hall spent its whole life wondering what elven hands would find in the metal, given the chance. And the law said we'd die before we ever saw it."
Kaelira stood very still in the red-gold light.

Quinlan watched the verdict she'd carried since her sentencing, the one she'd braced for at the gate, in the salon, in every elven street, the one that said what you are is a crime, come apart in the one hall where it should have been strongest.

All those years of hiding her hands, and the people whose law had hunted her had spent those same years wishing they could watch her work. The room that was supposed to hate her had been waiting for her.
Her eyes had gone bright, and her voice, when she found it, came out smaller than her shoulders. "...Given the chance," she repeated.
Then she turned, and the whole smithy watched the heretic elf's attention land on the stock racks of the lowest tier.
"Oi, lass..." the murmurs began.
Kaelira sent Quinlan a look, mischief all over her face. "Will you...?"
Quinlan's response was pulling his sleeves up. "Just a quick little piece."
"Yes!" she smiled, heart beating rapidly.
"Wait, what are you-" Elowen began, but was interrupted when the duo said together in perfect sync:
"We're crafting."
The elf's face scrunched just as hundreds of dwarven eyes shone as they leaned forward, curious.
It was time to show the royal smithy how a primordial and his elven lover went about the dwarf race's sacred craft!
