chapters.title: Chapter 1823 Display of Mastery
paragraphs: The stock racks of the royal smithy's lowest tier held everything the mountain worked with, and Kaelira walked their rows with three hundred dwarves tracking her every step.

What stopped her sat in the open, because down here it didn't need guarding: a short rack standing apart from all the others, holding a handful of metals that drank the forge-light and gave nothing back. She drifted toward it with the tour forgotten, and when her fingers stopped a polite distance from the nearest core, Brokk answered before she could speak.

"Adamantite. Raw cores, unrefined." The First Hammer's voice took on the flat tone of an old wound. "The best of our mines only give up a ton of it in a good decade, and the crown reserves every gram, by the same council that counts anvils. A master petitions for the right to attempt a working the way you'd petition for a duchy. Old Dain there has asked the crown every year for the last twenty years."
"Twenty two," Dain corrected, from his bench.
"It is the rarest of metals..." Kaelira's fingers hadn't moved. Neither had her eyes. "Parts of Quin's armor are made from adamantite."

"Oh...?" Brokk raised an eyebrow. "So you know how to wield it... Since you're about to show us what you can do, why don't you take some? It's not like the king or the council will punish us now, will they?"
"Nope," Quinlan confirmed. "They won't."
"..." Those words sat funny with quite a few listeners. It meant they lost the war and their conqueror made it clear the old powers no longer had the authority they used to, but it also meant that...
The greedy fuckers on the council no longer had the authority they needed to force them into using their talents for unreasonable requests.

"So, Kaelira?" Quinlan asked nonchalantly, picking up a hefty ore and tossing it high into the air. A hundred dwarves went wide-eyed, resisting the collective urge to lunge at the metal and protect it with their very bodies.
"Is this what you'd like to use?" he finished, catching the ore without difficulty.
The words brought the smithy to a standstill all over again.
Brokk had offered it herself, but this... This was the rarest metal on Iskaris. He showed zero humility and even took the offering from the dwarf to make it himself.

He said it the way he'd offer fruit from his own orchard, already turning to look for where the crucible tongs were racked, and the sheer, breathtaking entitlement of it rippled up the tiers in real time. Crown-reserved adamantite, handed to an elf, in front of three hundred dwarves...
But nobody stopped him. That was the point, and everyone understood it at once. Nobody could.
'The whole mountain is his now, as far as he's concerned,' Brokk thought as the giant rolled his shoulders loose. 'His entire body language screams it.'
It should have enraged her. She'd expected, when she finally met the mountain's new master, to grovel or to burn. She had not expected him to hand out the crown's treasury like table bread.
And the elf refused it.

Kaelira stood before the rack that held her people's every written dream about the deep metals, hand hovering an inch from a core of raw adamantite, and the hall watched her want it with her whole body. Then her fingers curled closed on nothing, and dropped back to her side, and she stepped away.
"Not today," she said. "I promised you that it'd be a quick little session."
Quinlan set the core back on its rack with a small smile, and three hundred dwarves quietly started breathing again.

She walked past the crown's rack, past the orichalcum stock and the coiled mithril drawing-wire, down to the common racks where the hall's daily working steel lived, and began flicking her fingernail along the bars.
*Tiing. Tiing. Tonk.*
She pulled one out.
The murmurs started on the second tier and died of confusion halfway down, because nobody could build a sentence out of what they were watching.
The elf had been handed the mountain's holiest rack, and she was down in the cheap stock, choosing hearth-steel by ear like a housewife thumping melons at a market stall.
Two bars of plain hearth-steel.

A length of old cart-spring iron, the kind apprentices ruined their first punches on. And a single dark bar of starforged steel, the meteor-metal the hall kept for mid-grade commissions, the only thing in her arms worth more than a good dinner.

One bar she flicked, frowned at, and slid back with a click of her tongue. Later that night, a master would pull that bar out, cut it open, and find the cold shut hiding at its heart, and would sit alone with the discovery for a long time.
Quinlan, meanwhile, was done with his shirt.

He never touched a button. The weave stirred against his shoulders like something waking from a nap, poured down his arms and chest in one silken sheet, and gathered itself around his neck as a plain grey work towel, because [Synchra] had been listening and knew forge work when she heard it coming.
The Primordial Villain stood in the red-gold light of the royal smithy in nothing above the waist but the towel and a necklace of woven leaves, two meters of scarred, sculpted primordial physique.

"Holy Son!" Elowen's cry cracked across the hall. She had been holding her composure with both hands for what felt like an eternity in this dusty, smelly, heated place meant for filthy midgets, and this was the blow it broke on. "What are you... that is LABOR! Forge work! There is soot, there are sparks, it is beneath you, you are the Holy Son of the First Elf, nobles do not..." Her voice achieved a pitch that made two apprentices wince. "Your hands!"
"I'm afraid my hands are a lot dirtier than you presume."
"N-no, that..." Her protest sailed on, but the hall had gone deaf to it, because the upper tiers were having a crisis of their own.

The female half of them hit the railings as one, three tiers of apprentices and more than one master leaning out over the drop for a better angle. On the third tier a rail groaned in honest warning as an apprentice went half over it and had to be hauled back by her apron strings.
The male half saluted the shirt.

A hammer-butt knocked twice against an anvil's horn, then a second answered from the racks, the smith's salute offered in perfect sincerity to a garment, to the shirt that had cleared itself off the instant real work came calling.
"Now that," an old master declared to the tiers at large, sooty eyes wet with feeling, "is clothing made for real men."
Brokk looked at Elowen's stricken face and smiled for the first time since the sealed door had opened, slow and deeply satisfied.

"Dirty hands are what legends are made with, lass," the First Hammer said. "Sit your delicate little butt down and be a good girl, okay? Pay attention to your Holy Son instead of screeching. I have the feeling you'll learn something interesting about him today..."
"Hah?! Watch what you say, you dirty little-"
"Sit," Quinlan spoke up all of a sudden, his tone carrying zero tolerance for refusal.
Elowen sat down.
On a dwarven bench.
Without checking it for soot first, which by her standards constituted a spiritual crisis, but there were larger ones underway.
Kaelira had claimed a forge. The first bar went into the coals, and the shy, stiff-shouldered elf who had walked into the hall an hour ago disappeared, and the smith came out.
The population of the royal smithy of Elvardia arranged itself around one forge like a theater, masters in front, apprentices hanging off the rails, and the dead standing silent guard by the door.
She worked the hearth-steel alone first, breaking each bar down, driving the grain straight, and the muttering began on the second fold.
"She shortened her stroke."
"Watch the elbow. Watch the elbow. She felt the shear plane."
"Who taught her that? Her technique is unorthodox..."
"She's self taught, lass. That's the point. Were you even paying attention?"
"Umm... It's hard..." a young apprentice muttered bashfully, sending the shirtless giant a quick glance.

On the second tier, Vorn discovered his arms had come unlocked somewhere around the fourth fold. He locked them back. By the fifth they'd come loose again on their own, and this time they stayed that way.

As for the Primordial Villain, the conqueror, the terror of the age, the man Brokk had promised would teach Elowen something: he had stationed himself directly behind his smith lover, wrapped both arms around her from behind, spread his palms flat over the ridges of her abs, hooked his chin over her head, and settled in to watch her hammer, content as a dragon on a hoard and exactly as shameless.
The hall stared.

She pulled one out.
The murmurs started on the second tier and died of confusion halfway down, because nobody could build a sentence out of what they were watching.
The elf had been handed the mountain's holiest rack, and she was down in the cheap stock, choosing hearth-steel by ear like a housewife thumping melons at a market stall.
Two bars of plain hearth-steel.
A length of old cart-spring iron, the kind apprentices ruined their first punches on.
And a single dark bar of starforged steel, the meteor-metal the hall kept for mid-grade commissions, the only thing in her arms worth more than a good dinner.
One bar she flicked, frowned at, and slid back with a click of her tongue.
Later that night, a master would pull that bar out, cut it open, and find the cold shut hiding at its heart, and would sit alone with the discovery for a long time.
Quinlan, meanwhile, was done with his shirt.
He never touched a button.

The weave stirred against his shoulders like something waking from a nap, poured down his arms and chest in one silken sheet, and gathered itself around his neck as a plain grey work towel, because [Synchra] had been listening and knew forge work when she heard it coming.
The Primordial Villain stood in the red-gold light of the royal smithy in nothing above the waist but the towel and a necklace of woven leaves, two meters of scarred, sculpted primordial physique.
"Holy Son!" Elowen's cry cracked across the hall.
She had been holding her composure with both hands for what felt like an eternity in this dusty, smelly, heated place meant for filthy midgets, and this was the blow it broke on.
"What are you... that is LABOR!
Forge work!
There is soot, there are sparks, it is beneath you, you are the Holy Son of the First Elf, nobles do not..." Her voice achieved a pitch that made two apprentices wince.
"Your hands!"
"I'm afraid my hands are a lot dirtier than you presume."
"N-no, that..." Her protest sailed on, but the hall had gone deaf to it, because the upper tiers were having a crisis of their own.
The female half of them hit the railings as one, three tiers of apprentices and more than one master leaning out over the drop for a better angle.
On the third tier a rail groaned in honest warning as an apprentice went half over it and had to be hauled back by her apron strings.
The male half saluted the shirt.

A hammer-butt knocked twice against an anvil's horn, then a second answered from the racks, the smith's salute offered in perfect sincerity to a garment, to the shirt that had cleared itself off the instant real work came calling.
"Now that," an old master declared to the tiers at large, sooty eyes wet with feeling, "is clothing made for real men."
Brokk looked at Elowen's stricken face and smiled for the first time since the sealed door had opened, slow and deeply satisfied.
"Dirty hands are what legends are made with, lass," the First Hammer said.
"Sit your delicate little butt down and be a good girl, okay?
Pay attention to your Holy Son instead of screeching.
I have the feeling you'll learn something interesting about him today..."
"Hah?!
Watch what you say, you dirty little-"
"Sit," Quinlan spoke up all of a sudden, his tone carrying zero tolerance for refusal.
Elowen sat down.
On a dwarven bench.
Without checking it for soot first, which by her standards constituted a spiritual crisis, but there were larger ones underway.
Kaelira had claimed a forge.
The first bar went into the coals, and the shy, stiff-shouldered elf who had walked into the hall an hour ago disappeared, and the smith came out.
The population of the royal smithy of Elvardia arranged itself around one forge like a theater, masters in front, apprentices hanging off the rails, and the dead standing silent guard by the door.
She worked the hearth-steel alone first, breaking each bar down, driving the grain straight, and the muttering began on the second fold.
"She shortened her stroke."
"Watch the elbow.
Watch the elbow.
She felt the shear plane."
"Who taught her that?
Her technique is unorthodox..."
"She's self taught, lass.
That's the point.
Were you even paying attention?"
"Umm...
It's hard..." a young apprentice muttered bashfully, sending the shirtless giant a quick glance.
On the second tier, Vorn discovered his arms had come unlocked somewhere around the fourth fold.
He locked them back.
By the fifth they'd come loose again on their own, and this time they stayed that way.

As for the Primordial Villain, the conqueror, the terror of the age, the man Brokk had promised would teach Elowen something: he had stationed himself directly behind his smith lover, wrapped both arms around her from behind, spread his palms flat over the ridges of her abs, hooked his chin over her head, and settled in to watch her hammer, content as a dragon on a hoard and exactly as shameless.
The hall stared.

chapters.title: Chapter 1824 One Smith In Two Bodies
paragraphs: Kaelira didn't so much as break rhythm, as if fully used to it.

She drew, struck, folded, and turned with two meters of half-naked primordial hanging off her torso like the world's most decorated apron, and her only acknowledgment of him was leaning back into his chest a degree on the long draws.
'No, not only is she used to it... She prefers it!' many female apprentices squealed inwardly, suddenly feeling an overwhelming urge to try a certain unorthodox crafting style themselves.
"Is he..." a master began, scandalized on at least four separate levels.
"What in the Ancestors' name is he doing," Brokk said flatly.
"Charging up," Quinlan replied, not moving an inch. "It's part of the process."
"..." The First Hammer of the royal smithy opened her mouth, found nothing in the entire dwarven language up to the task, and closed it.

Up on the rails, an apprentice whispered the word "degenerate" with an awe usually reserved for scripture, and the hall's assessment of the Villain quietly rearranged itself once more: monster, war-ender, flue-listener, and now, apparently, a pervert.

"How are you feeling~?" Seraphiel purred, petting Elowen's lush hair with the most amused of grins. As someone who personally snuck close many times to witness this exact 'smithing style,' she was not one bit surprised.
Elowen was speechless, her big, expressive eyes closed and opened on repeat, but a healthy color soon reached her cheeks.
Then Kaelira reached the lamination.
Three metals, three tempers, one weld. The fool's errand.

Every master in the hall knew the arithmetic by heart: hearth-steel and cart-spring iron ran different fires, and starforged steel drank heat the other two couldn't survive. Fold them together and one of the three always cracked. Always.
It was why nobody folded them together, and why the hall leaned in, three tiers going still at once, as the elf reached for the impossible with her ears flat with focus.
The Villain moved.
No word passed between them. He came off her like a wave leaving a beach, and by the time her tongs touched the starforged bar, the bellows were already in his hands.
The draw quickened the instant her rhythm called for it and eased the moment the color turned.
"Is he taking instruction?" a master beside Brokk whispered, hunting for the mechanism. "Hand signs? Is it the ears? Elves do things with the ears, right?"
"He's not taking anything." Brokk's eyes narrowed on the pair. "Look closer. Nobody's leading."
"Look at the coal bed," an old voice said from the rails, gone hollow with disbelief. "He's banked it in steps. He's running three heats in one hearth and holding them apart by hand."
"That's not possible on one draw..."
"Well, he's doing it."
Brokk had drifted back to the forge's edge with a correction on her tongue, because coaching was involuntary for a First Hammer, and a smith attempting an impossible weld needed her colors called.
She never got a word out.

Three times she drew breath to call a temper, and three times the fire had already moved before the breath ended, the bellows easing or the coals banking at exactly the moment her centuries of experience demanded it, as if her correction had been heard before it was spoken. The third time, Brokk shut her mouth and hooked her thumbs in her belt.
"First Hammer?" the master beside her asked, quiet.
"I wanted to offer some dwarven knowledge but... they don't need me." It came out half diagnosis, half surrender.
It crept up on the hall after that, the thing unfolding in front of them, gradually and then all at once.
Kaelira's hand opened behind her, empty, and the flux was in it, because he'd started moving before she reached.

He turned the billet a half-beat before her hammer wanted the new face, and she struck the instant the tongs settled, no glance exchanged, no signal given, nothing for three hundred professionals to catch.

When she paused between folds to flick the steel and listen, the bellows froze mid-stroke, the whole forge holding its breath with her, and the moment the note satisfied her the fire was already climbing, because he'd read the verdict off the angle of her ears.
*Tiing... tiing...*
*WHAM.*
Masters elbowed each other. Apprentices forgot to blink. The rails filled with smiths hunting for the signal, the nod, the code the two of them had to be using, and they came up empty.

The two of them had stopped being two of anything. What stood at that forge was one craftsman occupying two bodies, a single mind that had split itself down the middle for efficiency and handed the hammer to one half and the fire to the other.
And the royal smithy of Elvardia, which had measured every partnership in its history against the benchmark of a master and their own two hands, watched the benchmark quietly change owners.

Somewhere in the crowd a hammer-butt knocked twice against an anvil's horn, and this time a dozen answered it, then more, the same low double-knock rolling around the tiers like slow thunder and refusing to die out.
On her bench, Elowen made a small, strangled sound. Kings waited whole reigns for that salute. The heretic elf at the forge was collecting it mid-fold.
Then the weld turned on her.

Three metals met. The masters nearest the forge saw the grain begin to argue with itself and made the collective sound of smiths watching a friend step off a cliff: the starforged steel was drinking the heat out of the seam faster than the iron could bear, exactly as every treatise promised.
"There it is. The crack's coming."
"It always cracks. Nothing holds those three together. Nothing ever has."
"Pull the iron, lass! Save your folds!"

Kaelira did not pull the iron. She planted her feet the way a tank plants them to take a lance charge, stopped asking the steel nicely, and under the soot on her smithing arm, thin lines of light woke and began to climb.
*WHAM!*

The blow landed wrong, and every master in the hall heard it: far too heavy for the stock, far too heavy for her, the kind of strike that should have torn the lamination open and scattered her folds across the floor. The billet did not tear. It compressed, the three layers driven into one another as if her hammer had brought the weight of a hillside down through her arm, and where the crawling light reached her grip, script no dwarf had ever read sank glowing into the steel.
"What... WHAT?!" Old Dain was on his feet.
"Runes! She's setting runes MID-STRIKE!"
"You inscribe after the shape! Everyone inscribes after the shape!"
"She's not inscribing, per se..." Brokk said slowly as the impossible weld closed blow by rune-weighted blow. "She's... persuading."

At the forge, low against Kaelira's stomach, Quinlan's mark ignited, shining through the soot-streaked linen with a deep crimson heat that owed nothing to the coals, and in the same breath an answering glow lit at the hollow of his chest, banked and steady, one hearth acknowledging another.
"WHAT IN THE GODDESS IS GOING ON?!" a dwarven master screamed, having fully lost his composure.

chapters.title: Chapter 1825 Showing Off
paragraphs: To the dwarves it read as forge-light. To the royal guard on the guests' bench, who had spent the whole day re-learning her Holy Son one impossibility at a time, it read as one more thing that would never fit in her report.
Quinlan felt the draw on the reservoir like a hand squeezing his heart, and approved of it completely, feeding the bellows while his smith pulled deep and struck true.
'Lucille and the others have already started topping it back off,' he mused, a small, private smile tugging at his mouth.
The weld closed. Clean. Somewhere in their shelves, several venerable treatises quietly became fiction, and the roar that went up shook soot from rafters that had kept their peace for generations.

Sweat ran down Kaelira's spine and gathered along the ridges of her abs, her shoulder-length hair sticking to her neck, violet eyes reflecting forge-light. She'd never in her life been more purely herself. The work sang under her hands like it had never once sung in the hidden forge she'd almost died for.
And her man worked the bellows for her.

That was the part the smithy would never stop talking about, long after the details of the folding blurred. The Conqueror of the Continent, half-naked and soot-streaked, sweat sheeting down a physique that belonged on a war monument, pumping the bellows of a mid-tier forge to a rhythm nobody had heard anyone give him.
He fed her coals, fetched her flux, held the billet steady for the punishing folds, and did it all with visible, shameless pride, watching his lover conquer a mountain of her own.

Elowen, on her bench, was no longer entirely certain what she believed about anything. The dread of him had drained out of the hall somewhere in the last hour, and what filled the vacancy had no precedent in her training. He was sweat and soot and monstrous ease, hauling a bellows-arm that took four dwarves on a normal shift, laughing at whatever the terrifying First Hammer growled.
Firelight moved over the muscles of his back like the light had opinions. Elowen realized she had been staring for some time, and made no move to stop.
Her posture melted by degrees from parade attention into something that belonged on a tavern bench. A dwarven apprentice offered her water. She drank it without checking it for anything.
"He is..." she began, to no one.

"Mm~ he is," Seraphiel agreed warmly, from right beside her, and Elowen jolted hard enough to slop the water. The Holy Son's first elf had settled onto the same bench at some point, chin propped on her palm, thoroughly enjoying both shows at once. "Terrible, isn't it? He does this everywhere we go. You spend an hour deciding what he is, and then he ruins your notes."
"I have no idea whatever you might be talking about," Elowen said, with enormous dignity, watching him wipe his forearm across his brow.
"Is that so~"

It was the question that finally pulled the First Hammer off the forge's edge. Brokk crossed to the guests' bench, planted herself in front of the lounging first elf with her arms folded, and asked it with the growl scraped down to honest bafflement.
"The crown's rack stood open to her. Adamantite. Cores no hammer alive has been granted, and she walked past them for hearth-steel and cart-spring iron." Her eyes never left the forge. "Why."

"What do you mean~? Kaeli already said it, weren't you paying attention?" Seraphiel's purring reached new heights, enjoying her role in this showoff. "Those two have a rule about the good stuff. The piece has to deserve the metal, and today's..." she gestured at the forge, at the sweat and the fire and the impossible weld, with the same lazy warmth she'd give a picnic spread, "...just a quick little piece to show off, basically. They don't spend adamantite on a souvenir."
Brokk stared at her.

Then she looked back at the forge, at the one craftsman in two bodies, at the lamination her hall's treatises called impossible, at the salute still rolling around the tiers, and did the math every master in earshot was doing whether they wanted to or not.
That was the doodle. Then what was them being serious?!
As if perfectly reading the dwarf's thoughts, Seraphiel pointed toward Quinlan with one dainty finger. "She is~"
Or, to be more specific, she was pointing at the towel soaking up sweat on her half-naked lover, the garment that was previously his armor.
"...Ancestors preserve us," the First Hammer said, with feeling, and went back to her post. Then she caught herself. "Wait, she?"
"She has too much personality to be a mere thing, so Quin decided Synchra was a female," Sera giggled.
"..." A hundred butts suddenly found the nearest seat, which, for many, turned out to be the ground itself.

The forging ran on for the better part of an hour. When the folding was done and the shape emerged, a hammer head, drift-punched and true, the layered grain of three humble metals flowing through its faces like current-lines in dark water, Kaelira laid the newborn craft down on the anvil's face with both hands, careful as a midwife, and squared it to the light.
Then she straightened, chest heaving, and tossed her own working hammer backward over her shoulder without so much as a glance. "Quin."
Quinlan was already there.
He plucked the tool out of the air mid-stride, and the hall understood the gesture at once, because it was a smith calling in her finisher.
What the hall did not understand was what he did next, which was give the venerable forge hammer a lazy flip.

Then another. Then a slow spin across the back of his hand, the tool of the sacred craft twirling like a street performer's baton as the half-naked giant strolled up to a newborn masterwork like he was arriving at breakfast.
The temperature of the room's respect dropped tier by tier. Masters' eyes narrowed all around the hall. Swagger. Actual swagger, in the royal smithy.
"He'd better not..."
"If he ruins her piece playing circus, powerful villain or not..."
Dain's knuckles had gone white on his cane. Brokk said nothing, but her thumbs came out of her belt.

The hammer stopped spinning at the top of one last insolent flip, his right arm flaring with veins and hand settling onto the haft in a grip that was suddenly, chillingly correct, and came down square on the newborn head.
*CLANG!*
The sound went through the hall's bones, but it was nothing beside what came with it.

Quinlan's eyes ignited, all seven elements burning in them at once, flame and tide and gale and stone and frost and storm and magma, and light in the same seven colors detonated down the hammer's path and poured into the steel.

This was no smithing blow. Raw mana crushed itself into the newborn head, compressed under the strike until it folded into the grain along every rune-channel his smith had laid, and the anvil screamed under a pressure it had never been asked to hold.
The wash of it rolled off him in a visible tide, and the whole front rank of masters took an involuntary step back.
"Ancestors above! What is that output?!"
"He's pouring his entire pool into ONE STRIKE?!?! Is he dumb?!"
An old rune-master on the second tier was doing frantic arithmetic on his fingers. "Nobody sustains that. Three more of those and he's dry, I don't care what he is..."
*CLANG!*
"Two more!"
*CLANG!*
"That's it, he's done, no man alive..."
Quinlan, mid-swing, took a sharp breath.

The hall felt it before it saw it. The mountain's deep mana turned like a tide reversing, bending toward the man at the anvil from every direction at once, wisps of it going faintly luminous as they crossed the last span to his skin and sank in.

He was refilling. In plain sight, mid-work, sweat sheeting down his back, the deepest well any of them had ever stood near topping itself back up like a spring, and then the hammer rose again and the seven-colored blaze rose with it.
*CLANG!*
The rune-master sat down on the stairs.
"That's not a mortal being..." someone said faintly from the rails. "That's a calamity in human skin."
"No wonder our armies lost..."
"Unbelievable..."
"Someone wake me up!"

It became a rhythm, and the rhythm became the kind of spectacle that gets embellished for a century despite needing no embellishment: strike, blaze, the impossible expenditure, the breath, the tide of power crawling home across his skin, strike again. Magic, smithing, and raw endurance braided into a single act, performed at full burn by Quinlan, sweating like a dockhand and enjoying himself with a satisfied grin all master smiths recognized, the expression you made when you felt fully in control of your work.
And then, while the hall was still reeling, the elf walked into the blast radius.
"My part's done..."

Kaelira crossed the floor at her own unhurried pace, stepped through a mana-wash that had the front row shielding their beards, and wrapped herself around her lover from behind: arms sliding around his waist, palms spreading flat over the ridges of his abs, cheek coming to rest between his shoulder blades. It was his own hold, given back.
Except he had grinned through his version, loudly proud of himself, embracing what was his without a care for who watched.

Kaelira's face stayed buried against his spine, hidden from the entire hall, and the only part of her that confessed anything was her ears, which twitched once, hard, and then kept twitching, broadcasting to the upper tiers everything her hidden face refused to.
The hall noticed her one section at a time, conversations dying mid-word.
"Is... is she doing it now?"
"She is."
"The mana-wash! It'll cook her..."

The piece has to deserve the metal, and today's..." she gestured at the forge, at the sweat and the fire and the impossible weld, with the same lazy warmth she'd give a picnic spread, "...just a quick little piece to show off, basically.
They don't spend adamantite on a souvenir."
Brokk stared at her.

Then she looked back at the forge, at the one craftsman in two bodies, at the lamination her hall's treatises called impossible, at the salute still rolling around the tiers, and did the math every master in earshot was doing whether they wanted to or not.
That was the doodle.
Then what was them being serious?!
As if perfectly reading the dwarf's thoughts, Seraphiel pointed toward Quinlan with one dainty finger.
"She is~"
Or, to be more specific, she was pointing at the towel soaking up sweat on her half-naked lover, the garment that was previously his armor.
"...Ancestors preserve us," the First Hammer said, with feeling, and went back to her post.
Then she caught herself.
"Wait, she?"
"She has too much personality to be a mere thing, so Quin decided Synchra was a female," Sera giggled.
"..." A hundred butts suddenly found the nearest seat, which, for many, turned out to be the ground itself.
The forging ran on for the better part of an hour.

When the folding was done and the shape emerged, a hammer head, drift-punched and true, the layered grain of three humble metals flowing through its faces like current-lines in dark water, Kaelira laid the newborn craft down on the anvil's face with both hands, careful as a midwife, and squared it to the light.
Then she straightened, chest heaving, and tossed her own working hammer backward over her shoulder without so much as a glance.
"Quin."
Quinlan was already there.
He plucked the tool out of the air mid-stride, and the hall understood the gesture at once, because it was a smith calling in her finisher.
What the hall did not understand was what he did next, which was give the venerable forge hammer a lazy flip.
Then another.

Then a slow spin across the back of his hand, the tool of the sacred craft twirling like a street performer's baton as the half-naked giant strolled up to a newborn masterwork like he was arriving at breakfast.
The temperature of the room's respect dropped tier by tier.
Masters' eyes narrowed all around the hall.
Swagger.
Actual swagger, in the royal smithy.
"He'd better not..."
"If he ruins her piece playing circus, powerful villain or not..."
Dain's knuckles had gone white on his cane.
Brokk said nothing, but her thumbs came out of her belt.

The hammer stopped spinning at the top of one last insolent flip, his right arm flaring with veins and hand settling onto the haft in a grip that was suddenly, chillingly correct, and came down square on the newborn head.
*CLANG!*
The sound went through the hall's bones, but it was nothing beside what came with it.

Quinlan's eyes ignited, all seven elements burning in them at once, flame and tide and gale and stone and frost and storm and magma, and light in the same seven colors detonated down the hammer's path and poured into the steel.
This was no smithing blow.

Raw mana crushed itself into the newborn head, compressed under the strike until it folded into the grain along every rune-channel his smith had laid, and the anvil screamed under a pressure it had never been asked to hold.
The wash of it rolled off him in a visible tide, and the whole front rank of masters took an involuntary step back.
"Ancestors above!
What is that output?!"
"He's pouring his entire pool into ONE STRIKE?!?!
Is he dumb?!"
An old rune-master on the second tier was doing frantic arithmetic on his fingers.
"Nobody sustains that.
Three more of those and he's dry, I don't care what he is..."
*CLANG!*
"Two more!"
*CLANG!*
"That's it, he's done, no man alive..."
Quinlan, mid-swing, took a sharp breath.
The hall felt it before it saw it.

The mountain's deep mana turned like a tide reversing, bending toward the man at the anvil from every direction at once, wisps of it going faintly luminous as they crossed the last span to his skin and sank in.
He was refilling.

In plain sight, mid-work, sweat sheeting down his back, the deepest well any of them had ever stood near topping itself back up like a spring, and then the hammer rose again and the seven-colored blaze rose with it.
*CLANG!*
The rune-master sat down on the stairs.
"That's not a mortal being..." someone said faintly from the rails.
"That's a calamity in human skin."
"No wonder our armies lost..."
"Unbelievable..."
"Someone wake me up!"

It became a rhythm, and the rhythm became the kind of spectacle that gets embellished for a century despite needing no embellishment: strike, blaze, the impossible expenditure, the breath, the tide of power crawling home across his skin, strike again.

Magic, smithing, and raw endurance braided into a single act, performed at full burn by Quinlan, sweating like a dockhand and enjoying himself with a satisfied grin all master smiths recognized, the expression you made when you felt fully in control of your work.
And then, while the hall was still reeling, the elf walked into the blast radius.
"My part's done..."

Kaelira crossed the floor at her own unhurried pace, stepped through a mana-wash that had the front row shielding their beards, and wrapped herself around her lover from behind: arms sliding around his waist, palms spreading flat over the ridges of his abs, cheek coming to rest between his shoulder blades.
It was his own hold, given back.
Except he had grinned through his version, loudly proud of himself, embracing what was his without a care for who watched.

Kaelira's face stayed buried against his spine, hidden from the entire hall, and the only part of her that confessed anything was her ears, which twitched once, hard, and then kept twitching, broadcasting to the upper tiers everything her hidden face refused to.
The hall noticed her one section at a time, conversations dying mid-word.
"Is... is she doing it now?"
"She is."
"The mana-wash!
It'll cook her..."

chapters.title: Chapter 1826 Everwright
paragraphs: It was not cooking her. The torrent broke around the elf like current around a bridge pillar, and she stood rooted in it, comfortable, a tank in her own element letting her partner's power roll over her shoulders.
A scandalized master rounded on his neighbors, beard bristling, demanding sense from somebody. "What in the Ancestors' name is she doing?!"
The fairer half of the hall answered him at once, flat, fluent, without taking their eyes off the anvil.
"Charging up."
"It's part of the ritual," someone added helpfully from the rails. "Weren't you paying attention?"
The master opened his mouth, closed it, and turned back to the forge, educated.
On the guests' bench, Elowen had both hands pressed to her mouth.
"She is... they are... during labor," she managed. "In public. In front of dwarves!"

"Isn't she amazing? Inside the forge, she is always more comfortable..." Seraphiel had her chin propped on both palms, watching her best friend like a proud coach. "Look at that form. Head placement, hand placement, the lean. She learned it all from watching me. I taught her."
"That is not a technique!"
"It's absolutely a technique."
"...Does it require being his lover?" she asked the air, with enormous, doomed dignity. "The hearth-tending."
"Mm~?" Sera's head turned very slowly, her grin arriving ahead of it. "Why do you ask?"
"For the report."
"Of course~ For the report."

Elowen achieved a posture rigid enough to shame a parade manual and said nothing further, which said everything, and Seraphiel added another flustered royal guard to a collection that was coming along beautifully.

At the anvil, the final strike fell, and the seven lights banked themselves in Quinlan's eyes like lamps turned down for the night. He rolled the haft once in his grip, set the hammer aside, and gave the steel one long, satisfied look, and the air above the anvil shivered with a power none of them could name yet.

Brokk was moving before anyone else dared, because some offices cannot be delegated. The First Hammer of the royal smithy called the final quench herself, her voice cracking across the hall as if the masterwork were her own, and the whole hall leaned in.
Steam went up like a curtain rising.
The steam stood over Kaelira's borrowed anvil at the heart of the royal smithy, and for three long breaths nobody moved, three hundred professionals holding themselves still for the sake of a cloud.
When it thinned, the hammer sat in the quench-mist, finished. And it was humming.

Faintly, deep in the metal, at a pitch felt rather than heard: a finished thing announcing itself. The water-grained faces of three humble steels ran with rune-script that glimmered as the metal cooled, settling into the grain like the last words of a long argument, won.
Quinlan stood over the quench-anvil while the last of the steam curled off it, in nothing but the towel and the heat rising off his own back, and studied the humming hammer.

Behind him, the tip of an overly long ear poked out from under his arm before Kaelira had fully let go of his waist. She ducked through, came around to stand between the Villain and the anvil, and settled inside the circle of his arms while his chin came to rest over her head. Neither of them appeared to find this worth remarking on.
The smith went to work with her eyes first.

She tracked the rune-script down one face and up the other, tipped her head to read how the light moved through the layers, and only then touched the hammer to turn it three slow times against her wrist and find where the weight wanted to sit. Her hands were rock steady. Three hundred dwarves watched a woman run a full acceptance inspection while pressed spine-to-chest against two meters of half-naked primordial, and not one degree of her focus slipped.
'She isn't even breathing differently,' Brokk thought, somewhere between awe and grief.
"Well?" Quinlan's voice rumbled down over the top of her head, warm and unhurried. "What's the verdict?"
Kaelira turned the hammer one last quarter-turn, felt the balance seat exactly where she'd built it to, and delivered her judgment on the masterwork three hundred masters had just wept over.
"You did a good job," she nodded, proud of his work.
"We did."
"Me?" the Runeweaver shook her head. "I only-"
"Kaelira."
"..." silence overtook the tomboy elf, but only for a few stretching seconds. Then, the most honest, simple, joyous grin the dwarves had ever seen on an elf materialized on her lips.
"We did a good job!" she beamed.
"Good. Want to do the honors?"
She went still. Then she smiled, small and soft, entirely to herself, the shy elf surfacing under the smith for just long enough to matter, and both hands closed around the haft.
"...Yeah."

She stepped out of his arms and raised the hammer high over her head. The hall's noise dropped off a cliff, forge-light running the length of the water-grain and waking the rune-script where the glow crossed it.
"I think I'll call it Everwright," Kaelira said, her voice carrying to the top tier without her having to push it. "This is not a war hammer."
The gallery had no idea what to do with that, a relic humming with a conqueror's whole element-set, raised overhead like a war-banner, and the elf holding it telling them plainly it wasn't a weapon.
"Then what in the deeps is it?" a master got out.
"Everwright is a tool for master smiths with more mana than time on their hands."
"Huh?" came the gasps from all around.

Elemental infusion was a lengthy process, taking a great deal of time and resources. The most common method was to have a 'Mancer-type' mage expend their element into a special artifact made for compressing and storing it, a Pyromancer striking fire into the vessel, for example. The smith would then extract that stored fire and imbue it into the piece on their anvil.
"Could I borrow a few plain shields, First Hammer?" Kaelira asked, knowing it would be easier to show than tell. "Whatever your hall turns out on an ordinary day."

Brokk didn't ask why. She barked a name, an apprentice bolted for the common rack, and five plain dwarven wall-shields came skidding out across the floor, hall-forged and unlovely, the honest output of an ordinary shift.
Quinlan lifted two fingers.

A low gale peeled off his palm and slid under the shields where they lay, and all five lifted off the flagstones at once to hang in a slow, patient rotation at the height of Kaelira's shoulder, turning in his wind like leaves that had forgotten to fall.
Kaelira picked one with her eyes and reached into the hammer instead of into herself.
"Magma."
The rune-channels answered.

Of the seven elements folded into the grain she called up exactly one, and the hammer's head woke red, then deeper, then molten, magma-light bleeding up the water-grain until the whole tool ran the color of a fresh pour.
She struck the hanging shield once, and the magma took, heat spreading from the point of impact in a slow bloom that the plain dwarven steel drank down and held.
The second blow drove it deeper, the bloom running to the rim, veins of banked fire threading the surface and down the straps until an apprentice on the rail forgot every rule of the hall and yelped.
On the third she swung full-arm, the way she'd driven her last folds, and Everwright's glow guttered out the instant the blow landed, every ember of it gone from the hammer and into the shield.

The shield rang off the flagstones no longer plain and no longer cold, a common wall-shield off a common rack now banked with a magma heat, while the other four spun on in Quinlan's wind, untouched and waiting their turn.
For one heartbeat the hall couldn't make sense of what they'd seen. Then the rune-master who'd sat down on the stairs got there first, and he came back off them slow.
"Ancestors," he breathed. "They forged a tool that bypasses the whole pain-in-the-ass enchanting procedure?!"
Silence held for exactly as long as dwarven lungs could bear it.
"Impossible!"
"There must be a drawback!"
"How many uses?!"
"How much mana needed?!"
"What's the output?!"
"Am I out of a job?!"

Then the royal smithy came apart. Masters surged in around the anvil, protocol dead and terror forgotten, shouting over each other in dwarvish and trade-tongue at once. Someone demanded to know the fold count. Someone else had produced calipers from somewhere. An entire delegation was interrogating Kaelira about the shear plane, and she answered six of them at a time with her ears blazing and her spine straight.
Dain got a hand on the hammer's haft, just laid it there, the way you'd touch a shrine, and his shoulders shook once.

"Twenty-two years I begged the crown for the best metal and cursed them for forcing my craft to get stale," the old master said, to nobody, his voice cracking around an apprentice's grin. "...Perhaps it was never the metal."

Brokk stood over the anvil, thumbs hooked back in her belt, studying the finished work for a long, wordless stretch. Then she raised her head and looked across it at Quinlan. The question that had been building in the First Hammer's chest all day finally came out, and the hall heard it coming and went quiet to make room.
"You didn't come with terms," she said. "You came, you asked good questions, you opened the crown's racks like they were yours, you worked my bellows. Fine. I've stopped trying to make sense of you."
She stood iron-grey and unbowed under his gaze. "So I'll just ask it, since every hammer in this hall is afraid to. What do you want from the dwarven people, Conqueror?

chapters.title: Chapter 1827 Unga Bunga
paragraphs: "So I'll just ask it, since every hammer in this hall is afraid to. What do you want from the dwarven people, Conqueror?"

The towel at Quinlan's neck stirred, poured back down over his chest and arms, and rewove itself into his shirt, and he took his time settling the cuffs while the royal smithy of Elvardia held its breath around him.
"What do the dwarven people want to do?" he finally asked with a sly grin.
"...We want to live our lives honestly. Work hard mastering our craft, drink good booze, and sleep in our beds without fear."
"Sounds like the kind of people any sane ruler would want to support."
Brokk looked at him for a long moment. Then she nodded, once, to the Conqueror of the Continent, smith to smith.
"... Any sane ruler, hmm?" she said.
Sera reappeared at his side without any of them catching her cross the floor, nestled her cheeks into his shoulder, and let a wounded little sound out against his ear.

"Are you forgetting about me...?" She melted in against his skin, the pout in her voice with nothing whatsoever behind it, her eyes warm and dancing. "I can't beat metal into behaving the way Kaeli can, I know that. But I love you plenty too, and I was so patient and so good all afternoon, and you haven't looked at me even once..."
Quinlan chuckled at that, apologetically looking at Brokk. "Gotta go. Duty calls."
Sera's chin came off his shoulder. "Did you just call spending time with me a duty?!"
He answered by raising one hand, and the [Warp Gate] unfolded at the hall's heart, pale and silent. Not a muscle in his face moved while he did it. Sera pouted so hard her ears folded down flat.
An arm settled around each elf's waist, Sera on one side still mourning her stolen honor and Kaelira on the other, and he turned the three of them toward the seam.

Kaelira went with him a step before she set her heels. She leaned out of the circle of his arm just far enough to lay the humming hammer down on the anvil, settled the magma-banked shield beside it, and squared them both to the light the way she'd squared every piece she finished that day. Then she looked up and found hundreds of gazes staring right at her.

"Thank you for your hospitality, royal smiths." The words came quiet, and for once she let the whole hall hear all the way to the bottom of them. "Seeing these forges was a dream I've held since I was small enough to hide under a workbench. I won't forget it."
She never said keep it. She simply left it there, humming on the anvil, and let Quinlan draw her the rest of the way to the gate.
Behind them, three hundred dwarves slowly worked out that the relic was not leaving with the people who'd made it.
The gate swallowed the Villain and his women and folded shut without a sound.
For a moment the royal smithy just stood there, three hundred professionals and one First Hammer alone with a humming artifact their guests hadn't thought worth carrying home.
Brokk didn't move. She stayed rooted where she was with her arms folded, turning his words over in the quiet behind her eyes.
The others had no such dignity left to guard.

Old Dain moved first, because some things do not wait for a committee. The most venerable master of the mountain hobbled to the anvil, hauled his hammer up in both hands, and knocked its butt against the horn twice, hard, right beside the humming relic. The double-knock cracked through the hall like a starting gun, and the mountain came off its leash.

Every hammer in the room found something to beat on. The horn, the nearest anvil, an inspection plate, a support pillar, a neighbor's pauldron, a neighbor's helmet with the neighbor still inside it, and three hundred hammer-butts came down at once in no rhythm anyone agreed on and none anyone needed, until somewhere under the din the first voice went up, wordless and enormous, straight from the chest.
"OHHH... OH-OH... OHHHH!"

It was not a song. Nobody wrote it and nobody agreed to it, it just came up out of them, from somewhere underneath every treatise the day had murdered, from the same floor of the dwarven soul where the first smith watched lightning hit a rock and decided to argue with it.

The hall took it up in one breath and gave up on words entirely. The same masters who had spent the afternoon calculating mana thresholds and shear planes were stamping in a slow circle around the anvil now, beards swinging like censers, tools thrust overhead, grunting at a masterwork like it was the first moon any of them had ever seen.
"OHHH... OH-OH... OHHHH!"
A rune-master who a minute ago could not stand now could not stop, and headbutted a support column affectionately on his way past it without breaking stride.
Somebody hauled Dain up onto a bench, where the most dignified craftsman in the deep kingdom sang with streaming eyes and both fists beating the air, and did not miss one single knock.
The channel-master gave up on her inspection plate and drummed it against her own breastplate instead.
Vorn, whose arms had locked at the sight of the Villain and come loose for good somewhere around the fifth fold, stomped into the circle bellowing at the rafters.
"OHHH... OH-OH... OHHHH!"

Two apprentices grabbed the youngest of their number and hoisted him overhead like a battle standard, and he shrieked the chant down at all of them, already living inside the story he would still be telling when he was old.

The noise went down through two feet of living stone. The freshly mortared flue caught the din and carried it note-perfect into every gallery, stair, and drinking hall of the deep city, where dwarves who had no idea what had happened felt the beat rise through their boots and, being dwarves, started stamping right along.
The royal smithy of Elvardia danced around the hammer the way the first dwarves had danced around the first fire.
"OHHH... OH-OH... OHHHH!"
At the edge of it all, Brokk watched her hall lose its mind over a hammer three cheap metals had no business becoming, and she neither joined the circle nor moved to break it up.
It could have gone the other way.

Had the two of them pulled some legendary artifact out of hearth-steel and cart-spring iron, every master in this hall would've gone home knowing their life's work had been a child's game played at the foot of gods. That hammer would have emptied the mountain's forges within a generation.

Instead they'd made a tool. A quality of life utility tool for working smiths, left humming on a royal anvil like a promise that the ceiling of the craft sat higher than any treatise had dared to draw it, and that the road up ran through plain honest steel her people already owned.
The Villain and his elf hadn't shown them their smallness. He'd shown them the mountain still had rooms they'd never opened.
"Wait, he just left me here?" Elowen gasped as she finally realized what was going on. "In enemy territory?!"
"Enemy territory?" Brokk scoffed. "Open your eyes, you insufferable cunt."

sentences.text: "So I'll just ask it, since every hammer in this hall is afraid to.
What do you want from the dwarven people, Conqueror?"

The towel at Quinlan's neck stirred, poured back down over his chest and arms, and rewove itself into his shirt, and he took his time settling the cuffs while the royal smithy of Elvardia held its breath around him.
"What do the dwarven people want to do?" he finally asked with a sly grin.
"...We want to live our lives honestly.
Work hard mastering our craft, drink good booze, and sleep in our beds without fear."
"Sounds like the kind of people any sane ruler would want to support."
Brokk looked at him for a long moment.
Then she nodded, once, to the Conqueror of the Continent, smith to smith.
Any sane ruler, hmm?" she said.
Sera reappeared at his side without any of them catching her cross the floor, nestled her cheeks into his shoulder, and let a wounded little sound out against his ear.
"Are you forgetting about me...?" She melted in against his skin, the pout in her voice with nothing whatsoever behind it, her eyes warm and dancing.
"I can't beat metal into behaving the way Kaeli can, I know that.
But I love you plenty too, and I was so patient and so good all afternoon, and you haven't looked at me even once..."
Quinlan chuckled at that, apologetically looking at Brokk.
"Gotta go.
Duty calls."
Sera's chin came off his shoulder.
"Did you just call spending time with me a duty?!"
He answered by raising one hand, and the [Warp Gate] unfolded at the hall's heart, pale and silent.
Not a muscle in his face moved while he did it.
Sera pouted so hard her ears folded down flat.
An arm settled around each elf's waist, Sera on one side still mourning her stolen honor and Kaelira on the other, and he turned the three of them toward the seam.
Kaelira went with him a step before she set her heels.

She leaned out of the circle of his arm just far enough to lay the humming hammer down on the anvil, settled the magma-banked shield beside it, and squared them both to the light the way she'd squared every piece she finished that day.
Then she looked up and found hundreds of gazes staring right at her.
"Thank you for your hospitality, royal smiths." The words came quiet, and for once she let the whole hall hear all the way to the bottom of them.
"Seeing these forges was a dream I've held since I was small enough to hide under a workbench.
I won't forget it."
She never said keep it.
She simply left it there, humming on the anvil, and let Quinlan draw her the rest of the way to the gate.
Behind them, three hundred dwarves slowly worked out that the relic was not leaving with the people who'd made it.
The gate swallowed the Villain and his women and folded shut without a sound.
For a moment the royal smithy just stood there, three hundred professionals and one First Hammer alone with a humming artifact their guests hadn't thought worth carrying home.
Brokk didn't move.
She stayed rooted where she was with her arms folded, turning his words over in the quiet behind her eyes.
The others had no such dignity left to guard.
Old Dain moved first, because some things do not wait for a committee.
The most venerable master of the mountain hobbled to the anvil, hauled his hammer up in both hands, and knocked its butt against the horn twice, hard, right beside the humming relic.
The double-knock cracked through the hall like a starting gun, and the mountain came off its leash.
Every hammer in the room found something to beat on.

The horn, the nearest anvil, an inspection plate, a support pillar, a neighbor's pauldron, a neighbor's helmet with the neighbor still inside it, and three hundred hammer-butts came down at once in no rhythm anyone agreed on and none anyone needed, until somewhere under the din the first voice went up, wordless and enormous, straight from the chest.
"OHHH...
OH-OH...
OHHHH!"
It was not a song.

Nobody wrote it and nobody agreed to it, it just came up out of them, from somewhere underneath every treatise the day had murdered, from the same floor of the dwarven soul where the first smith watched lightning hit a rock and decided to argue with it.
The hall took it up in one breath and gave up on words entirely.

The same masters who had spent the afternoon calculating mana thresholds and shear planes were stamping in a slow circle around the anvil now, beards swinging like censers, tools thrust overhead, grunting at a masterwork like it was the first moon any of them had ever seen.
"OHHH...
OH-OH...
OHHHH!"
A rune-master who a minute ago could not stand now could not stop, and headbutted a support column affectionately on his way past it without breaking stride.
Somebody hauled Dain up onto a bench, where the most dignified craftsman in the deep kingdom sang with streaming eyes and both fists beating the air, and did not miss one single knock.
The channel-master gave up on her inspection plate and drummed it against her own breastplate instead.
Vorn, whose arms had locked at the sight of the Villain and come loose for good somewhere around the fifth fold, stomped into the circle bellowing at the rafters.
"OHHH...
OH-OH...
OHHHH!"

Two apprentices grabbed the youngest of their number and hoisted him overhead like a battle standard, and he shrieked the chant down at all of them, already living inside the story he would still be telling when he was old.
The noise went down through two feet of living stone.

The freshly mortared flue caught the din and carried it note-perfect into every gallery, stair, and drinking hall of the deep city, where dwarves who had no idea what had happened felt the beat rise through their boots and, being dwarves, started stamping right along.
The royal smithy of Elvardia danced around the hammer the way the first dwarves had danced around the first fire.
"OHHH...
OH-OH...
OHHHH!"
At the edge of it all, Brokk watched her hall lose its mind over a hammer three cheap metals had no business becoming, and she neither joined the circle nor moved to break it up.
It could have gone the other way.

Had the two of them pulled some legendary artifact out of hearth-steel and cart-spring iron, every master in this hall would've gone home knowing their life's work had been a child's game played at the foot of gods.
That hammer would have emptied the mountain's forges within a generation.

chapters.title: Chapter 1828 Majestic Forest
paragraphs: Seraphiel came through the [Warp Gate] first, walking backward, conducting the royal smithy happenings with both hands and a mesmerizing grin.

"...and old Dain was crying hehe! Kaeli, did you see him? The most venerable master under the mountain, weeping into a hammer you made out of cart parts. The one with the calipers had to sit down on the stairs. And the First Hammer's face when you left Everwright on the anvil, I thought she was going to propose. To you, to the hammer, unclear, but there was marriage in her eyes somewhere..."
Her bare feet sank to the ankle in snow, and the rest of the sentence went out like a lamp.

Sera had never owned a pair of boots. They suffocated her outright, pinched closed the contact between her soles and the ground that she needed open, and her Vitality was high enough that a little winter had never been a convincing argument.

Winter held the continent of Iskaris. The gate had opened onto a white field before a treeline, fat unhurried flakes drifting down through the grey, her breath blooming silver in front of her face. And past the field stood the forest.
Even from outside, it refused to fit in her eyes. The trees rose like the roots of the sky, trunks wider than watchtowers, climbing until the snowfall blurred them into the white above.

Whole fields of snow rode the canopy's shoulders the way a mountain range carried them, a second white country hanging overhead, and beneath that impossible roof the spaces between the trunks glowed faintly green.
Green. In midwinter.

Sera stood in the snow with her arms loose at her sides and let the legend look back at her. She had been born in Elvardia and conscripted out of it on her hundredth year, marched from a barracks to a slave block without once being shown her own country's heart.

The deep forests surrounding Luminareth, the deepest parts of the elven heritage, had reached her anyway. They did so in fragments, in the homesick rambling of older conscripts, in songs that got the details wrong. None of the songs had mentioned that it was this big.
"Kaeli," she breathed. "Kaeli, look. It's really here... It's actually..."
Behind her, somebody moaned. It was not a moan of scenic appreciation.
Sera turned around.

Quinlan had Kaelira against a snowbank, or Kaelira had dragged him down into one, the order of operations had stopped mattering several seconds ago. The shy smith of the family was kissing her man with both fists in his collar, steam curling off the two of them where the snow gave up on their skin, and the sound she was making into his mouth, low and starving, belonged to some other elf entirely. Some elf who had definitely never blushed at hand-holding.
*Smooch.*
Sera's left eye twitched.

The oldest, most culturally significant forest of elvenkind stood twenty steps away, ancient beyond every song she'd ever been sung, and her best friend was devouring their lover in a roadside snowdrift.
"You two are UNBELIEVABLE!" The first elf of the harem descended on the pair and got a fistful of collar in each hand. "The forest is right there! Have at least this much decency, you animals! Up!"

She hauled. They came up still attached at the mouth, which she chose not to dignify. She marched the conjoined disgrace across the white field and under the eaves of the oldest living thing on the continent, scolding the whole way and not slowing down.
Then the forest happened to all three of them at once.
The cold stopped dead at the treeline, the way noise stopped when a door closed, and warmth rose from the earth underfoot like the breath of a banked hearth. The snow stayed outside.

Miles overhead the canopy held its white country against the sky, and what slipped through the gaps came down as light instead: a soft, silvered snow-light that drifted between the trunks in slow columns and laid itself over the moss like frost that had forgotten how to be cold. The air belonged to another season entirely, green and sweet and so dense with the smell of living things that breathing it felt like a meal.
Somewhere far above, a bird sang, and another answered it, unbothered, as if nobody had told the forest what season it was.
Kaelira surfaced from the kiss because the air had changed.
"It's warm." She blinked at the green around her.
"It is." Quinlan had his head tilted toward the nearest trunk, the same way he'd listened to the dwarves' flue. "The old trees run their own hearth of sorts. How curious."
Sera wasn't listening to either of them.
She was already deeper in.

She stepped into a bank of deep moss and her whole body stopped. Warm. The earth of her homeland's heart was warm under her naked soles in the dead of winter, alive the way a sleeping animal was alive, and the mana of the place rose up through her arches like a tide finding a channel it had been missing.
Her eyes drifted shut. Her arms floated out from her sides, palms open. Pollen, actual pollen, drifted gold through the silver light-columns around her.
"Oh..." she whispered, and her ears trembled.

For a long moment the cheeky grin was nowhere on her, and the first elf of the Villain's family simply stood in the middle of her homeland's heart with her toes curled into the warm earth, breathing it in until her breath ran out of room.

"This is what I mean, Kaeli." Her voice had gone soft and drunk. "Feel it with your feet. You have to feel it with your feet. Isn't nature amazing? You poor thing, you spent your whole life in cellars and forges, and I love you, but a smithy simply can't compare to..."
*Smooch.*
She opened her eyes and turned around, holding the moment out to her best friend with both hands.

Round two had started without an intermission. Her fingers were buried in his hair, one of his hands had already hiked her thigh up over his hip, and her ears, blazing red, were angled forward the way they angled at a promising billet.
"I don't believe you two!" Sera's scoff sent a choir of birds off a branch. "In the holy elven forest! That's the soul of our people!"
Kaelira broke the kiss by a centimeter. Her eyes had gone dark, and her voice came out in the blunt register she used for load tolerances.
"The soul of our people is warm and soft." She looked pointedly at the moss underfoot. "Good ground. It'll hold."
"In the name of..." Sera pressed both hands to her face. Between her fingers, a grin was already winning. "Unbelievable. Simply unbelievable."
But from one moment to the next, her expression changed. "Okay, I'm done pretending I care so much about all this nonsense. I sound like Mom. Ugh."

The fight went out of Sera all at once, because it had never really been in her. She looked at her best friend, pinned and glowing and shameless, ears broadcasting on every frequency at once, and the pout melted into the warm, wicked thing that lived at the bottom of all her performances.
"Leave some of him for me, you greedy girl!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1829 Expressed Desire
paragraphs: "Leave some of him for me, you greedy girl!" She shouted, running close to the ferocious pair. "Quin~ how about we build Kaeli a bower?"
Quinlan didn't put her down.
He shifted her weight to one arm, palm settling under her backside, and walked them both to the hollow between two great roots where the snow-light pooled. His free hand rose, and the earth answered.

The floor of the hollow breathed in and swelled into a broad, moss-deep couch between the roots, its edges rolled like a bedframe grown rather than built. Magma, banked to a whisper, slid into the stone far beneath until the moss went from warm to sun-warm.

A sphere of flame the size of a heart pinched itself into being above the hollow and hung there, small and patient as a private sun, and a curtain of moving air drew itself around the whole of it, keeping the heat in and the winter's opinions out.

Halfway through, he kissed her again, unhurried, one hand still shaping the bower while his mouth found better uses for itself, and Kaelira made a sound against his lips that had nothing to do with the forest and everything to do with the arm holding her up like she weighed nothing.
"Are you kidding me," Sera said. The pout was enormous. The grin underneath it was bigger.

It took him less than half a minute. Seven elements, the same seven that had brought down armies, taught to do bedroom furniture one-handed, because putting his smith down wasn't something he felt like doing.

Kaelira felt every element pass through him while he held her, all of it traveling through his chest into hers. Being pressed against him while he worked was a cruelty she had no interest in surviving.
He laid her down into what he'd built.

The moss took her weight like it had been expecting her all day. He came down over her slowly, forearms bracketing her head, and the ferocity they'd been trading since the snowbank gentled into a stillness that held. His thumb traced her cheekbone. He knew exactly what was underneath him. The last first of his family.
"You're sure," he asked, and there was no tease anywhere in it.
Sera, folding herself down at the hollow's edge with her chin on her palms, had the grace to stay quiet.
"Am I sure?" Kaelira repeated it flatly, like he'd asked whether steel was hard. Then she inhaled, and it all came out at once.
"I asked you to wait, yes. But... I've been ready for a while. It's just the world kept getting in the way and I never found the chance..."

Her voice was climbing, and her ears had passed red and were working on crimson. "And then Nyxara, who joined the harem LONG after me, strolls past the queue like it isn't there... A demon older than the language I'm complaining in. Do you have any idea what that does to an elf's confidence?"
"Kaeli," Sera managed, but was interrupted.

"I'm not finished." The smith's finger came up between their faces, trembling with conviction. "If Black Fang laps me too, I'm done. I mean it. I'll renounce having bodily needs altogether. I'll take orders, join Isveth's maidens, and worship you from a respectful distance for the rest of my unnaturally long life. A shrine maiden." A pause. "A shrine smith tank maiden."
"..." Quinlan remained silent, listening to this wonderful girl put her thoughts out there for once. Always so shy, always content to remain in the smithy while he was having fun with his girls.

Both of her calloused hands came up and framed his face, and under all the ranting her eyes were steady and bright and serious, because that was the confession beneath the comedy: she had wanted him for a while now, quietly, thoroughly, with the same patience she gave a long fold, while duty and war kept taking her turn away from her.
She had never once complained about the waiting. She was complaining now because it was finally over, and she could at last afford to admit how heavy it had been.
Sera moved first.
"Let me help you~" She slid in behind Kaelira, fingers finding the shirt's hem, and her voice dropped low, meant for no one but Kaelira. "Is it okay? Me being here for this."
Kaelira's hand found Sera's wrist and held. "Yes... Please stay. I need you to stay." A shaky exhale. "I'd combust on my own."
Sera giggled at that, bright and warm, and patted Kaelira's hair. "Then let big sis Sera take care of you~" She gathered Kaelira's head onto her thighs, soft and unhurried.
"I'm older than you," Kaelira murmured, but she settled into Sera's lap and did not move a centimeter away.
"Shh~ Big sisters are a state of mind."

Sera took the shirt's hem in both hands and peeled the forge-smudged linen up and over her best friend's head in the half-second Quinlan's mouth left hers, and his mouth was back before the linen hit the ground. Then the wraps beneath, unwound turn by turn, Sera's fingers patient and practiced along the bindings, each discarded layer folded once and set aside. The snow-light received what the forge-light never had.

She was built the way she built things, nothing wasted: the sweat-sheened plane of her stomach with its chiseled ridges, the hard taper of her waist into hips set like a stance, the smithing arm with its cords of quiet muscle, and above all of it, freed of their binding, the surprisingly heavy curve of her breasts, a softness the wraps had been flatly lying about for all those months.
Kaelira did not cover herself. She planted her palms in the moss on either side of Sera's knees, chin up, flushed to the collar, and let him look until looking visibly stopped being enough for him.
"Say something," she soon begged.
He wasted absolutely no time and decreed with a straight face: "I'm looking at the best thing a smithy ever produced."
"Quin... I can't do this..." Kaelira whimpered.

His mouth started at her throat and worked down without hurrying, and he handled her exactly the way she'd always suspected he would. Thoroughly, patiently, in the correct order. He learned the weight of her breasts with both hands and then with his mouth until her spine came up off the moss and her gasp rang off the roots.

He traced the ridges of her stomach with his tongue like they were a personal gift to him, which, judging by the low sound he made against them, was his honest position on the matter. Muscle earned over a lifetime at the anvil jumped and trembled under his lips, and he took his time with every ridge, murmuring his appreciation into her skin, shameless about how much he liked them, until she was squirming from the praise as much as the touch.
Then he found the faint old scars along her forearm and kissed those too, one by one, and that, of all things, was what made her eyes sting.
Above her, Sera's thumb caught the first tear before it reached her ear, and said nothing, and kept combing.
Then, as he shifted to settle lower, Kaelira's hand closed on his shoulder and pushed.
He let her push. "Oh?"

Two meters of primordial rolled over into the moss, interested, and the smith sat up, swung a thigh across his hips, and looked down at her naked lover, flushed and resolute, like she'd rehearsed this decision in her head a hundred times.
"My turn."
"Oh my~" Sera's eyebrows climbed, delighted. "And here I sat, ready to hold your hand through the scary parts. Look at you go~"

"He's my lover." Kaelira's palms spread flat over his chest and started mapping, slow and thorough, reading him the way she read everything worth reading, hands first. Her ears were incandescent. Her touch did not waver at all.

"I find him..." one hard swallow "...extremely attractive. I have watched this body across a forge for months. Today it worked a bellows for me, half-naked, for an hour. I am not going to lie back and just receive like some... some dead fish woman." Dignity and blush fought over her face. "I want to feel him too. Why should he get all the... the doing?"
She bent, and put her mouth on him.

Do you have any idea what that does to an elf's confidence?"
"Kaeli," Sera managed, but was interrupted.
"I'm not finished." The smith's finger came up between their faces, trembling with conviction.
"If Black Fang laps me too, I'm done.
I mean it.
I'll renounce having bodily needs altogether.
I'll take orders, join Isveth's maidens, and worship you from a respectful distance for the rest of my unnaturally long life.
A shrine maiden." A pause.
"A shrine smith tank maiden."
"..." Quinlan remained silent, listening to this wonderful girl put her thoughts out there for once.
Always so shy, always content to remain in the smithy while he was having fun with his girls.

Both of her calloused hands came up and framed his face, and under all the ranting her eyes were steady and bright and serious, because that was the confession beneath the comedy: she had wanted him for a while now, quietly, thoroughly, with the same patience she gave a long fold, while duty and war kept taking her turn away from her.
She had never once complained about the waiting.
She was complaining now because it was finally over, and she could at last afford to admit how heavy it had been.
Sera moved first.
"Let me help you~" She slid in behind Kaelira, fingers finding the shirt's hem, and her voice dropped low, meant for no one but Kaelira.
"Is it okay?
Me being here for this."
Kaelira's hand found Sera's wrist and held.
"Yes...
Please stay.
I need you to stay." A shaky exhale.
"I'd combust on my own."
Sera giggled at that, bright and warm, and patted Kaelira's hair.
"Then let big sis Sera take care of you~" She gathered Kaelira's head onto her thighs, soft and unhurried.
"I'm older than you," Kaelira murmured, but she settled into Sera's lap and did not move a centimeter away.
"Shh~ Big sisters are a state of mind."

Sera took the shirt's hem in both hands and peeled the forge-smudged linen up and over her best friend's head in the half-second Quinlan's mouth left hers, and his mouth was back before the linen hit the ground.
Then the wraps beneath, unwound turn by turn, Sera's fingers patient and practiced along the bindings, each discarded layer folded once and set aside.
The snow-light received what the forge-light never had.

She was built the way she built things, nothing wasted: the sweat-sheened plane of her stomach with its chiseled ridges, the hard taper of her waist into hips set like a stance, the smithing arm with its cords of quiet muscle, and above all of it, freed of their binding, the surprisingly heavy curve of her breasts, a softness the wraps had been flatly lying about for all those months.
Kaelira did not cover herself.
She planted her palms in the moss on either side of Sera's knees, chin up, flushed to the collar, and let him look until looking visibly stopped being enough for him.
"Say something," she soon begged.
He wasted absolutely no time and decreed with a straight face: "I'm looking at the best thing a smithy ever produced."
"Quin...
I can't do this..." Kaelira whimpered.
His mouth started at her throat and worked down without hurrying, and he handled her exactly the way she'd always suspected he would.
Thoroughly, patiently, in the correct order.
He learned the weight of her breasts with both hands and then with his mouth until her spine came up off the moss and her gasp rang off the roots.
He traced the ridges of her stomach with his tongue like they were a personal gift to him, which, judging by the low sound he made against them, was his honest position on the matter.

Muscle earned over a lifetime at the anvil jumped and trembled under his lips, and he took his time with every ridge, murmuring his appreciation into her skin, shameless about how much he liked them, until she was squirming from the praise as much as the touch.
Then he found the faint old scars along her forearm and kissed those too, one by one, and that, of all things, was what made her eyes sting.
Above her, Sera's thumb caught the first tear before it reached her ear, and said nothing, and kept combing.
Then, as he shifted to settle lower, Kaelira's hand closed on his shoulder and pushed.
He let her push.
"Oh?"

Two meters of primordial rolled over into the moss, interested, and the smith sat up, swung a thigh across his hips, and looked down at her naked lover, flushed and resolute, like she'd rehearsed this decision in her head a hundred times.
"My turn."
"Oh my~" Sera's eyebrows climbed, delighted.
"And here I sat, ready to hold your hand through the scary parts.
Look at you go~"
"He's my lover." Kaelira's palms spread flat over his chest and started mapping, slow and thorough, reading him the way she read everything worth reading, hands first.
Her ears were incandescent.
Her touch did not waver at all.
"I find him..." one hard swallow "...extremely attractive.
I have watched this body across a forge for months.
Today it worked a bellows for me, half-naked, for an hour.
I am not going to lie back and just receive like some... some dead fish woman." Dignity and blush fought over her face.
"I want to feel him too.
Why should he get all the... the doing?"
She bent, and put her mouth on him.
