paragraphs: "I want to feel him too. Why should he get all the... the doing?"
Kaelira bent, and put her mouth on him.
"'The doing,'" Sera repeated reverently, committing it to memory forever.
"Shut up..." Kaelira murmured against his skin, tongue out.

There was nothing tentative about what came next, only inexperience burning itself away in real time. She kissed his chest, dragged her lips along his collarbone, licked the salt of the day's work off his skin and hummed at the taste, low and satisfied, the note she usually saved for good steel.

She found the pale old seams scattered across the sculpted plates of him and gave each the same grave attention he'd given hers. Her palms read the ridges of his stomach, the swell of his arms, the shift of muscle when he breathed, and her own breathing grew audibly less steady the further she mapped, and she kept going anyway, red to the ear-tips, entirely undeterred.
Quinlan lay in the moss under his shy elf's blazing-eared inspection, smug as a dragon being appraised by exactly the right person.
It was when her explorations reached his waistband that the afternoon found its next lesson.
She got him free of the last of his clothes, sat back on her heels, and stilled completely, violet eyes fixed on the hefty shaft standing against his stomach.
"...Hm." The flush rolled down past her collarbones. "I've heard a lot about it..."
"Blossom?" Sera asked.

"What do you mean, 'Blossom?'" The healer elf was given the wryest of looks. "All of you keep going on and on about it, teasing me endlessly... Blossom speaks eagerly about 'Quinlan Junior' but so are Lucille, Aurora, Kitsara and..." Her eyes narrowed. "You."
"...Me? I'd never tease my friend," Sera told the canopy warmly.
"Mhm."

"Alright, Kaeli, stop pouting at me like that, you're way too adorable." The cheeky elf flowed up out of her lounging, shedding her dress along the way with a shrug the garment simply agreed to, and settled in at Kaelira's side, warm skin against warm skin. She cracked her knuckles with theatrical ceremony. "Hearing isn't the same as knowing. Which means it's time for big sis to give you the practical portion, before you hurt yourself with enthusiasm. Watch closely."
While the gals were having their adorable little pouting warfare, Quinlan leaned back, hands behind his head, manhood ready, and just watched, far too content with his life right now.
"Look at the smugness~" Sera giggled.
"...He's very happy," Kaelira replied, half looking at his grin, half at the eagerly waiting entity between his legs.
"Of course he is. Do you know why?" The question was theatrical, but its recipient answered nonetheless, ears twitching.
"The two of us are about to pamper him..."

"Right on~" Sera purred as she wrapped her fingers around the base of his cock with the easy confidence of long practice, and her lecture voice was a purring, tilde-laced disgrace from the first syllable.

"Foundations first. I'll be honest with you, Kaeli, I'm no Lucille. Nobody is Lucille. That woman is a natural phenomenon when it comes to the art of pleasing Quin with her mouth and the rest of us have made peace with it~ But I am very, very far from a rookie. So. Pressure at the base, like this, patience at the top. He pretends he's above all of it, but the underside, just below the crown, right here..."

She demonstrated. Her lips closed over the crown, her tongue found the exact spot she'd just lectured about, and she sank down his length by slow, practiced degrees until her nose brushed his stomach, held there, humming, and drew back up slow.
*Pop.*
Her eyebrows arched at Kaelira in silent lecture.

Quinlan, the big bad Primordial Villain, terror of powerful rulers all across the continent, exhaled hard through his nose, betrayed by his own body, and both elves noted the sound with identical satisfaction, a theory just confirmed.
"See~?" Sera came back up looking unbearable. "Eye contact is optional but devastating."
"So it's not optional," Kaelira noted, prompting Seraphiel to smile brightly.
"Indeed. If you're competitive about it, then it's not."
Seeing the determination on her friend's face, she knew she was looking at a future great of the art of blowing. This girl would not rest until she mastered the technique.

So, instead of yapping more, knowing both her friend and lover were eagerly awaiting, she only added a few important tips. "Breathe through your nose. Mind the teeth. It's okay to make sloppy sounds, that only makes him happier."
"Base pressure. Crown patience. Teeth... Sloppy." Kaelira nodded along, filing it all away. "Understood."
Then she gulped her nerves down, audibly, bent, and went to town.
*Slurp. Schlop.*
As technique went, it was a massacre.

She forgot the base almost immediately, applied patience nowhere at all, took him far too deep on the second pass, choked, and refused with visible fury to retreat a single centimeter, glaring up along his body as if daring him to comment. She did everything in the wrong order and some things in no known order.
Well, at least she got the sloppy part right.

But none of her shortcomings mattered, because what she lacked in craft she replaced with a sincerity so total it bordered on violence. Every drag of her mouth said it plainly: making this man feel good was the only job in the world.
Quinlan's head went back into the moss, and his groan scattered birds off three tiers of branches.
"...I don't believe this." Sera pressed a hand over her heart, mortally wounded. "It took me months of technique and refinement to get this over-pampered guy to make that sound for me."
Kaelira, mouth occupied, answered with a small, vicious hum of triumph.
It was a little after that, cheeks hollowed, eyes watering, thoroughly in over her head and refusing all rescue, that she did the thing neither of them expected.
She reached up, took both of Quinlan's hands, and placed them on her ears.
"...Hold me here," she managed, barely above a whisper, not meeting his eyes at all. "Please."
The hollow went quiet in a way that had nothing to do with sound.

Her ears. The one part of her that had never once obeyed her. They had betrayed her at the forge in front of three hundred dwarves, betrayed her in the salon, betrayed her every single time he so much as looked at her warmly, broadcasting everything her face refused to sign.
A lifetime of hiding what she was had taught her to armor everything else, her expression, her voice, her hands. Never the ears. And every elf alive guarded them by instinct because of it.
She had just handed them over.

Quinlan's hands closed around them with a gentleness that had no business belonging to hands his size, thumbs settling along the long ridges, and the sound Kaelira made around him at the contact was wrecked and grateful and shameless all at once. He held her exactly where she'd asked to be held, steady and certain, and she melted the rest of the way into him.
Sera watched her best friend hand over her oldest secret, and for once in her loud life commented absolutely nothing. 'This girl... She's a player.'

chapters.title: Chapter 1831 Big Sister's Generosity
paragraphs: What followed was not quick, because Kaelira had never once rushed a piece she cared about.

The frantic edge burned off and she settled in, unhurried and rhythmic, learning him one slow pass at a time, and what replaced the massacre was far worse for him: a devoted, wet, thorough patience that was utterly unembarrassed by its own sounds, exactly as instructed.
*Mm... schlop... mmh~*

And she watched him the entire time. Big, happy, violet elven eyes stayed mashed into his and never once let go, shining up along his body with open delight at every hitch of breath she managed to cause, and Sera's most devastating technique turned out to require no technique at all when the eyes doing it meant everything they said.

The forest kept them company. The light-columns between the trunks slid by slow degrees, the birds came back one wary branch at a time and resumed their afternoon arguments, and the little sun over the bower crackled softly to itself while the Primordial's lover worshipped at her own pace.

Sera stayed at the hollow's edge with her bare feet dangling into the air, toes swinging in small absent arcs while she watched, chin on her palms, her whole face gone soft. Somewhere along the way she'd started humming, an old elven melody, pretty and wandering, and it wove itself beneath the sounds of the work as if it had always belonged there.

Now and then her hand drifted over to pet Kaelira's hair, smoothing it back from her working cheeks, tucking a strand behind one crimson ear, and Kaelira leaned into each touch without ever breaking stride or eye contact.
"Look at you," the blue-eyed elf murmured, to one of them, or both, or neither. Nobody asked her to clarify.

He lasted a long time, because upgrades or not, the stamina that came with the Primordial Breeding Physique had never gone anywhere. But that only gave her more time to practice, and by the end his hands were weakening around her ears, the most ominous creature on the continent coming apart by inches under a rookie's devotion.
"Kaelira." Gravel had come into his voice, and his hands tightened around her ears exactly as steady as she'd asked for. "It's coming."
Violet eyes flew wide, then darted sideways to her self-appointed big sis, asking for guidance with everything a face could ask while her mouth was this full.

Sera had never looked smugger in her life. Chin on her palms, bare feet swinging merrily, she delivered the final lesson like it was a nursery rhyme. "Keep your tongue moving diligently around the shaft~ And then it's just gulp~ gulp~ gulp~"

The last three words came with a little roll of her throat that was somehow the lewdest thing anyone had said all day, and Kaelira went scarlet from hairline to shoulders without surrendering a single centimeter of her work.
"Aww~" Sera's grin softened at the edges. "Want big sis to hold your hand?"
A weak nod, tiny and instant and entirely without shame left to spend.
Sera's hand slid into hers and squeezed, and that settled that.

Kaelira answered him with a hum, her free hand digging into his hip, anchoring the way she anchored against a pour gone violent. Then he pulsed hot against her tongue and gave his newest lover her first load, thick and generous and shamelessly primordial in volume.
"Mmph!?"
She struggled with it. Her throat worked in long, laboring swallows, one bead escaped the corner of her mouth and was chased back in with a knuckle.
*Gulp. Gulp. Gulp.*
Exactly as taught, she stayed planted, resolute, drinking him down swallow after stubborn swallow and refusing to surrender a single drop of her first commission.
Then, chest heaving and eyes glassy, she sat back on her heels, looked him dead in the eye, and opened her mouth wide to show him her hard work: empty, finished, signed.

Quinlan's heart skipped a beat. Genuinely skipped, the same heart that had kept perfect time through duels and wars and the collapse of kingdoms stumbling once, hard, because a shy smith with blazing ears had just presented her work for his inspection.
"...I didn't teach her that part," Sera whispered, somewhere between religious awe and career concern.
"Well?" Kaelira rasped, wiping the corner of her mouth with the back of her hand, ears incandescent and gaze unwavering. "Did I pass?"

He answered by hauling her up his body and kissing her, deep and unhurried. By the time she surfaced, she could feel the answer pressed against her stomach, as ready as if the last few minutes had been a warm-up stretch. His bottomless stamina was not a rumor. The day would run out before he did.

He laid her back into the deep moss of the bower, the little sun burning low above them, and settled between her thighs, and the forest went soft around them as if it knew: the birdsong easing, the light-columns leaning, the warmth of the earth rising to meet her spine.
Her heels found the backs of his legs. Her hands gripped his shoulders like a haft she was testing for balance. He waited, one last time, asking with nothing but the stillness.
"Quin. Thank you for being so considerate, but..." Kaelira looked up at him, violet eyes enormous and clear. "I really am ready. Move, please. Make me yours..."

He nodded and pressed into her, slow and inexorable, opening her around him one held breath at a time, and her nails bit crescents into his shoulders as her breath tore on the sharp sting of a threshold crossed and gone.

He stopped there, buried to the hilt in her heat, holding his weight off her on his forearms, giving her the stillness. Her breath came in ragged pulls. Her thighs trembled once against his hips, then steadied.
Then he saw them: twin lines of wet sliding from the corners of her eyes, back toward her crimson ears, catching the light.
Everything in him went still at once, his voice dropping soft and urgent. "K-"
"I did it!" It came out wet and it came out laughing, both at once.

She caught his face in both hands so he could see it plainly: she was crying, and underneath the tears she was grinning like her whole soul had come loose. "I'm not hurt, you enormous idiot. I'm happy. I finally lost it. Finally. FINALLY." A hiccup of a laugh escaped her, and her voice cracked and dropped to almost nothing. "And so much more importantly than that... I lost it to you."
For a few seconds Quinlan didn't move at all.

Then he came down off his forearms, slid his arms under her back and around her shoulders, and hugged her, tight and complete, her face pressed into his neck, his buried in her hair, holding his smith like the world outside the bower had been cancelled. He didn't move and he didn't speak, just held on, hard, while she shook once against him and clung right back with all the strength her forge had ever built into her.

Because it had never really been about the milestone. Her whole life had been things taken out of her hands: her craft made criminal, her future sentenced into a conscript wave, her first forge hidden in a cellar like a shame.

This one thing she had kept, guarded, and given away herself, on a day she judged worthy, to the man she had chosen. Nobody had taken it from her. She had handed it over, and it had been received like treasure.
"You're far too precious..." he said into her hair, rough.

"Hehe..." Her arms cinched tighter around his neck. "...I assume we don't just lie here like this until you finish, right?" she asked, but her voice was pure eagerness, ready to take the full package and experience everything being with this man entailed.
"Right." Quinlan laughed, and moved.

The afternoon stopped being gentle by increments. She caught his rhythm faster than any book had promised and then began answering it, hips rolling up to meet him, forge-built strength giving as good as it got, and there was laughter at first, hers, breathless and disbelieving at how good it was.
"Ah...! Ahn... mm... that's..." Every moan out of her sounded like a discovery, cute and blunt at once, exactly like her.

"Harder." It came out exactly like her forge instructions, blunt and certain even with her voice shaking at the edges. "I'm not made of glass. I have one real advantage over the others, and I intend to make full use of it..."
He grinned into the crook of her neck, low and delighted. "It's not a competition, but..."

He gave her precisely what she'd ordered, and it kept getting better. An arm hooked under the small of her back to lift her into every stroke, moss tearing under her grip, his name breaking in her mouth in a register no forge had ever heard. Her hands left his shoulders for his back, holding on with everything the anvil had ever built into her. When she felt him grin against her throat at the strength of it, she dug in harder on purpose, marking what was hers.
"Hie!? Ah! Ahn... Quin...!" Her yelps chased each other up the trunks, climbing higher with every stroke.
Somewhere in the middle of it, Sera's hand found hers in the moss and laced through, and Kaelira gripped it without ever opening her eyes, and neither elf said a word about it.
And the forest answered them.
Neither of them noticed it begin. The moss of the bower deepened and went lush under her clawing hands, and the light-columns leaned closer.

Then, chest heaving and eyes glassy, she sat back on her heels, looked him dead in the eye, and opened her mouth wide to show him her hard work: empty, finished, signed.
Quinlan's heart skipped a beat.

Genuinely skipped, the same heart that had kept perfect time through duels and wars and the collapse of kingdoms stumbling once, hard, because a shy smith with blazing ears had just presented her work for his inspection.
"...I didn't teach her that part," Sera whispered, somewhere between religious awe and career concern.
"Well?" Kaelira rasped, wiping the corner of her mouth with the back of her hand, ears incandescent and gaze unwavering.
"Did I pass?"
He answered by hauling her up his body and kissing her, deep and unhurried.
By the time she surfaced, she could feel the answer pressed against her stomach, as ready as if the last few minutes had been a warm-up stretch.
His bottomless stamina was not a rumor.
The day would run out before he did.

He laid her back into the deep moss of the bower, the little sun burning low above them, and settled between her thighs, and the forest went soft around them as if it knew: the birdsong easing, the light-columns leaning, the warmth of the earth rising to meet her spine.
Her heels found the backs of his legs.
Her hands gripped his shoulders like a haft she was testing for balance.
He waited, one last time, asking with nothing but the stillness.
"Quin.
Thank you for being so considerate, but..." Kaelira looked up at him, violet eyes enormous and clear.
"I really am ready.
Move, please.
Make me yours..."

He nodded and pressed into her, slow and inexorable, opening her around him one held breath at a time, and her nails bit crescents into his shoulders as her breath tore on the sharp sting of a threshold crossed and gone.
He stopped there, buried to the hilt in her heat, holding his weight off her on his forearms, giving her the stillness.
Her breath came in ragged pulls.
Her thighs trembled once against his hips, then steadied.
Then he saw them: twin lines of wet sliding from the corners of her eyes, back toward her crimson ears, catching the light.
Everything in him went still at once, his voice dropping soft and urgent.
"I did it!" It came out wet and it came out laughing, both at once.
She caught his face in both hands so he could see it plainly: she was crying, and underneath the tears she was grinning like her whole soul had come loose.
"I'm not hurt, you enormous idiot.
I'm happy.
I finally lost it.
Finally.
FINALLY." A hiccup of a laugh escaped her, and her voice cracked and dropped to almost nothing.
"And so much more importantly than that...
I lost it to you."
For a few seconds Quinlan didn't move at all.

Then he came down off his forearms, slid his arms under her back and around her shoulders, and hugged her, tight and complete, her face pressed into his neck, his buried in her hair, holding his smith like the world outside the bower had been cancelled.
He didn't move and he didn't speak, just held on, hard, while she shook once against him and clung right back with all the strength her forge had ever built into her.
Because it had never really been about the milestone.
Her whole life had been things taken out of her hands: her craft made criminal, her future sentenced into a conscript wave, her first forge hidden in a cellar like a shame.
This one thing she had kept, guarded, and given away herself, on a day she judged worthy, to the man she had chosen.
Nobody had taken it from her.
She had handed it over, and it had been received like treasure.
"You're far too precious..." he said into her hair, rough.
"Hehe..." Her arms cinched tighter around his neck.

"...I assume we don't just lie here like this until you finish, right?" she asked, but her voice was pure eagerness, ready to take the full package and experience everything being with this man entailed.
"Right." Quinlan laughed, and moved.
The afternoon stopped being gentle by increments.

She caught his rhythm faster than any book had promised and then began answering it, hips rolling up to meet him, forge-built strength giving as good as it got, and there was laughter at first, hers, breathless and disbelieving at how good it was.
Ahn... mm... that's..." Every moan out of her sounded like a discovery, cute and blunt at once, exactly like her.
"Harder." It came out exactly like her forge instructions, blunt and certain even with her voice shaking at the edges.
"I'm not made of glass.
I have one real advantage over the others, and I intend to make full use of it..."
He grinned into the crook of her neck, low and delighted.
"It's not a competition, but..."
He gave her precisely what she'd ordered, and it kept getting better.
An arm hooked under the small of her back to lift her into every stroke, moss tearing under her grip, his name breaking in her mouth in a register no forge had ever heard.
Her hands left his shoulders for his back, holding on with everything the anvil had ever built into her.
When she felt him grin against her throat at the strength of it, she dug in harder on purpose, marking what was hers.
"Hie!?
Ah!
Ahn...
Quin...!" Her yelps chased each other up the trunks, climbing higher with every stroke.
Somewhere in the middle of it, Sera's hand found hers in the moss and laced through, and Kaelira gripped it without ever opening her eyes, and neither elf said a word about it.
And the forest answered them.
Neither of them noticed it begin.
The moss of the bower deepened and went lush under her clawing hands, and the light-columns leaned closer.

chapters.title: Chapter 1832 Pleading For Mercy
paragraphs: Along the great roots that cradled them, out of season and out of reason, buds swelled and opened, small white blossoms unfolding by the dozen in the silver snow-light, as if the oldest ground in Elvardia had decided that whatever was happening in that hollow counted as spring.

Mana rose with them, dense and warm and approving, pouring up through the earth into two bodies built to conduct it. Low on Kaelira's bare stomach, Quinlan's crimson mark woke and glowed like a banked coal against all that silver and green.
"They're blooming," Sera whispered from the hollow's edge.
Kaelira, extremely occupied, did not care even slightly about the trees.
"Ah... ahh! Quin, I'm... it's...!"

The smith who finished everything she started chased her finish with single-minded focus and found it hard, spine bowing off the moss as she clamped down around him in waves. Her cry went up through the canopy and shook snow loose somewhere miles above. He worked her through every last tremor of it, then followed her over the edge with a groan pressed into her throat, filling her while she held him locked in with both legs and hummed, low and sated, like her own hammer had.
The blossoms kept opening for a while after that.
For a while afterward the bower held still, just breath and silver light and the far-off patience of the snow.

Kaelira lay poured into the moss where he'd left her, ears at half-mast, one forearm flung across her eyes, smiling like every number had come in high. Sera gathered her best friend's head back onto her lap without being asked and resumed the slow combing, humming to herself, pleased with the whole world.
Quinlan then looked at his first elven lover.

She had been patient all day in a smithy that wasn't hers, tender all afternoon through a milestone that wasn't hers, and quiet at every moment that needed her quiet, which for Sera was the expensive part. None of it had escaped him.
"Sera."
"Mm~?" She glanced up from her work, caught what was in his eyes, and slowed. "...Oh."
"Good girls deserve a reward."

The Dawnbringer lit up from somewhere well beneath the skin. Then, because she was Sera, she immediately set about ruining it. "Well, naturally~" she purred, laying a modest hand over her heart. "I am always perfect. It is a heavy burden, but somebody in this family has to... Quin?" The combing stopped. "Why are you looking at me like-"
He was on her before the sentence found its ending.
"Kyaa~!"
The pounce took her clean off Kaelira and down into the deep moss, and the yelp Sera loosed on the way was, by any honest measure, the happiest noise the forest had heard all day.

"Mercy~!" she wailed, making no attempt whatsoever to escape, arms already winding around his neck in open contradiction of everything her mouth was doing. "Mercy, dreaded primordial! I am but a helpless elven maiden, alone and defenseless in the deep woods! Whatever shall become of my poor, innocent... ah. Ahh~"
"Time to feast," the Villain of the continent decreed, straight-faced, and set about keeping his word.
What followed was, by the standards of Sera's theater, a masterpiece with a very short run.

She fluttered her lashes, she pleaded her innocence, she beat two dainty protests against his chest that both ended with her fingers gripping him closer, and she held the helpless-maiden voice through an admirable amount of begging that fooled no one, least of all the maiden herself.

Then he hooked her knees over his arms, folded her down into the moss, and drove into her in one long, merciless stroke, granting her petition exactly as filed: none. The performance cracked straight down the middle, the tildes losing their curl first, then the words losing their order, until there were no words left at all, just Sera, loud and unscripted, heels locked at the small of his back, being thoroughly relieved of her veteran's composure.
"Hyan~! Ah! Ahn! W-wait... don't wait... ahn~!"
Kaelira watched the whole production from one arm's length away, propped on an elbow in the wreck of her own afterglow, and forgot to blink.
She had known Sera was shameless. Everyone knew Sera was shameless; the reputation traveled ahead of her like perfume.

But knowing it and watching it turned out to be two different disciplines entirely, because the veteran of the family, the lecturer, the composed author of today's tutorial, was currently begging a primordial for a mercy she had specifically arranged not to receive, and enjoying herself more honestly than Kaelira had ever seen her enjoy anything.
'The tales were censored,' the smith realized, somewhere between scandal and awe.
"You weren't like this when you were teaching," she observed aloud, flat as an inspection report.
"Sh-shut up~!"
Kaelira did not, as it happened, shut up. But watching had its limits, and Kaelira had never in her life been content to watch a craft she could learn.

The smith pushed herself up on arms that still trembled faintly, crawled the arm's length over, and settled at the head of the moss, gathering Sera's disheveled golden head onto her bare thighs and steadying it there with both palms, exactly the way it had been done for her.
"Shh." She stroked her best friend's hair back from her damp forehead, ears blazing, voice level as a load rating. "This big sis will take care of you."

Sera's eyes flew open and found her upside down. For one whole second the self-declared big sis looked genuinely, cosmically betrayed, and then the next wave hit and betrayal stopped being an available emotion.
"Cheeky little sisters... deserve to be... punished!" she managed, in pieces, half moan and half promise, and that was the end of the lecture.
They went at it for hours.
The silver light between the trunks warmed toward the amber of a day winding down, the little sun over the bower burned patiently on, and nobody anywhere suggested stopping.

Kaelira came back for seconds with the shameless directness of a new convert, then thirds. She rode him with her palms braced on his chest and her ears flat with concentration, adjusting her hips by degrees until she found the angle that made her vision white out, and announced it out loud, like a measurement. After that she stopped announcing anything, because the angle did the talking, and the deep forest learned exactly what a smith sounded like when her discipline finally lost an argument.
"AHN~! Hyah... ah...!"
Roughly like that.

The tutorial continued in installments just like that, Sera demonstrating and Kaelira mastering, until the geometry stopped being worth tracking: a tangle of three in a moss hollow under a private sun, two elves and the man they'd chosen, warmth below and winter miles above, the birds long since resigned to the noise.

Much later, Kaelira lay in the middle of the pile, listening to two heartbeats and the enormous, patient quiet of the trees. Sera was draped over her back, boneless, one arm flung across them both, and the dusk around them smelled like spring. One foot dangled past the bower's edge, toes drawing slow lines through the moss, still talking to the forest.

The day ran back through her in slow flashes: a sealed door opening, adamantite offered and declined, humble steel singing under her hammer, an old dwarf tearing up seeing her work, the law that had sentenced her to die dissolving in the one hall where it should have been strongest, a hammer left humming on an anvil.
And then this.
Her fingers found the woven necklace at Quinlan's throat in the fading light, the leaves and seedpods and fanatic geometry of it, and settled there.
'Worth the wait,' she murmured to herself. 'I'm so glad I waited for the right moment, instead of rushing it...'
Quinlan lay under his two elves and watched the blossoms glow faint in the day's last light, one arm around each of them, and let them drift a while longer before he said it.
"When you two are rested," he said to the canopy, quiet, "It's time we turn serious again."
Kaelira smiled, nodding into his skin. Against his side, she felt Sera's lashes lift too.
"Myrasyn must be waiting." Above the bower, the little sun banked itself low. "Let's go claim the elven race, shall we?"

chapters.title: Chapter 1833 Back in the Royal Elven Palace
paragraphs: Quinlan stepped out of the [Warp Gate] and onto the high terrace of Luminareth's palace with an elf under each arm and the deep forest's traces still clinging to all three of them.

The capital met them with its best hour. The sun was going down somewhere beyond the canopy, and its light came in low and sideways, strained through a million leaves until the whole city ran amber and rose.

Walkways of living wood glowed like banked coals, the great trunks wore the evening on their western faces, and far below, in the blue shadows between the roots, the first lantern-buds were waking one by one.
"Sweet Goddess's Lacy Panties~" Sera arched against his arm and drank the view down. "Fine, I'll say it. The palace evenings are almost as good as our home's."
"It's beautiful, but nothing beats a sunset happening from under Rosie's tree," Kaelira said.
"Exactly!" Sera nodded, joyous.
Somewhere behind them, a tray nearly died.

The yelp came first, then the rescue: a young maid caught her own tray out of the air with reflexes her posture immediately apologized for. Then the terrace staff converged on the three of them with the speed and coordination of a practiced strike team.

Cool cloths appeared. Chilled fruit wine appeared. A cushioned bench was aimed at Quinlan's general direction and deployed with military urgency, and a dozen elven maids in palace livery arranged themselves into a half-circle of trembling readiness, ears high, eyes shining.
"Welcome back, Holy Son!" the eldest of them said, bowing deep to Quinlan while the rest of the half-circle sank with her. "Welcome back, honored... Ladies of the Line?"
"Holy Consorts?" another whispered from the second rank, testing it.
"Sacred Companions?"
Sera let the titles pile up a moment longer, savoring every one, then raised a gracious hand and stopped the auction.
"You can call me," she said, letting it purr, "the First Elf."

The half-circle went white. A dozen spines locked at once, and the youngest maid's lips started moving in what was unmistakably prayer. The whisperer from the second rank swayed where she stood, eyes flicking from Sera's face to Sera's ears and back while a life of theology tried to rearrange itself around a blue-eyed healer with moss in her hair.
Quinlan's hand tightened on her butt.
"...of the Holy Son~" Sera finished.
The exhale that traveled down the line was strong enough to stir the lantern-buds.
"Kaelira is fine," Kaelira then spoke her own preferred title.
Nobody was going to call the Holy Son's woman just Kaelira, and the resulting negotiation carried them across the terrace in a warm, fussing cloud.

A maid relieved Quinlan of nothing, because he carried nothing, and looked briefly devastated about it. Another crouched to brush moss dust from the hem of Kaelira's trousers and found the trousers largely made of moss dust at this point. A third reached up to pluck a small white blossom from Kaelira's hair.
She froze with it between two fingers.
The petals were fresh. It was midwinter. That flower barely bloomed at all, and every elf on the terrace knew where the old trees grew that it fell from.

The maid looked at the blossom, then at the moss, then at the three of them, all that monstrous, half-dressed, forest-smelling contentment, and arrived, with an audible swallow, at the only conclusion the evidence allowed: the Holy Son had spent the better part of a day rutting his two consorts senseless in the Progenitor's own deep forest, on the sacred moss, under the sacred trees, and then all three of them had warped directly from the scene to a royal ceremony without so much as a comb between them.
Very carefully, with both hands, she tucked the blossom back into Kaelira's hair like a relic being reshelved.
"...Don't," Kaelira warned, ears already heating.
"I said nothing, honored lady."
"Loudly," Sera added.
Quinlan drained his cup, handed it back to a maid who received it like a holy vessel, and rolled his shoulders against the last of the forest's pleasant ache.
"So." He looked over the half-circle. "Is Myra ready for us?"
The terrace stopped.
It was a warm sort of stop. A dozen elven maids stood there while the syllables settled over them, and their ears did the talking, tilting one by one toward some private, wistful horizon.
"...Myra," the youngest repeated under her breath, tasting the shape of it, as though checking whether saying it secondhand required penance.

"Your Queen," Quinlan clarified, but that was not the problem. All of them understood who he was referring to, their ancient, legendary matriarch who had been ruling over them for four thousand years, the bringer of light, one of the strongest mages their people ever produced.
And that woman...
"The Queen has a pet name...!!" someone whispered from the back.
"What a lucky woman," someone else whispered, with feeling, and half the line nodded before their discipline caught up.
The line's composure buckled down its entire length until the eldest maid clapped twice, order snapped back down the line, and she turned back to Quinlan with her dignity reassembled.
"Her Majesty is in the final preparations, Holy Son. She asks for a little more of your patience, and commands us to see to your every comfort until she sends for you."
"Daddy!"

The shriek arrived ahead of its owner. Rosie rounded the terrace corner at a full sprint, flanked by two royal guards who were trying to escort her with ceremony and failing at a jog, and behind them a palace clerk clutched a leaf-paper folio to her chest like it held state secrets. Which, in a sense, it did.
Quinlan crouched, caught the incoming dryad princess, and stood up with her already halfway through her report.
"Papa, Rosie GOVERNED!"
She had flowers threaded through her curls and the unmistakable air of a professional. "Rosie attended four meetings! Rosie only slept in one! Auntie Myra let Rosie sign real documents, look, look!"

The clerk, summoned by a small imperious hand, presented the folio. On the top sheet, beneath dense elven legal script, sat an enormous, laborious ROSIE in letters of three different sizes, decorated with a small drawing of a root.
"That one makes a road wider," Rosie explained gravely.
"A fine road it'll be," Quinlan said, equally grave, studying the signature like a connoisseur. "Strong signature. Good root."
"Rosie knows." She preened. Then her whole body lit up with the next thing, and she grabbed a double fistful of his collar. "Daddy, tonight there's a... mmmph."
Both of her hands had clamped over her own mouth.
The terrace held its breath. Rosie held her breath. Her eyes bulged with the effort of containment, and when she finally spoke again it was through her fingers, muffled and solemn.
"Nope. Rosie is not a snitch."
"Is that so?"

"Yes!" She wriggled down out of his arms, landed, and smoothed her ceremonial sash with two tiny palms, composure restored. She held up one finger at him, a perfect miniature of a lecturing minister. "No asking."
And with that she marched back to her guards, who fell in around her with straight faces and shaking shoulders, and the delegation departed the way it had come.
Sera watched her go, misty-eyed. "How can she be such an adorable cutie? If Mom saw this, she would've fainted on the spot. Or suffered a heart attack."
"Probably both?" Kaelira asked.
"Probably both," Sera agreed.

It was then that the eldest maid stepped forward again, folded her hands, and made the evening's real opening move. Her gaze went to Sera and Kaelira, took in the moss, the petals, the forge-and-forest state of them, and turned tactfully, delicately hopeful.
"Honored ladies. The ceremony tonight is... significant. If you would permit it, the palace would be honored to prepare you." A breath. "Baths are drawn. The salon is ready. Everything is ready."
The two elves looked at each other.
"Oh."

It was in this moment that the two of them realized they looked like naughty elves who'd just had hours of raunchy sex and, once done, had arrived at a royal ceremony without even brushing their hair.
Which was exactly what had happened.
Kaelira's ears had gone scarlet at the tips, and the color was still traveling, down her jaw and heading for territory her collar wouldn't cover.

Sera's grin spread slow and shameless, but a telltale pink had crept up her neck too, because there was being shameless behavior and also pure trashy behavior, and the Dawnbringer knew perfectly well which faction she wanted to be a part of.
"...Well, if it's for the ceremony," Sera decided, chin up, entirely failing to sound casual.
"Please take care of us," Kaelira managed, sheepish.

"You can call me," she said, letting it purr, "the First Elf."
The half-circle went white.
A dozen spines locked at once, and the youngest maid's lips started moving in what was unmistakably prayer.

The whisperer from the second rank swayed where she stood, eyes flicking from Sera's face to Sera's ears and back while a life of theology tried to rearrange itself around a blue-eyed healer with moss in her hair.
Quinlan's hand tightened on her butt.
"...of the Holy Son~" Sera finished.
The exhale that traveled down the line was strong enough to stir the lantern-buds.
"Kaelira is fine," Kaelira then spoke her own preferred title.
Nobody was going to call the Holy Son's woman just Kaelira, and the resulting negotiation carried them across the terrace in a warm, fussing cloud.
A maid relieved Quinlan of nothing, because he carried nothing, and looked briefly devastated about it.
Another crouched to brush moss dust from the hem of Kaelira's trousers and found the trousers largely made of moss dust at this point.
A third reached up to pluck a small white blossom from Kaelira's hair.
She froze with it between two fingers.
The petals were fresh.
It was midwinter.
That flower barely bloomed at all, and every elf on the terrace knew where the old trees grew that it fell from.

The maid looked at the blossom, then at the moss, then at the three of them, all that monstrous, half-dressed, forest-smelling contentment, and arrived, with an audible swallow, at the only conclusion the evidence allowed: the Holy Son had spent the better part of a day rutting his two consorts senseless in the Progenitor's own deep forest, on the sacred moss, under the sacred trees, and then all three of them had warped directly from the scene to a royal ceremony without so much as a comb between them.
Very carefully, with both hands, she tucked the blossom back into Kaelira's hair like a relic being reshelved.
"...Don't," Kaelira warned, ears already heating.
"I said nothing, honored lady."
"Loudly," Sera added.
Quinlan drained his cup, handed it back to a maid who received it like a holy vessel, and rolled his shoulders against the last of the forest's pleasant ache.
"So." He looked over the half-circle.
"Is Myra ready for us?"
The terrace stopped.
It was a warm sort of stop.
A dozen elven maids stood there while the syllables settled over them, and their ears did the talking, tilting one by one toward some private, wistful horizon.
"...Myra," the youngest repeated under her breath, tasting the shape of it, as though checking whether saying it secondhand required penance.
"Your Queen," Quinlan clarified, but that was not the problem.

All of them understood who he was referring to, their ancient, legendary matriarch who had been ruling over them for four thousand years, the bringer of light, one of the strongest mages their people ever produced.
And that woman...
"The Queen has a pet name...!!" someone whispered from the back.
"What a lucky woman," someone else whispered, with feeling, and half the line nodded before their discipline caught up.
The line's composure buckled down its entire length until the eldest maid clapped twice, order snapped back down the line, and she turned back to Quinlan with her dignity reassembled.
"Her Majesty is in the final preparations, Holy Son.
She asks for a little more of your patience, and commands us to see to your every comfort until she sends for you."
"Daddy!"
The shriek arrived ahead of its owner.

Rosie rounded the terrace corner at a full sprint, flanked by two royal guards who were trying to escort her with ceremony and failing at a jog, and behind them a palace clerk clutched a leaf-paper folio to her chest like it held state secrets.
Which, in a sense, it did.
Quinlan crouched, caught the incoming dryad princess, and stood up with her already halfway through her report.
"Papa, Rosie GOVERNED!"
She had flowers threaded through her curls and the unmistakable air of a professional.
"Rosie attended four meetings!
Rosie only slept in one!
Auntie Myra let Rosie sign real documents, look, look!"
The clerk, summoned by a small imperious hand, presented the folio.
On the top sheet, beneath dense elven legal script, sat an enormous, laborious ROSIE in letters of three different sizes, decorated with a small drawing of a root.
"That one makes a road wider," Rosie explained gravely.
"A fine road it'll be," Quinlan said, equally grave, studying the signature like a connoisseur.
"Strong signature.
Good root."
"Rosie knows." She preened.
Then her whole body lit up with the next thing, and she grabbed a double fistful of his collar.
"Daddy, tonight there's a... mmmph."
Both of her hands had clamped over her own mouth.
The terrace held its breath.
Rosie held her breath.
Her eyes bulged with the effort of containment, and when she finally spoke again it was through her fingers, muffled and solemn.
"Nope.
Rosie is not a snitch."
"Is that so?"
"Yes!" She wriggled down out of his arms, landed, and smoothed her ceremonial sash with two tiny palms, composure restored.
She held up one finger at him, a perfect miniature of a lecturing minister.
"No asking."
And with that she marched back to her guards, who fell in around her with straight faces and shaking shoulders, and the delegation departed the way it had come.
Sera watched her go, misty-eyed.
"How can she be such an adorable cutie?
If Mom saw this, she would've fainted on the spot.
Or suffered a heart attack."
"Probably both?" Kaelira asked.
"Probably both," Sera agreed.
It was then that the eldest maid stepped forward again, folded her hands, and made the evening's real opening move.
Her gaze went to Sera and Kaelira, took in the moss, the petals, the forge-and-forest state of them, and turned tactfully, delicately hopeful.
"Honored ladies.
The ceremony tonight is... significant.
If you would permit it, the palace would be honored to prepare you." A breath.
"Baths are drawn.
The salon is ready.
Everything is ready."
The two elves looked at each other.
"Oh."

It was in this moment that the two of them realized they looked like naughty elves who'd just had hours of raunchy sex and, once done, had arrived at a royal ceremony without even brushing their hair.
Which was exactly what had happened.
Kaelira's ears had gone scarlet at the tips, and the color was still traveling, down her jaw and heading for territory her collar wouldn't cover.

Sera's grin spread slow and shameless, but a telltale pink had crept up her neck too, because there was being shameless behavior and also pure trashy behavior, and the Dawnbringer knew perfectly well which faction she wanted to be a part of.
"...Well, if it's for the ceremony," Sera decided, chin up, entirely failing to sound casual.
"Please take care of us," Kaelira managed, sheepish.

chapters.title: Chapter 1834 Twink Garbs
paragraphs: The half-circle of maids lit up like a festival, a joy wildly disproportionate to the task, the joy of people who had won something.

They closed around the two women in a warm tide of guiding hands and reverent chatter, and they were already halfway to the archway when Quinlan pushed off the bench he had eventually been herded onto and followed.
The tide stalled.

A dozen sets of ears swiveled toward him. The maids looked at the Holy Son, then at each other, and a silent crisis moved down the line like weather. Protocol said nothing about this. Scripture said nothing about this. Nobody breathed until the eldest maid turned, bowed to him carefully, and ventured, with the courage of her office:
"Holy Son. Do you... require something?"
Quinlan raised an eyebrow, honestly confused.
"What, I don't get scrubbed?"
A tray hit the terrace somewhere to the left. Nobody went to pick it up.

For three full seconds the royal household of Luminareth stood in perfect, ringing silence, processing the blessing that had just been dropped on it without warning, and then a maid in the second rank sat down.
Just sat, right there on the terrace boards, one hand pressed to her sternum, while her neighbor made a sound that had last been heard from Isveth in the presence of relics.
"The Holy Son," the eldest maid said slowly, like handling live runes, "wishes for us... to prepare him. Ourselves."
"Is it a problem?" Quinlan asked with a straight face. He was not, whatever that face claimed, a dense man. He was having fun with these turbo loyal and expressive maids.

"A problem." She said the word from very far away. Then her spine straightened, her chin rose, and she accepted the field promotion with the gravity of a general being handed a war. "Ladies. Second shift to the honored consorts. First shift, with me."
The wing of the palace they took him to smelled of warm cedar and blossom oil, and what followed was less a bath than a coronation with soap.
He let them have all of it.

Synchra came off first, at his word, "Take the evening off, let them work," and the living garment rippled once with unmistakable sulk before pouring off his shoulders and coiling herself into a black torc around his wrist, radiating the air of a cat relocated from the one chair she wanted.

The maids inhaled as one. Then there were two meters of half-bare primordial standing in the steam, scarred and monumental in the lamplight, and the first shift of the royal household briefly forgot every procedure it had ever drilled.

They recovered like professionals, working in rotation by some unspoken schedule enforced with elbows in ribs, so that every maid in the wing would be able to say, for the rest of her long life, that she had once attended the Son of the Progenitor, and no sister could say she hadn't.
One maid combed his wet hair back with the focus of a scholar restoring a manuscript.

Another, evidently the shift's self-appointed dignity, worked oil into his shoulders with brisk professional strokes that told the entire wing someone here was above all of this. Quinlan rolled the shoulder under her hands, and she went to check on the towels.
A third found the pale old seams scattered across his back, hesitated, and then traced one with a fingertip so light and so reverent that it tickled.
"You can press harder," Quinlan said lazily, eyes closed, arms draped along the rim of the bath, treating being worshipped as a perfectly reasonable use of an evening.
"Yes, Holy Son," she whispered, and did not press harder, because the scar was scripture and you do not lean on scripture.

The drying very nearly caused a schism. The maid who won the right started at his shoulders with a warmed towel and total composure, made it as far as the ridges of his stomach, and had to be relieved of duty by a colleague when her hands simply stopped moving, ears pinned flat, eyes gone somewhere her training couldn't follow.
Her replacement lasted two ridges longer.

Down the hall, behind screens and steam, a parallel operation announced its own progress. Sera's laughter rolled through the wall at intervals, bright and scandalized. Kaelira's voice arrived only once, a flat, carrying "that stays where it is," followed by giggling that suggested it had not stayed where it was.

It was somewhere in the middle of the drying and the combing that Kaelira's head appeared around the edge of the connecting screen, hair pinned up off her neck, expression puzzled by something other than the four maids currently orbiting her.
"Quin. Didn't we have an escort?" she said. "Royal. Armored. Hissed a lot."
A pause with genuine thought in it.
"Elowen!" Sera's face appeared above Kaelira's, lit with delight.
Both elves looked at Quinlan, ears twitching in wait.
Quinlan, horizontal under three sets of devoted hands, shrugged with the shoulder no one was currently oiling.
"She could use some time in the smithy," he said. "Builds character. I'll pick her up when I feel like it."
Far away under a mountain, at that exact moment, the royal guard Elowen was being taught her third dwarven drinking song against her will.
The heads withdrew, somehow deciding his response was acceptable.
The operation continued. And then, with the sun's last direct light going bronze on the windowsills, the operation hit the wall that everyone with functioning eyes should have seen coming.
The clothes.

They brought him the finest ceremonial menswear the palace held, and the palace held wonders: robes of leaf-silk that shimmered like standing water, high-collared court coats embroidered past all reason, garments that would have made any elven lord weep with vanity.
Every one of them had been cut for elven men, which was to say, for willowy creatures whose shoulders had never argued with anything heavier than a harp.
A seam gave first: the finest robe made it over one arm before the shoulder surrendered with a sound like a snapped bowstring, and the maid holding the other sleeve flinched as if wounded herself.
Next came the largest formal coat in the royal wardrobe, which refused to close across his chest by a handspan. The sash reached. Technically.
"He's bulging," a maid reported from behind him, in a tone unsuitable for tailoring.
"Out of it, or in it?"
"Yes."
The wing descended into beautiful, blasphemous chaos.
Runners were dispatched to farther wardrobes and returned defeated.

Someone proposed summoning the tailors' hall, and someone else pointed out the ceremony was in under an hour. Someone proposed, very quietly, that the Holy Son could attend as he was, a suggestion that was scandalous, heretical, and seconded twice before the eldest maid killed it with one look.
Quinlan stood in the middle of the storm, arms out, thoroughly enjoying himself while elven maids swarmed him with pins and measuring cord and despair.
"I've conquered dwarven forts with less resistance," he told the ceiling.
"Please don't move, Holy Son."
"No need to fret so much. If you don't have apparel that fits, I'll just have Synchra take on a form you'll find fitting."
"Please don't say such a thing, Holy Son."
His proposal was shut down instantly, all maids being far too invested in getting him into actual elven garb by now.

It was the oldest of them, a silver-haired maid who had said almost nothing all evening, who suddenly went still in the middle of the panic. Her eyes lost focus, tracking something down a corridor of years, and when they came back they were wide.
"...The weavers' vault," she said.

chapters.title: Chapter 1835 The Big Surprise
paragraphs: The room stopped.
"The old measure," she said, louder, already moving. "Send a runner to the weavers' hall. Run."

Nobody asked what she meant. Two maids simply detonated out of the room, and the wing waited out the longest quarter hour of its collective life until the hall answered, in the form of a cedar chest carried in by two silver-robed elders of the weavers' guild, borne on their arms with the pace and posture reserved for the bones of saints.
The chest was old. The wax seals on it were older. The senior weaver broke them with hands gone careful with age, folded back layers of cloth soft as breath, and lifted out the garment inside.

White, and gold. A long ceremonial vestment of heavy leaf-silk, its every hem worked with thread-of-gold in the pattern of leaves and seedpods, the geometry of the deep forest made formal wear. It was beautiful work by masters, and it was enormous, cut for a chest like a gate and shoulders like a lintel, its sleeves sized for arms that could carry a fallen tree, or a war.
The room had gone silent around the comedy's grave.

"There is a story," the old weaver said into that silence, her voice worn smooth from telling it a thousand times to children, and never once to a man who might make it true. "That our men were not always as they are. That long ago, before something broke in our race, an elven man could stand eye to eye with his wife. Match her strength. Grow old beside her, all ten thousand years of it, instead of leaving her behind before her youth was even spent. That some among them could even sport your physique."
She smoothed the folded silk with one flat palm. "A curious old tale. No scholar credits it, but every generation, our hall weaves one garment to the old measure anyway."
She lifted it before Quinlan with her arms at full stretch, and her eyes were bright.
"Forgive an old woman her presumption. It would mean a great deal to some very patient ghosts."
Quinlan looked at the vestment for a long moment. He knew the story. He knew better than any elf alive that it was no story at all. He knew what had broken, and when. None of it reached his face.
"It'd be my honor," he replied, putting out his arms. With trembling fingers, they dressed him in it. It fit to the seam.

The shoulders sat where shoulders sit, the chest closed without complaint, the hems broke at exactly the height of a man no elf alive had ever seen, and the wing of the palace watched the old tale fit him like tailoring.
The eldest maid let out a shaky breath. The silver-haired one simply nodded, once, like a debt had been paid on schedule.
The screens at the connecting archway folded aside then, and the second shift presented its own work.

Sera came through first in white and pale gold, leaf-silk cut low across her collarbones and gathered at her waist with a cord of braided sunlight-thread, her hair brushed to a molten shine and crowned with a thin circlet of white blossoms.

Kaelira followed in deep forest-green shot with bronze, high-collared and elegant, the silk fitted close over the shoulders the forge had built her, dark hair pinned up off her neck with two long copper needles.
Quinlan's breath stopped. Both of them saw it happen, and neither of them would ever let him forget it.

They were stunning. This was an older, more formal beauty than the warm, familiar one he woke up beside, two elven ladies in the old style, dressed by a palace that adored them, and Quinlan simply looked, kept looking, and made no attempt at all to be subtle about it.
"We're taking these home," he said at last.

It wasn't a question, and it wasn't addressed to the maids. Sera's grin came out crooked and pink at the same time. Kaelira reached up and adjusted one of her copper needles, very slowly, as if it required her whole attention. Neither of them asked what for, but they knew he wanted to do more than keep observing them in it.
Myrasyn was waiting for them in the antechamber of the great doors, and she had ambushed him with ceremony before he had even cleared the corridor.

The Queen of the Elves stood in regalia no court had seen in living memory, robes of deep evening-green shot through with silver, a crown of living braided wood that must have been grown for the occasion, and a stillness that had been rehearsed all day and was already losing to her ears.
They angled toward him the moment he entered, quivered once, and gave the entire operation away.
At her side waited Isveth, Head Maiden of the Faith, in white and gold that answered his own, hands laced at her waist, serene as deep water.
The serenity lasted until she saw what he was wearing.

Isveth's breath left her in one long, shaking exhale, both hands rising to her lips, and the Head Maiden of the Faith, who narrated miracles the way clerks read inventory, stood staring at two meters of primordial dressed in the old cut of her people, white and gold and impossible, and forgot every word of her office.
She bowed to him, deeply, and did not entirely manage to straighten all the way, as though the geometry of standing fully upright before that sight had stopped being available to her.
Myrasyn fared no better. She only failed more royally.
"You look..." she started, and then visibly discarded the sentence as understating it.

Her eyes made the journey from his shoulders to the gold-worked hems and back with a thoroughness no throne room would ever hear about, and by the time they arrived, her composure was running on ceremony alone.

The Queen of the Elves cleared her throat and reassembled her opening line. "Quinlan Elysiar. Thank you for coming back to me. To us," she corrected, half a heartbeat too late, and her ears folded back in mortification while her face carried on being royal.

"Myra." He grinned and took her in properly, the evening-green and silver, the living crown, all that majesty scrubbed and braided and nervous. "This dress looks good on you. You should wear it more."
The compliment went through her regalia like an arrow through paper. Myrasyn opened her mouth, closed it, and lost a short, vicious internal war over whether queens were permitted to giggle.
"The old cut suits you, Holy Son," she returned at last, with immense dignity and a voice half a tone too warm, and her eyes betrayed her by making the journey one more time. "Far too well."
"You going to tell me what all this is?"
"No." The word arrived instantly and with immense satisfaction.

She had been guarding this word all day, and delivering it clearly ranked among the finest moments of her reign. "You have been surprising me since the day you crashed into my war. Every plan I ever made, you arrived from some impossible angle and made it a footnote." She lifted her chin, eyes bright. "Tonight I get one. Allow me it."

"What took you so long?!" A small ceremonial whirlwind rounded the queen's skirts. Rosie, re-dressed in a miniature version of the court's evening finery with her sash somehow already askew, planted herself between the adults and vibrated. "It's almost time!"
"The pretty elven ladies bathed me," Quinlan replied nonchalantly.
Rosie's eyes lit up. "Rosie too! Very talented," the little princess decreed with a nod.
"Very talented," her father nodded back.
A few steps back, two bodies had to be caught before they hit the ground.
Then the group walked.
It was finally time.

It wasn't a question, and it wasn't addressed to the maids.
Sera's grin came out crooked and pink at the same time.
Kaelira reached up and adjusted one of her copper needles, very slowly, as if it required her whole attention.
Neither of them asked what for, but they knew he wanted to do more than keep observing them in it.
Myrasyn was waiting for them in the antechamber of the great doors, and she had ambushed him with ceremony before he had even cleared the corridor.

The Queen of the Elves stood in regalia no court had seen in living memory, robes of deep evening-green shot through with silver, a crown of living braided wood that must have been grown for the occasion, and a stillness that had been rehearsed all day and was already losing to her ears.
They angled toward him the moment he entered, quivered once, and gave the entire operation away.
At her side waited Isveth, Head Maiden of the Faith, in white and gold that answered his own, hands laced at her waist, serene as deep water.
The serenity lasted until she saw what he was wearing.

Isveth's breath left her in one long, shaking exhale, both hands rising to her lips, and the Head Maiden of the Faith, who narrated miracles the way clerks read inventory, stood staring at two meters of primordial dressed in the old cut of her people, white and gold and impossible, and forgot every word of her office.
She bowed to him, deeply, and did not entirely manage to straighten all the way, as though the geometry of standing fully upright before that sight had stopped being available to her.
Myrasyn fared no better.
She only failed more royally.
"You look..." she started, and then visibly discarded the sentence as understating it.

Her eyes made the journey from his shoulders to the gold-worked hems and back with a thoroughness no throne room would ever hear about, and by the time they arrived, her composure was running on ceremony alone.
The Queen of the Elves cleared her throat and reassembled her opening line.
"Quinlan Elysiar.
Thank you for coming back to me.
To us," she corrected, half a heartbeat too late, and her ears folded back in mortification while her face carried on being royal.
"Myra." He grinned and took her in properly, the evening-green and silver, the living crown, all that majesty scrubbed and braided and nervous.
"This dress looks good on you.
You should wear it more."
The compliment went through her regalia like an arrow through paper.
Myrasyn opened her mouth, closed it, and lost a short, vicious internal war over whether queens were permitted to giggle.
"The old cut suits you, Holy Son," she returned at last, with immense dignity and a voice half a tone too warm, and her eyes betrayed her by making the journey one more time.
"Far too well."
"You going to tell me what all this is?"
"No." The word arrived instantly and with immense satisfaction.
She had been guarding this word all day, and delivering it clearly ranked among the finest moments of her reign.
"You have been surprising me since the day you crashed into my war.
Every plan I ever made, you arrived from some impossible angle and made it a footnote." She lifted her chin, eyes bright.
"Tonight I get one.
Allow me it."
"What took you so long?!" A small ceremonial whirlwind rounded the queen's skirts.
Rosie, re-dressed in a miniature version of the court's evening finery with her sash somehow already askew, planted herself between the adults and vibrated.
"It's almost time!"
"The pretty elven ladies bathed me," Quinlan replied nonchalantly.
Rosie's eyes lit up.
"Rosie too!
Very talented," the little princess decreed with a nod.
"Very talented," her father nodded back.
A few steps back, two bodies had to be caught before they hit the ground.
Then the group walked.
It was finally time.

chapters.title: Chapter 1836 Their Truth
paragraphs: Myrasyn led them down the processional hall with Rosie enthroned back on her shoulders, and the palace had dressed itself the way its people had: garlands of white blossom wound the pillars, lamps burned low and warm, and staff in ceremonial white lined both walls, each of them bowing to the Holy Son as he passed, deep and held.

Nobody spoke. A palace that housed thousands made no sound but their footsteps, and above the queen's crown Rosie hummed a tiny tune and vibrated with the effort of containment, both hands clamped over her own mouth for safety so she wouldn't spoil anything.
The great doors stood shut at the end of the hall, and from beyond them came a sound like the sea, if the sea wore silk.
Voices. Thousands on thousands of voices, held low, waiting, a pressure of presence that leaned on the doors from the far side.
Myrasyn stilled for a breath, melancholy plain on her face.
Then she turned toward the doors, and everything else fell away from her by degrees. Her shoulders set, her hands folded, and whatever had been rehearsed all day rose up in her and stood ready.
"Isveth."
"My Queen."

Myrasyn lifted Rosie down from her shoulders and set her at Quinlan's side. Then the two women walked ahead, alone, the queen and the Head Maiden, matched step for step down the last length of the hall, and laid their hands on the great doors together, one leaf each.

"Quinlan Elysiar, Son of Luminara," Myrasyn said, without turning around. Her voice had changed. This was the voice from the sky above a battlefield, the one that had ended a nation. "Please face your people."
The doors parted, and the evening poured in.
High on the palace's living face the balcony ran wide as a courtyard, and beyond its rail lay the heart of Luminareth, and the heart of Luminareth was full.

The square below was packed to its edges, wall to root to tree-line, and it did not end at the square: elves filled the terraces above it, the walkways, the great branches themselves, tier upon tier rising with the canopy until faces became points of pale gold in the leaves. Hundreds of thousands. All in ceremonial garb, whites and greens and golds, entire districts dressed like festival day, and all of them silent.
Sunset came in level across the canopy, lighting the whole gathering from the side, and the horns of shaped heartwood sang out over the city, one long note from every quarter at once.

No one cheered. Quinlan noted that the way he noted a drawn blade. Hundreds of thousands of elves watched him step out onto the balcony without a single voice rising, because whatever this was, it had not happened yet, and every soul in the square knew it.
"Oh," Sera breathed at his left, all the theater gone out of her.
Kaelira said nothing at all. Her hand found the back of his sleeve.
Myrasyn stepped to the rail.
When she spoke, the canopy itself seemed to carry her, the living acoustics of the city bearing her voice out and down until it reached the farthest branch without her ever seeming to raise it.
"Elves of Luminareth. Elves of every wood, every den, every hollow of Iskaris. You know me."
A movement through the crowd like wind over wheat.

"I was Queen of the Elves under the Elvardian Alliance. I ruled you under its law, I sent your daughters to its wars, and when its council found me inconvenient, it named me traitor and chained me in the dark, and not one clause of all that fine law lifted a finger for me."
Her voice held a flat, carrying calm, somewhere far past wavering.
"You have heard what I declared above the battlefield. I will say it again tonight, on holy ground, so there is no elf alive who doubts it. Elvardia is dead. I killed it."
The square did not cheer that either. It exhaled, thousands of chests at once, the sound of a people letting a dead thing finally hit the ground.
"And I do not come to resurrect it under a new coat of paint." Her hands settled on the rail.
She turned toward him, though her voice still reached every leaf.
"Elvardia made criminals of its finest smiths." Kaelira's breath stopped.
"It sold its healers to slavers with contracts and called it conscription." Sera's chin came up.

"It chained its own queen and voted itself righteous while it waited for the strong to come and eat it. That was what we built, the last time we built a nation on law and council and crown. Law can be rewritten by whoever holds the pen. Councils can rot. Crowns," and her mouth curved, rueful, "can be inconvenient."
Myrasyn's eyes returned to the square.

"So we asked ourselves, Isveth and I, and every magistrate and matron and mother we spoke to through these long hours of quiet work: what does an elf actually kneel to? Not a document. Not a chair. We are an old people. We remember. In the deepest memory of our race, we were not founded by a law."

Her voice dropped, and the acoustics carried the drop like thunder rolling away. "We were founded by a person. We grew from her hand. We are, all of us, one family's garden, and the family came home."
Beside her, Isveth stepped forward, and the Head Maiden's voice rose clear and unshaking, in the register she reserved for scripture, because tonight it was.

"For time immemorial, my order kept faith with a memory," Isveth said. "We tended it the way you tend a grave: with love, and no expectation of an answer. And then the memory came back to us with a voice, and a face, and a family. It fought for this land while its council hid. It wept the Progenitor's own light over a battlefield of her children."
Her hands rose, palms open, toward Quinlan.
"Tonight, we are admitting what is already true. The faith did not need a nation. The nation walked in the door."

"Hear the decision of the last Queen of the Elves," Myrasyn said, "made with the full assembly of magistrates, ratified by every surviving house, entered into the record by my own hand as the final act of the old law and the first act of the new."
The whole city leaned in. Quinlan felt it, the intake of one enormous breath.

"The crown is dissolved. The council is dissolved. The elven people rise tonight as a holy nation, one nation under one faith, and its founding truth is no document. The only truth we respect is one man."

She let it stand for a heartbeat. "Its law will be written in his name. Its courts will judge in his name. Its borders begin and end at his word. From this night, until the last tree falls, we are the Holy Dominion of Elysaria."
The name went off across the square like a struck bell.
"Elysaria."
Quinlan heard it travel.
He heard the crowd seize it and turn it over, heard the exact rolling instant when hundreds of thousands of elves worked out what the name was carved from.

The sound that tore through their sections then was half sob and half cheer, and it did not settle, it built, voices crashing into voices, his family name sung through elven vowels, a country baptized out of the House of Elysiar.

chapters.title: Chapter 1837 Pleading Elves
paragraphs: Sera had both hands pressed over her mouth, and above them her eyes were shining and enormous, because the healer bought from a slave block with zero rights to her name was standing on a balcony listening to her people rename themselves after the man she loved.
Myrasyn lifted a hand and the square hushed by degrees. Her voice gentled at last, and she let it shake.

"Quinlan Elysiar. Son of Luminara." She turned fully to face him, the sunset behind her, her back to her whole people. "We are not offering you a throne. Thrones are things men take, and you are no mere man. You fed our refugees and freed our slaves and put my crown back on my head when its own council had thrown it in the mud, and you never once asked us for anything at all."
Her hands gathered her robes.
"So we are not granting. We are asking." Her eyes were bright and level. "Please. Accept us."
And the last Queen of the Elves knelt to Quinlan.

She went down slowly, in full regalia, one knee to the balcony's living wood, head bowed, while the whole city watched. The woman who had dissolved an alliance, survived her own council's chains, and ruled her people through four ages knelt before him alone with the sunset on her crown.
Isveth knelt to him next, silent, both knees, hands folded, the way one kneels to what one worships rather than what one serves.
Behind them, in the doorway, every maid of both shifts sank down in a whispering of silk.
Below, the square drew breath, and the pleading rose up the palace face in a hundred thousand voices at once.
"Accept us, Holy Son!"
"Accept us!"
Mothers lifted children over the crowd toward the balcony.

Old soldiers pressed fists to hearts and shouted with the young. Somewhere in the mass a district began to sing the name, "E-ly-sa-ria," and three more picked it up off-beat, joy and begging fused into one enormous sound rolling up against the palace like surf.
And then the trees answered.

Rosie had slipped forward unnoticed, a tiny figure at the balcony's edge, and pressed both small palms flat to the living rail with her face screwed up in ferocious concentration, and the city bloomed.
It went out from the palace in a wave.

Down the great trunks, along every branch and walkway, across the canopy above upturned faces, buds swelled and split and opened by the million, small white blossoms, the deep forest's own, out of season and out of reason, until the whole of Luminareth stood flowering in midwinter with the last of the sunset caught pink and gold in every petal.
Petals came down over the square like warm snow.
The crowd's roar broke into a wordless, keening awe.

Elves fell to their knees mid-cheer just from the sight of it. The blossoming of the deep wood, the flower of the oldest stories, opening over a new nation on its founding night: no sign from any heaven could have said it plainer.
Rosie peeled her hands off the rail, wobbled once with the effort, and looked up at Quinlan with her whole face ablaze in triumph.
"Rosie's roots barely managed to reach close enough... She was trying to hurry it up the whole day..." she whispered up at him.
"...Thank you, Rosie." He reached down and ruffled her curls, and the most feared man on the continent had to take one breath before his voice agreed to stay level. "It's beautiful."
"Hehe~!!" she beamed.
Quinlan took a breath and stepped to the rail.

The square saw him move and the sound climbed. Then he raised one hand, and the noise cut off so fast the silence rang. Hundreds of thousands of faces stayed upturned in the petal-fall, Myrasyn unmoving on one knee at his side, and his mother's people waited, from wall to root to canopy, on one man's answer.
Quinlan wasn't big on lengthy speeches, and he did not reach for one now.
He let her out instead.
It rose off him slow and warm, Luminara's bloodline, the aura he had only ever loosed over battlefields, and this time there was no war in it at all.

It rolled out over the square like the first hour of spring, like a hand laid on every head at once, and every elf it touched felt her, the Progenitor, the mother of every root and ear and season of them, present and warm and unmistakably, impossibly proud.

The square wept. There was no shame in it and no exceptions to it. Hardened rangers wept. Magistrates wept. The districts that had been singing sank down all together, and this kneeling was nothing like surrender, faces up, eyes streaming, hands raised into the petal-fall as the warmth poured over them, an entire civilization folding to its knees in joy.
Elves had knelt to Quinlan before, on battlefields, weapons in the mud, dropped by shock and grief and an aura that had walked through their ranks like weather. Nobody had asked them.

Tonight they had dressed for it, rehearsed it, wanted it, begged for the right to do it, and the whole living city went down together, tier upon tier into the blossoming canopy, and stayed down, laughing and crying and holding their children up into the light, one people deciding, joyously, on its knees, to belong to him.
"I accept," Quinlan decreed, and the canopy carried it to every last leaf. "You're my people now."
The grin arrived, slow and villainous and warmer than any oath. "And I take care of what's mine."
The sound that rose back up off the square had no name. It shook petals from the canopy in sheets, and it startled birds off branches half a city away.
Sera was weeping openly and not bothering to hide it, and beside her Kaelira had both hands pressed over her heart, eyes streaking.
Myrasyn, still on one knee, looked up at him through the falling white with her whole reign paid off in her eyes.
And a window unfolded across Quinlan's vision.
There was no sound to it and no light.
It simply opened, mid-kneel, mid-roar, a pane of quiet, glowing script hanging between him and his cheering nation, and Quinlan Elysiar went very still.
[The elven people of Iskaris have acknowledged your dominion.]
[Peoples of Iskaris conquered: 1/4]
[Conquer the dwarven people, the human people, and the beastkin people to claim rulership of Iskaris.]
[Reward: ???]

[Peoples of Iskaris conquered: 1/4]

'Dwarves, humans, beastkin,' he mused. 'It even wrote me a to-do list.'
He flicked the window shut, question marks and all, and filed the whole thing away for a quieter hour, because the sound below him was changing.
