"I have three goals," he told the elves, and the canopy carried it to the farthest branch.
The hush deepened.

"First." He raised one finger. "Unite Iskaris. Every land and every people, elf, dwarf, human and beastkin, under one banner. And when the continent stands together, I will reach up and tear the Heavenly Restriction out of your sky."
A sound moved through the square, half gasp and half prayer. He kept going.

"Second." Another finger, and the villain's trademark grin came with it. "Your race. Do you know what the rest of Iskaris says about elves? That you are, without question, the prettiest people on the continent." He let the compliment settle. "And that you make good archers."
The square made a strangled sound, indignation and laughter colliding in mid-air.
Quinlan didn't smile with them. He let the laughter run one second too long, then asked, without raising his voice:
"Why are you laughing?"
The canopy carried the question to every last branch, and the laughter died where it stood.

"That's the entire entry. Everything the world bothered writing down about your race." He listed it out, flat as an appraisal. "Pretty faces. Decent bows. Reliable backliners. And down in the slave markets, the highest-priced sex slaves."
Across the square, hundreds of thousands of ears began to sink.

On the balcony, Sera held her chin up. The healer whose whole existence had once carried a price, body and years and name together, listened to her entire race summarized that way, in public, by the man she loved, and did not look at the floor once.
"Are you content with that?" He looked out over the silence he'd made, unhurried. "Because you reacted like a people who've made peace with it."
Down in the front rows, an old ranger's knuckles went white around her bow.
"I haven't."

The grin returned, and this time nobody in the square mistook it for a joke. "The world is due a very rude awakening on the subject of elven strength. My second goal is just that: to watch you blossom into the potential I know you have."
Across the square, the ears rose again, and the roar that tried to be born right there had teeth in it, thousands of chests filling with shame and defiance in the same breath.
"Third."
He let the word sit. The square leaned in. Up on the balcony, Sera stopped breathing for a second, because she could count on one hand the times that tone had come out of him.

"My mother has been gone from this world for a very long time." Quiet, level, matter-of-fact. "I will bring Luminara home, and when she steps into Thalorind again, I will show her everything her children built while she was away."
Myrasyn had prayed to the Progenitor her whole reign, and not one of those prayers had ever asked for her to come back in person. Her hand closed on the rail.
Beside her, Kaelira watched Quinlan and smiled, soft and small.
A different silence took the square, the sound of hundreds of thousands of minds arriving at the same wall together.
Behind him, Isveth made a sound like a hymn dying in her throat.
"...Home?" The whispers collided somewhere over the crowd. "He said he'll bring her home."
"He said it like she's at market..."
"The Progenitor is a prayer. She isn't a, a person who can simply..."
"He's her son. Would her son say it if..."
Nobody finished a sentence.
"That's all," said the man who had just promised his nation a returned divinity, and stepped back from the rail. "Let's get to work, shall we?"

Then he simply turned and walked, past Myrasyn's regalia and Isveth's trembling hands, collecting a wobbly, blossom-drunk Rosie off the rail with one arm on the way, and gave the most important address in elven history exactly zero closing ceremony.
For three whole steps, the only sound in the capital was petals landing.
Then an elderly magistrate in the front rows came up out of her kneel with tears shaking loose off her chin, and said it to no one and to everyone.

"All my life I served the crown. It promised us quiet borders. Peace with the dwarves, protection from beastkin, our old ways kept exactly as they were." Her voice cracked wide open. "He just promised us the sky."
"Promised? No, he demanded!" a soldier shouted, visibly energized. "He demanded we become a race he can proudly show off to his mother when she returns!"

The old ranger's bow was still in a white-knuckled grip. She said it down at the bow, not up at the balcony. "Every one of them told me elves make good archers." Her thumb moved once along the bowstring. "And I thanked them for it. Every time."
"Then what are we waiting for?!" a young voice shouted down from the walkways, cracking with laughter and tears at once. "Follow him! Just follow him!"
The square detonated.

The sound that went up had no words in it at first, only voice, joy with its skin off. Then the name found them again, E-LY-SA-RIA, E-LY-SA-RIA, rolling up the palace face in waves while the petals came down like a second snowfall, chasing their sovereign through the doors.
He didn't turn around, but his lips kept curling upward little by little until the maids saw a sight they'd never forget for the rest of their lives.

Inside, the processional hall was still lined wall to wall with staff, every one of them bowing to the Holy Son as he passed with Rosie now asleep against his shoulder, worn out from blooming a whole city. Sera and Kaelira fell in behind him, and Isveth glided after them with the doors' thunder at her back.
Myrasyn came last, and quietest.
She caught up to Isveth halfway down the hall, and when she spoke, her voice was pitched low, meant for one set of ears only.
"You are going to be very busy, my friend." She said it smiling. The smile reached nothing.
The melancholy underneath had been waiting all evening, patient as winter, and now that the ceremony was over it came up through her like groundwater.
Isveth's hand found her friend's sleeve. She opened her mouth with something gentle in it.
Quinlan stopped walking.
"What's that supposed to mean?"
The last Queen of the Elves straightened, caught out in her own palace, and then let it go, too tired to keep pretending.
"Look at what my reign amounted to, Quinlan. My own council chained me beneath my own palace, and my people had to be saved by a miracle to have any chance at a better tomorrow."

Her hand moved toward him and gave up halfway. "The faith held when the crown rotted. Isveth and her order never failed anyone. The new age deserves to be built by the hands that stayed clean. I do not deserve..."
The queen with droopy green eyes full of regret was interrupted.
"No."
Myrasyn blinked. "...No?"
"No, Myrasyn Ael'vyrn." Quinlan came around fully, Rosie snoring on undisturbed, and the whole attention of a primordial landed on her at once. "You don't get to self-pity your way out of work."
Her mouth opened. Nothing useful arrived in it.
"Fanatics are wonderful, but I'm not running this nation on faith alone. A country that runs on nothing but hymns starves with perfect posture. The elven people need a proper governor."
He tipped his head at Isveth. "No offense."
"None taken, Holy Son." The Head Maiden inclined her head, serene.
"Then you have Jasmine," Myrasyn tried. "Your Tyrant of Commerce. The whole continent has already begun whispering about her..."

"I do have Jasmine." The grin arrived, slow and merciless. "My amazing twenty-five-year-old human lover, who was a merchant girl haggling over silk margins when I met her, currently raising my domain out of raw wilderness, chronically overworked, and about to inherit a great deal more. Or..."
He let it hang for a second.
"...I have a four-thousand-year-old queen with a crown's worth of statecraft experience standing in front of me, fishing for permission to retire." A beat. "Guess you're out of luck."

chapters.title: Chapter 1839 Good Girl
paragraphs: Beside him, Isveth's gaze rested on her lord with open gratitude, because the Head Maiden knew how dejected Myrasyn was the whole day, riddled with the guilt of her past actions.
Her friend, meanwhile, had reached her limit.
"I have worked for four thousand years," Myrasyn said, volume climbing with every word, ears climbing with it, "and you stand there demanding I work more? What are you, a slaver?!"
"Yes." No pause at all. "Literally. I'm the Primordial Subjugator. Being a slaver is a major part of who I am."
Myrasyn stomped, actually stomped, one royal slipper cracking against the ancient living wood, and glared at him with her regalia still on. "You... I didn't..."
Quinlan turned and resumed walking, not waiting for her to hiss out a rebuttal.
Isveth flowed after him without a heartbeat of hesitation.

Sera hooked Kaelira's arm and followed, both elves grinning at nothing in particular, and the maids peeled off the walls to trail the procession at a reverent distance, leaving the Queen of the Elves standing alone in the middle of her own hall.
Myrasyn watched that tall, broad back recede, taking her entire people's future with it like the load weighed nothing.
Then, without turning around, Quinlan patted his thigh twice and whistled, short and bright. The universal signal for: come here, girl.
Somewhere along the wall, a maid walked into a pillar.
"I am NOT your dog!" The second stomp echoed off the distant ceiling.

Then the last Queen of the Elves picked up her hem and dashed after him with an enormous smile, crown and all, and wrapped her arms around him from behind, cheek pressed flat between his shoulder blades. The maids' eyes went wide down the entire length of the hall, and nobody remembered how to keep walking.
"Cruel bastard," she said into his back. "Hmph. Demeaning bastard. Hmph. Sadistic bastard. Hmph."
He kept walking. She kept holding and scoffing. For a while the procession moved like that, a nation's sovereign wearing its former queen like a cloak.
A cloak that cursed him out while adorably pouting the entire time.
The hmphs slowed, then stopped altogether. Her arms changed the way they held him. She walked a good stretch of corridor without saying anything.

"I want to say something." Her voice had gone quiet and serious. "I stood at your side while you faced the beastkin lords, named Luminara your cherished mother, and declared in the same breath: I am the Primordial Villain, I am called as such because that is who I am."

Her arms tightened around him. "Your words have been sitting wrong in me ever since and I wish to correct them. You are not a villain, Quinlan. You are the best thing that has ever happened to me and to every soul in Iskaris."
Quinlan was silent for three full steps.
"Tell that to the millions I've killed." He didn't slow down, and he didn't soften it. "And the billions I'm going to kill."
His women had told him he was good before. It had never once changed the number, and it did not change it now.
For a dozen steps, the only sound was the city still singing his name, far away behind the doors.
Then Myrasyn's gaze found Seraphiel and Kaelira walking ahead, arm in arm, and the sorrow that crossed her face was old and personal.

Two of her own. One conscripted and sold off to a slave block in dancer's silk, one sentenced to die for the crime of crafting, and every page of it signed under her seal while her own hands stayed clean.
"I never massacred anyone," she said at last. "I ruled lawfully. Gently. Righteously. And my righteousness did that."
A breath.
"Even the mighty must make sacrifices. A ruler only gets to choose what the sacrifice buys. Mine bought my council more years of rot and my people more years of slow decline."
Her cheek pressed harder between his shoulders. "Yours bought tonight. If you won't let me be dejected about my past, then I refuse to let you feel guilty about yours."
Quinlan said nothing. But hands came up and closed over the small ones clasped at his chest, and stayed there for a long stretch of corridor, and that was answer enough.
"...By the way." Myrasyn's voice returned to full volume against his back. "I still do not want to work."
"Tough luck. Your Holy Son demands it."
"Hmph! Slaver Son! I want a vacation!"
"Sure."
The arms around him loosened. She leaned out sideways to see his face, suspicion blooming. "...Wait. Really?"
"Yes. I'll enslave you and a few of your aides. Then you can take your vacation anywhere on the continent and keep working the entire time through [Master's Link]."
Myrasyn went completely still. Her arms slipped loose, and she let him walk out from under them.

"Subjugation," she repeated. "Me?" Her eyes were wide, and there was nothing in them resembling horror. His subject. His actual, marked, bound-by-power subject, the way his women were his. No elf alive could be granted a higher station than that.
Before she could assemble a response, two figures detached from the trailing column at speed.
"Holy Son." An aide with a treasury sash bowed to him mid-stride, deep and urgent. "I have served the crown's ledgers for five thousand years. My loyalty is absolute. Please choose me."
"I take dictation at any hour," a second aide announced over her, elbowing into the bow. "ANY hour."

"H-Holy Son." Isveth materialized at his other side, palms pressed flat together, dignity and hope having a visible fistfight across her face. "In a holy dominion, the head of the faith carries considerable burdens. The rites, the canonizations, my own court to establish. I would require... that is, it would only be proper if I were also..."
"Sure, Isveth. I'll enslave you as well." He never broke stride as a lazy tilt of his head took in the two aides. "As for you two, I'll let Myra decide."
A pane of quiet script unfolded in front of the Head Maiden mid-stride.
[The Primordial Subjugator, Quinlan Elysiar, offers you a place among his subjugated people.]
[Do you accept?]
Isveth's finger went through the accept button before the second line even finished forming, and the smile that broke across her face belonged to a girl a fraction of her age. "Thank you!"
At the same time, the two aides began looking at Myrasyn with pleading eyes.
He kept walking, and the corridor ahead of him kept wanting.
The maids lining the walls began to quiver in unison as he came level with them, hands pressed to skirts, not one of them daring to voice what the entire line was vibrating with.
"Want to be my slaves too?"
"As a maid, efficient communication..." the old maid began, but cut herself off. An uncharacteristic, sheepish nod replaced her lengthy speech alongside healthy pink cheeks. "Yes, please..."
"All of you?" Quinlan grinned.
"It'd be our greatest honor!!" the maids shouted in unison.
"Granted."
Down the length of the corridor, dozens of panes unfolded at once, the same quiet script blooming in front of every maid in the line.
The joyous shiver that followed traveled wall to wall, accept buttons lighting up one after another.
At the junction, a guard blinked at him through her visor, armored fists tight on her spear.
"H-Holy Son..." She bit her tongue, knowing she was well out of her station. She could lose her job, and worse, make a joke out of herself before him.
"Property of the Primordial Villain?" Quinlan asked.
"Property of the Primordial Villain!!" She shed all pretense, screaming her desire.
A pane unfolded in front of her visor, and a gauntleted finger rose and pressed accept with the solemnity of an oath.
And on the Primordial Villain walked through his brand-new palace, never once slowing, confiscating freedoms left and right and leaving a trail of rapture in his wake.
At the edge of his vision, subjugation confirmations had begun stacking like receipts.
Myrasyn caught back up to his side mid-glow with her own pane of script trailing her like a faithful hound, opened her mouth to accept the highest honor of her long life, and froze mid-step instead.
"...Wait." Her eyes narrowed, the arithmetic landing at last. "Did you just say I would be working the entire time I am on vacation?!"
"Rest is for the dead."
"Tell that to your Elite Souls..." Seraphiel snickered.
"Technically, they're not dead. They were only truly dead until Quin claimed them," Kaelira spoke up, defending her man from the cheeky gal.
"Exactly." Quinlan nodded. "You got it."
"..." Sera sent a scrutinizing look to her friend, who had rescued their lover instantly.
'Did getting plowed for hours on end,' Sera wondered, 'confuse the girl about where her loyalties lie?'
Kaelira avoided her gaze.
While the two friends conducted their wordless discussion, Myrasyn aimed Seraphiel's exact look at Quinlan himself.
'...Why,' the last Queen of the Elves wailed into the privacy of her own skull, 'is this cruel bastard so hot even while he sentences me to work myself to the bone for him?!'
Ahead of her, serene as deep water, Isveth did not break stride.
"We are going to be gloriously busy, my friend."
Myrasyn's groan chased the procession all the way down the hall.
Her finger, mid-groan, had already pressed accept.

With his business in Luminareth done for the time being, or rather, all his duties having been passed down to his two joint rulers of the elven people, Isveth and Myrasyn, Quinlan quickly made a strategic retreat before any work found his lap.
He stepped out of his [Warp Gate] and into a war.

His actual, marked, bound-by-power subject, the way his women were his.
No elf alive could be granted a higher station than that.
Before she could assemble a response, two figures detached from the trailing column at speed.
"Holy Son." An aide with a treasury sash bowed to him mid-stride, deep and urgent.
"I have served the crown's ledgers for five thousand years.
My loyalty is absolute.
Please choose me."
"I take dictation at any hour," a second aide announced over her, elbowing into the bow.
"ANY hour."
"H-Holy Son." Isveth materialized at his other side, palms pressed flat together, dignity and hope having a visible fistfight across her face.
"In a holy dominion, the head of the faith carries considerable burdens.
The rites, the canonizations, my own court to establish.
I would require... that is, it would only be proper if I were also..."
"Sure, Isveth.
I'll enslave you as well." He never broke stride as a lazy tilt of his head took in the two aides.
"As for you two, I'll let Myra decide."
A pane of quiet script unfolded in front of the Head Maiden mid-stride.
[The Primordial Subjugator, Quinlan Elysiar, offers you a place among his subjugated people.]
[Do you accept?]
Isveth's finger went through the accept button before the second line even finished forming, and the smile that broke across her face belonged to a girl a fraction of her age.
"Thank you!"
At the same time, the two aides began looking at Myrasyn with pleading eyes.
He kept walking, and the corridor ahead of him kept wanting.
The maids lining the walls began to quiver in unison as he came level with them, hands pressed to skirts, not one of them daring to voice what the entire line was vibrating with.
"Want to be my slaves too?"
"As a maid, efficient communication..." the old maid began, but cut herself off.
An uncharacteristic, sheepish nod replaced her lengthy speech alongside healthy pink cheeks.
"Yes, please..."
"All of you?" Quinlan grinned.
"It'd be our greatest honor!!" the maids shouted in unison.
"Granted."
Down the length of the corridor, dozens of panes unfolded at once, the same quiet script blooming in front of every maid in the line.
The joyous shiver that followed traveled wall to wall, accept buttons lighting up one after another.
At the junction, a guard blinked at him through her visor, armored fists tight on her spear.
"H-Holy Son..." She bit her tongue, knowing she was well out of her station.
She could lose her job, and worse, make a joke out of herself before him.
"Property of the Primordial Villain?" Quinlan asked.
"Property of the Primordial Villain!!" She shed all pretense, screaming her desire.
A pane unfolded in front of her visor, and a gauntleted finger rose and pressed accept with the solemnity of an oath.
And on the Primordial Villain walked through his brand-new palace, never once slowing, confiscating freedoms left and right and leaving a trail of rapture in his wake.
At the edge of his vision, subjugation confirmations had begun stacking like receipts.
Myrasyn caught back up to his side mid-glow with her own pane of script trailing her like a faithful hound, opened her mouth to accept the highest honor of her long life, and froze mid-step instead.
"...Wait." Her eyes narrowed, the arithmetic landing at last.
"Did you just say I would be working the entire time I am on vacation?!"
"Rest is for the dead."
"Tell that to your Elite Souls..." Seraphiel snickered.
"Technically, they're not dead.
They were only truly dead until Quin claimed them," Kaelira spoke up, defending her man from the cheeky gal.
"Exactly." Quinlan nodded.
"You got it."
"..." Sera sent a scrutinizing look to her friend, who had rescued their lover instantly.
'Did getting plowed for hours on end,' Sera wondered, 'confuse the girl about where her loyalties lie?'
Kaelira avoided her gaze.
While the two friends conducted their wordless discussion, Myrasyn aimed Seraphiel's exact look at Quinlan himself.
'...Why,' the last Queen of the Elves wailed into the privacy of her own skull, 'is this cruel bastard so hot even while he sentences me to work myself to the bone for him?!'
Ahead of her, serene as deep water, Isveth did not break stride.
"We are going to be gloriously busy, my friend."
Myrasyn's groan chased the procession all the way down the hall.
Her finger, mid-groan, had already pressed accept.

With his business in Luminareth done for the time being, or rather, all his duties having been passed down to his two joint rulers of the elven people, Isveth and Myrasyn, Quinlan quickly made a strategic retreat before any work found his lap.
He stepped out of his [Warp Gate] and into a war.

chapters.title: Chapter 1840 Brave Little Warrior
paragraphs: He stepped out of his [Warp Gate] and into a war.
A war of paper.

The central reading hall of the Vraven royal archive had been conquered wall to wall: ledger towers rising like siegeworks, squads of crown clerks moving in supply lines, estate maps of the Ravenshade duchy pinned across three joined tables with knives through their corners, and runners coming and going with document crates stacked to their chins.
A clerk saw the gate bloom, yelped, and baptized the floor with a full tray of files.
"Stop arriving like that," Alexios said from behind a desk that had annexed two smaller desks, sleeves rolled to the elbow, not looking up from what he was signing.
"Why?"
"Because it's disruptive."
"Oh." Quinlan nodded, not intending one bit to change his methods of arrival.
Alexios's vein bulged for a second before, through visible effort, he restrained himself from speaking back to this arrogant creature. "Not today..." he whispered under his beard.
Morgana sat at the correspondence table with her family's letters sorted into merciless piles, Ravenshade ink getting read by the one Ravenshade nobody had thought to lie to.
A table over, Lilith leaned over a ledger with her arms crossed, grinding through it column by column.
And in the middle of all of it stood Iris.
She had her red eyes on a map of the duchy's border holdings, and she was questioning a sweating archivist about missing years in the toll records with the exact courtesy of an interrogation.
The clerks orbited her at maximum possible radius. She looked like five days of no sleep held together by spite.
Quinlan drifted along the tables without announcing himself.
Nobody here needed him. He'd come with half a mind to offer gates, muscle, and a legion's worth of dead clerks, and one look at the room settled it.

The machine he'd handed her in a workshop full of blood and cauldron-steam was running at full draft, and it answered to the short woman with a generational vendetta. Hers, top to bottom. Exactly as promised.
Then he saw the folio.
It lay open on the central table under a clean sheet of glass, crown-sealed, positioned where every runner in the hall would pass it a hundred times a day.
An old page. Four sentences of tired bureaucratic script that had once dissolved a barony. And above the faded paragraph, in fresh dark ink, a single line had been entered at the head of the record.
Damian Ravenclaw.
The document that had erased a family and never once thought to mention a child now opened with his name, entered first, exactly as a king had promised in a freezing cellar.
Quinlan read it upside down across the table and allowed himself a long pause and a big smile.
"Good," he said to no one in particular. "That's the least of what you deserve, brave little warrior."
"..." Iris went very still and made a point of not looking at him, for her eyes moistened as soon as the words left his lips.
Brave little warrior, spoken the way one speaks to the honored dead, as if her brother were standing at the table to hear his due.

Her whole life, the world's paper had agreed that her brother had never existed, and she had built a knife of herself on top of that silence. Now his name led the crown's own record, and the most feared creature on the continent had just called him what no one else was left to call him.
Something that had sat clenched behind her ribs came loose, one knuckle at a time.

Quinlan crossed the hall and took up station behind her, and for a while the two of them just shared the silence. The hunt lay pinned under her hands, the name sat in fresh ink under glass, and everything worth saying about either had already been said to no one in particular.
Then his hands settled onto her shoulders, and his thumbs dug in.
"Ngh." It escaped her before she could kill it.

Long hours of hunched ledgers and swallowed fury had collected under his palms, and his fingers went after the knots one at a time, firm and patient and far better at this than a feared conqueror had any business being.
Iris blinked her eyes clear.
"...Where did you learn this?" she muttered at the map.
"Learn?" The man sounded far too entertained. "I'm just rubbing your shoulders, it's nothing special. I used to do this for my mom from time to time."
"Which one?"
Quinlan chuckled and actually gave it thought. "Come to think of it, I've rubbed every one of my mothers' shoulders by now."
To the dozens of human ears in range it was nothing, family small talk from a man with a complicated family. Iris did the calculations in silence, though: Mearie and Lumi had both come later.
The first shoulders he'd ever rubbed belonged to a mother a whole world away. He just didn't feel like turning himself into an open book in front of the room.
"You're right, by the way," she then scoffed, chin dipping forward to surrender more of her neck to his thumbs. "It's really nothing special."
"Mm."
"Mediocre. At best." Her shoulders had come down two full centimeters and were still descending.
"Noted," he said, and kept kneading. "How's the hunt?"
"Slow." She didn't look up. "I can't torture and demand answers from papers. You require something?"
"Just visiting my favorite secret agent."
"Then you've seen me. There's the gate."

He stayed exactly where he was, thoroughly pleased with himself. For a while the hall worked around them: runners, ledger-stacks, Morgana's pen scratching steadily through her own bloodline's correspondence.
Then Iris rolled one shoulder, irritated. The roll became a full-body twitch, and her scowl climbed off the map to land on him.
"Actually. Since you're not being of any use right now." She reached over her shoulder and jabbed a thumb at the top of her spine.
"Deal with your screeching midget. She's been getting on my nerves."
<Twitch, twitch, twitch, at all hours, like sharing a skull with a squirrel in a jar. I can't read a ledger without her nerves crawling up my back. Fix her, or I'll do it myself.>
"My screeching midget," Quinlan repeated.
He studied her instead of leaving. The shadows under her eyes, the maps of the duchy that had butchered her family spread out under her hands, and the fresh ink on old paper twenty steps away.

She was neck-deep in the reckoning of her own past, and from the middle of it she was shoving him at Ayame's, because nobody alive knew better than Iris what unfinished business did to a person. The crude mouth had never once managed to hide the good girl behind it.
"Alright. I'll handle it." Then, with malice aforethought, warmly: <You're a good friend, Iris.>
Her eyes widened into outraged saucers.
<FRIEND?!> The word came out strangled, an octave above her fighting voice. <Me and that slit-eyed, smug, bond-polluting... GET OUT!> The hiss turned fully feline on the last word. <Out, out, OUT!>

Quinlan was already stepping backward into his blooming gate, grinning like he'd gotten everything he came for and then some. "Eat something before sundown," he called as the light folded around him. "Ayame is a good girl too. She would hate to know you're starving."
The inkwell chased him through the gate thanks to a heaving woman's mighty throw.

A heartbeat later it drifted back out and set itself down on her map, empty. Its contents followed, her own ink hanging in the air in tidy script, rearranging itself into two words before the gate winked shut.
'Good luck.'
For a long moment, no one in the hall moved.
"He just..." Somewhere by the stacks, a runner put it into words, very quietly. "The Primordial Villain. He strolled into the royal palace. Uninvited. Massaged the scary woman. And left."
Nobody had a correction to offer. The continent's terror had conquered nothing but a set of shoulders, and fucked off.
Alexios signed another page. 'How nice it is to be ignored by that creature for once...' he mused inwardly.
Back home beneath Rosie's tree, Ayame Fujimori was losing a war against a travel case.

She had packed it twice and re-tied its straps three times, and the second-in-command of the most dangerous family on the continent was currently frowning at a buckle as if it had insulted her technique.
The [Warp Gate] bloomed at the garden's edge and delivered her lover.

"There you are." The strap got one final, unnecessary tug, and the brat arrived on schedule, chin first. "Mister Primordial, keeping his second-in-command waiting on departure day. Staying with the elves must've been enjoyable..."
"Yeah, it was great." Quinlan nodded, taking Ayame out of her groove. "They're very hospitable people."
"..." Ayame's eyes narrowed. "What about..."
"Elves, done. Dwarves, humans, and beastkin remain," he wasted no time, knowing exactly what she wanted to know.
"Beastkin, huh?" Ayame murmured, pondering.
Beastkin were a collective of people, consisting of various beastkin races. Unlike humans, elves, or dwarves, they were not a single race.
"I'm thinking it has to do with them being united under one beastkin banner," Quinlan said.

"Conquer the Beastman Confederation, and you conquer the beastkin people..." Ayame tried the logic on her tongue, then admitted. "It makes sense, I suppose. The beastkin species created a nation of their own, which in turn means they've chosen to become a collective of the beastkin people."
Quinlan merely nodded again, smiling. Theorizing with his beloved samurai was always a treat.
"But what about the treaty? It still has 'a few' years left on it."
"We'll deal with it."
"Of course we will. It was a rhetorical question," Ayame smirked. "I already have a few ideas."
"Me too. But shall we leave that for tomorrow and focus on today? I've long awaited this day..."
Ayame averted her gaze quickly, knowing full well he meant more than just visiting her hometown.
Her hands went back to the case, checked a buckle that was already closed, then checked it again.
Quinlan watched her do it and kept every observation to himself.
"Ready?"
"Obviously." It arrived a breath too fast, and both of them heard it, and neither of them touched it.
Black Fang was waiting against the tree.
"Was the sisterly bonding session fun?" Quinlan asked her.
Black Fang looked at him and said nothing, which from her was a complete sentence.
"We bathed," Ayame supplied across the lawn, not looking up from her case.
"Oh?"
"In poison."
Quinlan's eyebrows rose.

"She made me a 'rookie' blend." Ayame gave the buckle another entirely unnecessary tug, far too casual for the content she was delivering. "My skin has never felt this good, and I slept the whole night through for the first time in a long time." A pause. "She also washed my hair."
Quinlan looked at Black Fang.

chapters.title: Chapter 1841 Portal.
paragraphs: Quinlan looked at Black Fang.

Black Fang looked back, expression offering absolutely nothing, as if she had definitely not spent her evening kneeling behind her little sister in venom-steam, rinsing samurai hair with great patience.
"Portal," she demanded.
He didn't move. Instead the smile arrived, small at first, then spreading, deeply obnoxious, as he filed the image away for the rest of his very long life.
Black Fang pushed off the tree and simply started walking away from the two of them.
"Portal." It came back over her shoulder, flat as a knife laid on a table, without her breaking stride.
Quinlan and Ayame watched her receding back with matching grins, fond in a way neither of them would have dared say to her face.
Kaede trailed down the path last.

She was thinner than her reign had left her, dressed in plain traveling grey with her hair bound low, and guilt organized every inch of her: where she stopped, three steps short of the group and no closer; the depth of the greeting bow she offered them and refused to rush; the way she carried nothing, asked for nothing, presumed nothing.
She had run numbers on her own sister's life once, as a duchess. Now she held her place on a winter lawn, awaiting a sentencing that kept refusing to arrive, and the refusal was its own punishment.
Ayame crossed the lawn to her.

For a moment the two Fujimori regarded each other in the pale light, the elder settled and unhurried, the younger braced like a struck bell. Then Ayame deposited a cloth-wrapped bundle into her sister's arms, weight-first.
"You carry the offerings."
Kaede's arms closed around it on reflex. Rice wine, incense, white ash-paper, the shapes readable through the cloth to anyone raised in that house, and her breath went somewhere for a second.
"Yes, sis..." She caught the word halfway out, folded it smaller, and bowed her head over the bundle. "...Understood."
Ayame had already turned away.
Then the mansion doors opened, and the luggage marched out on its own.

"The head of the line does not carry baggage," Elder Chizuru of the Fujimori announced to the garden in general, crossing the lawn under a stacked tower of travel cases with her spine straight as doctrine. "The line carries for its elders. This arrangement dishonors the clan."
"Shut your mouth," Quinlan and Ayame demanded in perfect sync.
"..." The elder's mouth worked, hunting for a counter-doctrine and finding none, then closed with the dignity of a vault door.

Quinlan surveyed his travel party: a samurai with the most gorgeous of cheeky grins, an assassin already halfway across the lawn, a duchess holding grave-offerings like a verdict, and one very dignified filing cabinet.
Across the lawn, Black Fang was still walking, small with distance now and not slowing.
"Open it already, Quin." Ayame's eyes tracked her sister's course over the grass. "Before she marches into one of Yoruha's traps."
Quinlan grinned, and the [Warp Gate] bloomed.

To the north and a mile beneath the surface, Brokk, First Hammer of the royal smithy, climbed the long gallery to the main halls of dwarven governance with a requisition slate under one arm and half an hour of patience left, and heard the future of her people before she ever saw it.
It sounded like a tavern brawl wearing its best jewelry.

The news had arrived days ago: Ragnar captured, the elves had dissolved their own crown and knelt, all of them at once, to the Primordial Villain, the man who'd been on a warpath to destroy all their forts.
Every clan lord under the stone had been screaming at every other clan lord since.
No one had thought to close the great doors of the council hall, because what was boiling inside had long stopped caring who heard it.
"...the king ROTS in the Villain's keeping and you're already measuring his chair for your backside, Harrek!"
"Somebody had better measure it! Or do we wait for the long-ears' fake god to come do it for us?!"
"The army is BONES, you copper-counting vulture! Helmets with nobody under them! Whoever takes the seat inherits a graveyard with taxes!"
"And no allies to guard it! Or did you miss what little remains of our forces crawling back through the passes empty-handed?" A goblet went over.

"The old alliance died with Elvardia, the long-ears say! Generations of treaty, dead in ONE elven evening! And for what? One strong male strutted into their forest, and the entire race rolled over for him, crown, army, and temple!"

"What did you expect from long-ears?!" a fourth lord roared over the wreckage of his chair. "Weak-willed does in heat, the lot of them! A race that spreads its legs the moment it sniffs a stronger male, then dresses the smell up as scripture!"
"That description reminds me of your wife."
"I heard your daughter takes visitors late at night."

The lord of the Copper Vaults and the lord of the Iron Gates had each other by the beard-rings within the minute. A fist cracked across a rival's nose, a chair splintered to kindling under somebody's backside, and their retainers pretended very hard to be furniture.
Brokk halted in the doorway with her slate and watched the finest blood of her people eat itself.
Someone finally noticed her.

"First Hammer!" Lord Harrek untangled his beard from his rival's fist, straightened his chains, and his voice turned to syrup. He addressed the room over her head. "Let the record show the royal smithy stands with the Copper Vaults' claim! Every hearth, every hammer!"
Brokk's mouth opened.
"When the seat is mine," Lord Mogrun bellowed across him, "the smithy's quotas double! Siege plate by summer! The mountain rebuilds on its anvils, as it always has!"
Her mouth was still open. Neither of them was looking at her.

A third voice slid in from the side, oiled and reasonable, some cousin of a cousin with a thin claim and a strong perfume. "And who guards your smiths when the beastkin test our passes, hm, First Hammer? These are dangerous years for craftsmen. Remember whose soldiers stand guard so you can focus on your trade."
That one, at least, had the courtesy to threaten her directly.

Brokk stayed where she was, requisition slate under one arm, pig-iron and coal and copper for the rebuild itemized in a smith's neat columns, and waited to be asked a single question by a single soul in that hall.

She counted instead, because counting was what her hands did when they wanted to break something: four claims, two brawls, one king in a cell. Her half hour of patience had run out somewhere around the second brawl. She stayed anyway.

And zero questions, in a solid hour of shouting about the mountain's future, about what the mountain could still make. The smiths who would carry the whole rebuild on their backs had come up exactly three times, every time as somebody's property, indebted slaves who'd best do their bidding, or else.
Brokk gave the lords of her people one last, level look.
Then she turned around, tucked the slate under her arm, and walked, and not one voice rose to call her back, because not one of them noticed the royal smithy leave the room.

The gallery took her down through the lamplight one landing at a time, and somewhere on the long stair the shouting faded behind her and the memory arrived in its place, uninvited, warm and unhurried.
He hadn't come with terms.
He'd come asking about flue draw and quench-oil, and worked her bellows half-naked for an hour like the labor was a privilege.
The crown's racks had opened at one wave of his hand, and he'd watched her walk past adamantite for honest hearth-steel, then left the results of his sweat humming on her anvil.
And when the talk had finally reached her smiths, the most dangerous being alive had shrugged like it was obvious.
"Sounds like the kind of people any sane ruler would want to support."
The words had followed her home that day and never left.

The royal smithy met her the way it always met her: heat first, then the hammer-song. The song faltered tier by tier as she walked through the doors, because three hundred smiths knew exactly where their First Hammer had spent the last hour, and not one of them had yet run out of retellings of the time a conqueror worked their bellows.

Work slowed. Hammers stilled. Old Dain shifted around on his bench with both hands braced on his cane, and the apprentices collected along the second-tier rail like starlings, young master Vorn leaning further over it than any of them.
"Well?!" young Vorn blurted from the rail, and got cuffed by three masters at once for it.
On its anvil, where no one had presumed to move it, Everwright hummed.
Brokk stopped in the middle of her hall, thumbs hooking into her belt, and looked them over: the masters, the apprentices, the cold forges waiting on coal the lords were too busy brawling to approve.
Then the First Hammer of the royal smithy asked her smiths, plainly:
"Wouldn't it be better to be ruled by the Primordial Villain?"

sentences.text: Quinlan looked at Black Fang.

Black Fang looked back, expression offering absolutely nothing, as if she had definitely not spent her evening kneeling behind her little sister in venom-steam, rinsing samurai hair with great patience.
"Portal," she demanded.
He didn't move.
Instead the smile arrived, small at first, then spreading, deeply obnoxious, as he filed the image away for the rest of his very long life.
Black Fang pushed off the tree and simply started walking away from the two of them.
"Portal." It came back over her shoulder, flat as a knife laid on a table, without her breaking stride.
Quinlan and Ayame watched her receding back with matching grins, fond in a way neither of them would have dared say to her face.
Kaede trailed down the path last.

She was thinner than her reign had left her, dressed in plain traveling grey with her hair bound low, and guilt organized every inch of her: where she stopped, three steps short of the group and no closer; the depth of the greeting bow she offered them and refused to rush; the way she carried nothing, asked for nothing, presumed nothing.
She had run numbers on her own sister's life once, as a duchess.
Now she held her place on a winter lawn, awaiting a sentencing that kept refusing to arrive, and the refusal was its own punishment.
Ayame crossed the lawn to her.
For a moment the two Fujimori regarded each other in the pale light, the elder settled and unhurried, the younger braced like a struck bell.
Then Ayame deposited a cloth-wrapped bundle into her sister's arms, weight-first.
"You carry the offerings."
Kaede's arms closed around it on reflex.
Rice wine, incense, white ash-paper, the shapes readable through the cloth to anyone raised in that house, and her breath went somewhere for a second.
"Yes, sis..." She caught the word halfway out, folded it smaller, and bowed her head over the bundle.
"...Understood."
Ayame had already turned away.
Then the mansion doors opened, and the luggage marched out on its own.

"The head of the line does not carry baggage," Elder Chizuru of the Fujimori announced to the garden in general, crossing the lawn under a stacked tower of travel cases with her spine straight as doctrine.
"The line carries for its elders.
This arrangement dishonors the clan."
"Shut your mouth," Quinlan and Ayame demanded in perfect sync.
"..." The elder's mouth worked, hunting for a counter-doctrine and finding none, then closed with the dignity of a vault door.

Quinlan surveyed his travel party: a samurai with the most gorgeous of cheeky grins, an assassin already halfway across the lawn, a duchess holding grave-offerings like a verdict, and one very dignified filing cabinet.
Across the lawn, Black Fang was still walking, small with distance now and not slowing.
"Open it already, Quin." Ayame's eyes tracked her sister's course over the grass.
"Before she marches into one of Yoruha's traps."
Quinlan grinned, and the [Warp Gate] bloomed.

It sounded like a tavern brawl wearing its best jewelry.

The news had arrived days ago: Ragnar captured, the elves had dissolved their own crown and knelt, all of them at once, to the Primordial Villain, the man who'd been on a warpath to destroy all their forts.
Every clan lord under the stone had been screaming at every other clan lord since.
No one had thought to close the great doors of the council hall, because what was boiling inside had long stopped caring who heard it.
"...the king ROTS in the Villain's keeping and you're already measuring his chair for your backside, Harrek!"
"Somebody had better measure it!
Or do we wait for the long-ears' fake god to come do it for us?!"
"The army is BONES, you copper-counting vulture!
Helmets with nobody under them!
Whoever takes the seat inherits a graveyard with taxes!"
"And no allies to guard it!
Or did you miss what little remains of our forces crawling back through the passes empty-handed?" A goblet went over.
"The old alliance died with Elvardia, the long-ears say!
Generations of treaty, dead in ONE elven evening!
And for what?
One strong male strutted into their forest, and the entire race rolled over for him, crown, army, and temple!"
"What did you expect from long-ears?!" a fourth lord roared over the wreckage of his chair.
"Weak-willed does in heat, the lot of them!
A race that spreads its legs the moment it sniffs a stronger male, then dresses the smell up as scripture!"
"That description reminds me of your wife."
"I heard your daughter takes visitors late at night."
The lord of the Copper Vaults and the lord of the Iron Gates had each other by the beard-rings within the minute.
A fist cracked across a rival's nose, a chair splintered to kindling under somebody's backside, and their retainers pretended very hard to be furniture.
Brokk halted in the doorway with her slate and watched the finest blood of her people eat itself.
Someone finally noticed her.

Every hearth, every hammer!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1842 Return to Silverwind
paragraphs: Quinlan stepped out of the [Warp Gate] onto a snow-covered rise above the river country of Silverwind, and paused in the cold night, taking stock of a view he already knew.
He had been here before as an enemy.

When he was farming human settlements for XP and souls, he had gone through the duchy's countryside estate by estate. Silverwind's nobility had answered with barriers, quick-deployment veils bought on short notice and thrown over every hold that could afford one.

The kingdom's defenses being erected against him like that was what prompted him to join Elvardia's invasion to begin with. Knowing it'd take too long to destroy those barriers himself, he used the Elvardian war machine instead of brute-forcing things.
Those days were behind him. The barriers had stopped being an obstacle because he grew powerful enough to destroy them on his own.

Behind Quinlan the rest of the party stepped through: Ayame first, then Black Fang, then Kaede with the cloth-wrapped offerings held against her chest, and finally Chizuru, who stepped out of a tear in space with her spine straight and her dignity pre-assembled, as if arriving anywhere by a method other than palanquin was an affront she had decided to survive.
The gate folded shut behind them.

Below, the ducal seat filled a bend of the river, its gray walls and steep slate roofs picked out by lanterns climbing the slope in ordered rows. Tiled ridges curled at their ends like drawn bows, black against the snow.

Terraced fields slept under snow on the far hills, their white slopes catching the moon. Roads ran toward towns and holdings as thin chains of lamps. It was beautiful country, wealthy country, and even from a mile out it looked wrong.
The road to the western gate crawled with lanterns as carts moved away from the city, the ferries sat idle at their moorings, and watch-fires showed twice the men any peaceful duchy would pay for.
Ayame took position at the edge of the rise, looking down at the city where she had been born, raised, poisoned, and sold.
Her face was composed, and her thumb moved once along the strap of her sword belt.
"The western gate," she said. "Let's walk."

Captain Rin had been the highest-ranking officer in Silverwind's western quarter ever since everyone ranked above her marched north to Elvardia with the elite muster. For two days now, the north had stopped answering.
She lived on the western wall now. Sleeping in the tower saved an hour of walking, and the hour mattered, because the duchy unraveled a little more each bell and somebody had to be present for it.

Silverwind stretched far beyond this city. Towns, villages, and river ports lay scattered across clan land, every one of them writing to the ducal seat for instructions while the stack of unanswered petitions in the keep grew by a hand-span a day.

What the duchy received instead was rumor, hauled in with the trade carts and breeding in the markets faster than any quartermaster could ration it. The Alliance was dead. The dwarven king was frozen in a mountain of ice. Lady Kaede had conquered Elvardia, Lady Kaede was dead in a field, Lady Kaede had never existed at all and the clan had ruled through a mask.

Rin had given up correcting any of it. She kept the watch rotation full and the wall stocked, because the one point on which every version of the story agreed was that whatever came next would come up a road.
"Captain." The watchman's call fell from the tower, flat and careful. "Party on the western road. Five. On foot."
On foot was wrong. Nobody with business at a duchy's gate arrived on foot after dark.
She climbed the tower stairs with her glass in hand and found the road.
The wrongness got worse: no banners, no wagons, no escort, five figures crossing the moonlit road without a trace of hurry, the gait of people accustomed to everyone yielding the road.
She raised the glass. The five entered the reach of the gate braziers, and the skin on her arms tightened before her mind offered any reason for it.

The man at the center was enormous. Two meters and more of him, dark-haired, broad as a gate door, dressed in black that swallowed the firelight, and he carried no weapon. He advanced up their road like it already belonged to him.
To his left was a violet-eyed woman, and Rin's stomach dropped through the wall, because she had seen those wanted posters a million times.

Every guardhouse in the duchy hung that face. The reward under it could buy generational wealth, yet not many were suicidal enough to try collecting it. The Venomborne Terror was coming up the western road in the open, her face lit by the gate fires, unhurried.
To his right was a small woman in dark traveling clothes with a katana at her hip, and it was old Sergeant Daiki who made the sound, a strangled thing from a habitually silent man.
"That's..." His knuckles whitened on the parapet stone. "Goddess! That's Lady Ayame. The one who..."
He didn't finish. Nobody who had served under the old lord ever finished that sentence.
The whisper traveled down the wall anyway, low and disbelieving.
"The traitor."
"She's alive?"
"She came back..."

His name reached the wall by itself, whispered down the line like fire through dry grass, because every rumor out of the north had put the same figure at its center. He was the man who opened dwarven fortresses like ration crates, the man the elven race had knelt to, and the man the entire war had bent around, broken around, and ended around.
"The Primordial Villain," someone said, and the words cracked in the middle of it.
Bells rang down the wall, and drawn steel caught the torchlight along its whole length.
"Seal the gate!" Captain Rin's orders cut level and clear over the noise. "Bar the walk-door! Archers, hold! Nobody looses! Runner to the keep, now!"

Good orders, correct orders. She knew exactly what remained of the last walls that stood between that man and a thing he wanted, and she gave them anyway. The job was the job, whether or not it could be done.
Up the road, the Villain tipped his head back and considered the wall with mild interest, faintly bored, and that boredom frightened her worse than any war cry in her memory.
Rin filled her lungs to demand a parley.
"Stand down."
It was small. Level, worn, and small, and it went through Captain Rin like a blade through a paper screen, because she knew it, and she refused to know it.
Across the training yards, it had rung like a drawn bell.
Lady Kaede had used that same level tone to take the oaths and accept command of the finest army the duchy had ever mustered at eighteen, already matching ancient monsters of the highest level.
A slight figure stepped out from behind the Villain's arm, and the refusal collapsed.

She wore traveling gray. Her hair was bound low like a servant's, and she carried the thinness of long illness. She held a funeral bundle to her chest with both hands. Wine flask, incense, folded ash-paper, the shapes readable through the cloth to anyone raised inside these walls.
Down the length of the wall, bow arms slackened one by one.
The understanding arrived in Captain Rin all at once. There would be no relief column, because there was nobody left to send one. There had been no word from the north because the north was finished.

The war her duchy had spent bracing for had been over, so completely over that their lady, their invincible lady, was walking home on foot in servant's gray at that man's side of her own will. The order Rin had prayed nightly to receive from her chain of command had finally come up the western road.
And it was surrender.
"Open the gates," Lady Kaede demanded.

Rin's mouth worked. Protocol had one rung left on its ladder, and she grabbed for it: the figure at the rear of the party, ancient and immaculate, regarding the wall as if it had been raised for her inspection.
Her voice cracked, and she let it. "Elder Chizuru! Honored Elder, what are the clan's orders?!"

The Elder's gaze rose to her along the wall. An entire dynasty of replies assembled behind her sealed lips and died there as she glanced toward the man and the traitor, neither of whom so much as looked back.
Then Elder Chizuru of the Fujimori delivered unto the garrison of Silverwind the full and complete doctrine of her clan.
She nodded. Once.

Down the wall, hardened soldiers went gray. If whatever happened in the north had shut the mouth of that woman, the one their grandmothers had feared, then it was beyond asking about. And still nobody reached for the winches, because opening that gate felt like signing a treaty none of them had been allowed to read.
"Captain." Lady Kaede spoke again, and for two words the drawn bell came back into her voice. "Gates."
The wall obeyed her. It had been built to. The winches turned, the last nerve of the garrison broke without a single arrow loosed, and the gates of Silverwind groaned open.
Rin descended the tower stairs on legs she did not fully own and held herself at attention as the party passed beneath the arch.
The Villain went by close enough to touch, noticing her as a passing storm notices a fence post.
The Venomborne Terror looked at no one at all.
Beyond the arch, Silverwind learned.

chapters.title: Chapter 1843 I Claim Her
paragraphs: Beyond the arch, Silverwind learned. Rin heard it happen from her post: a crier's voice failing halfway through the name, cart wheels stopping, doors slamming, lanterns vanishing down the length of the gate street one after another, and beneath all of it a low human murmur spreading away into the city, thousands of doors and mouths passing the same impossible sentence inward, block by block.
But when Lady Kaede passed, slight and gray with the bundle in her arms, Captain Rin bowed to her lady, low, and held it.

The Fujimori buried their dead on a pine hill inside the walls, above the clan estate, where the wind blew off the river and moved through the trees at every hour. Paper lanterns burned at intervals along the path, casting warm pools across the snow as Ayame led them up beneath the pines.
The graves rose in ranks, oldest at the crown of the hill, their names worn soft by weather. Raijin Fujimori's stone sat in the newest row, black granite, the carving still holding its edges.
Kaede stopped at the shoulder of the hill, three steps short of the family rows, and planted her feet to hold there.

Black Fang left the path without a word and settled against a pine at the edge of the trees, inside earshot and outside everything else. Chizuru remained at the path head, fingers interlaced, and became her own memorial.
Quinlan walked the last stretch at Ayame's side.

He read the rows once, the way he read any ground he stood on, and his reading snagged. Beside Raijin's stone, where every other lord in these ranks had a wife's marker at his shoulder, there was only unbroken snow, bare of any stone or second name.

He hadn't asked Ayame about her mother. She'd offered nothing, and he'd shelved that silence as old grief best left where she kept it. Graves he understood. The absence of one, here, in a clan that carved its dead into ranked and ordered stone, was a different kind of quiet.
He said nothing. Ayame had reached her father.
She knelt on both knees, spine straight, palms flat on her thighs, in the report posture her father himself had drilled into her, and for a while the pines had the hill to themselves.

chapters.title: Chapter 1844 New Order in the Fujimori Clan
paragraphs: Ayame came down from her family's graves while holding Quinlan's arm, unhurried, while the snow filled their footprints behind them, and found the duchy waiting for her at the bottom of the hill in the shape of a single exhausted captain.
Captain Rin stood outside the low gate of the burial hill with her helmet under one arm, planted at an attention so rigid it was clearly holding the last of her composure up.
High behind them, a thread of incense smoke leaned off the hill's shoulder, marking where Kaede knelt.
Rin bowed to the two of them, low, and held it one breath past protocol.
"My lady... My... Lord..." The words came out level through visible discipline.
She straightened, looked the conquerors of her duchy in the eye, and asked for a chain of command the way drowning people ask for rope.
"What are my orders?"
Quinlan, instead of answering, looked at Ayame.
Ayame tilted her head, and the grin arrived a heartbeat later, small and entertained.
"Why are you asking us?"
Rin's mouth opened, then made a strategic retreat.
"Your clan leader is right up there." A tip of Ayame's chin sent the captain's gaze up the lantern path, to the incense thread bending in the wind. "And your elder is standing right behind me."

"Lady Kaede is..." Rin picked her words the way a courier crosses river ice, and the ice cracked anyway. "Forgive me, my lady. The city watched her walk in wearing servant's gray. The honored Elder has not spoken a single word inside these walls. I don't... I no longer know where my chain of command begins, or whether I still have one."
Her fist tightened on the helmet's rim, and the exhaustion she had been holding at attention finally leaked into her voice.
"Every bell, another town writes to a keep that doesn't answer. My soldiers ask me what happens to the clan now. To the duchy. To them. I have been inventing answers for days, and I have run out."
"And here you were, hoping the disgraced heir had come home to claim her rightful chair."
Ayame said it kindly, which was why it took a moment to land.

"I won't be taking the leader's role." She released Quinlan's arm and faced the captain fully, and the play drained out of her voice. "I am busy standing second in command to the man who shall rule this continent soon enough."
Rin's discipline came off her face all at once just as Ayame finished, "I intend to be very busy with all of it."

The guard's gaze flicked to Quinlan, then back, and what remained of her military bearing sagged around the question. "Then who rules us? My lady, the towns need someone to answer them, or by spring there won't be a duchy left worth handing to anyone."
Ayame sighed at the sky, deeply put upon.
"Fine."
She turned. "Elder Chizuru of the Fujimori."
Parade-even, each word laid down like a document being stamped.

"Restore order to the clan and to the duchy. Answer the petitions, feed the towns, pay the garrisons, keep the roads and the river open. Govern justly in the clan's name, protect the people of Silverwind as you would the clan's own honor, and ready its affairs for handover to the new age. You will not act against Quinlan Elysiar, his family, or his interests. Not in letter, not in spirit, not in silence, and not through another's hands."

The orders sank into the Elder clause by clause, the bond notarizing each one as it landed. A command from one of the Primordial Villain's enslaved women bound a lesser slave as absolutely as a command from the Villain himself, and every line of Chizuru's posture said she felt it.

The Elder inclined her head to Ayame, precisely as deep as doctrine required and not one hair deeper. Then she turned and set off toward the city, and it was the walk of a lifetime: each step arriving separately, as if approved by committee, her hands strangling one another behind her back, a dynasty's worth of etiquette fighting a full-body revolt and winning by a nose.
Ayame let her get three steps. The smirk that crossed her face as she watched the Elder go was pure, patient sadism, and she took her time enjoying it.
"Oh, and Elder." She pitched it sweetly across the snow. "You may speak now."
The Elder's stride hitched.

What came out of her, low and venomous and perfectly enunciated, was cursing of the highest doctrinal order. "Whelp of a disgraced line... clan custom trampled like tavern sawdust... the revered voice of the Fujimori, gagged and ungagged at a girl's whim, like a, like a house cat..."
"Did you say something, Elder?" Ayame asked pleasantly.

"Captain." Chizuru's voice arrived at full ceremonial volume, aimed at Rin, with no acknowledgment that it had been doing anything else whatsoever. "What are you standing there for? The duchy is drowning in unanswered paper. Follow."
Rin looked at the Elder's receding back. Then at Ayame. Then at the Elder again.

She had grown up on that woman. Officers Rin had spent her whole career admiring went quiet when Elder Chizuru's name entered a room, and counted their fear of her as a badge of service. And that woman had just been unmuted on order.

The new order of the world settled into Captain Rin only then, at the foot of the burial hill, later than the opened gates and the bells and the wanted posters had managed it. Everything she had sworn her life to now answered to the tall man in black and the short woman at his side.
She put her helmet on.

Then Captain Rin of the western wall bowed once more to Ayame and Quinlan, deep and unhurried, the bow of a surrender given honestly, and jogged off through the snow after the Elder, toward a duchy that had orders again.
Quinlan watched her go. "She looks promising."

"Mm. She'll do." Ayame reclaimed his arm, and her attention had already left the city entirely. When she looked up at him, the shine from the bottom of the hill was back, twice as bright and twice as dangerous.
"Now then~" she hummed. "About that debt of yours."
The Fujimori estate received its heir in silence.

What staff remained pressed themselves to the walls of the winter courtyards and bowed to Ayame as she passed. She acknowledged none of it. Her evening held only one item, and none of them were on it.
Black Fang came with them, a step off the path and silent.

She had fallen in with her sister somewhere on the way down from the pines, without being asked or invited. Now the estate her father had thrown her out of went by on both sides of her: the winter courtyards, the lantern posts, the bowing staff, the tiled roofs she had been born under and didn't remember sleeping beneath.

Her gaze crossed all of it at the same even pace it crossed everything else. Then she looked away from the last roof and did not look back, and the house of Fujimori got no more out of her than her father's grave had.
Ayame met her sister's eyes and held them for a breath. Nothing crossed between them that a third person could have named, but Black Fang turned toward the dark and disappeared.
Quinlan considered the nothing she left behind. "So that's what the poison bath bought."
"Hehe~ Yes, I asked her for privacy when the time came..."
Quinlan's grin came out slow, and his hand found the small of her back.
The dawn dojo stood at the head of the estate's oldest courtyard.

Ayame slid its doors open with both hands, and the hall breathed out at her: brazier warmth, pine smoke, a floor polished dark by generations of bare feet, and racks of training steel and ironwood lining the walls in ordered ranks. On the far side, a second set of doors stood open to the snow garden, where moonlight lay across the veranda like a second floor.

"The dawn dojo." She said it quietly, without turning. "Every Fujimori is tested on this floor, and every duel fought here is fought before the ancestors. Their verdicts are truth. This is the most sacred ground my clan owns."
"From what I remember, your desired dress code doesn't quite fit such an occasion..." Quinlan mused.
"The leader sets the terms."
"So we should ask Kaede."
She sent him a sly look, stepping forward, one pointer finger landing on his stomach. "Stop playing dumb with me, Quin. I know I said Kaede was the leader, but we all know..."
Her finger raced up and found his heart. "...that just like with the rest of the continent, we are the real bosses. Or will be soon enough~"

On the far side, a second set of doors stood open to the snow garden, where moonlight lay across the veranda like a second floor.
"The dawn dojo." She said it quietly, without turning.
"Every Fujimori is tested on this floor, and every duel fought here is fought before the ancestors.
Their verdicts are truth.
This is the most sacred ground my clan owns."
"From what I remember, your desired dress code doesn't quite fit such an occasion..." Quinlan mused.
"The leader sets the terms."
"So we should ask Kaede."
She sent him a sly look, stepping forward, one pointer finger landing on his stomach.
"Stop playing dumb with me, Quin.
I know I said Kaede was the leader, but we all know..."
Her finger raced up and found his heart.
"...that just like with the rest of the continent, we are the real bosses.
Or will be soon enough~"

chapters.title: Chapter 1845 Ceremonial Preparation
paragraphs: Her hand then came off and she turned around. She looked back over her shoulder at him, and the quiet cracked open into wickedness. "Get ready, Quin. And please bring out a few of my clanswomen first."
"Sure," Quinlan smiled. "[Awaken]."
Pale flame stood up out of the floorboards in five places and cooled into women.

They wore the elite muster's armor they had died in, and the seniormost of them, a scarred veteran with an old white line through one brow, took in the hall, the brazier, and the heir standing in the middle of it, and understood the assignment before anyone explained a thing.
Whatever the five of them had died believing about the clan's disgraced daughter, none of it survived the sight of her. They bowed to Ayame as one.
"Lady Ayame."
"Come with me, I need your help." She was already walking toward the preparation room off the hall's east side. "I have to look like a most treasured heirloom."
The door slid shut on the six of them.
Quinlan, left alone in the most sacred hall of the Fujimori, consulted his orders.
He remembered the terms exactly, because she had only ever managed to say them once, almost a year ago, in a small voice that had needed three separate attempts to leave her.
"We'll be naked... With trainer swords... the loser will submit to the winner..."
He kept his promises.
He undressed all the way down, folded nothing, took a practice blade off the nearest rack, and leaned against a support pillar to wait.
"Hmm." The blade turned against the brazier light, balanced across two of his fingers while he read it.
Black ironwood, dense past all argument, with a core that sang thinly of steel when he flicked a nail against it. He pressed his thumb into the grain, and the grain won.
A proper practice weapon, made for high level duels. It wouldn't break on him after a few hits.
From the east room came the sounds of ceremony: water being poured, cloth whispering, the small clicks of lacquered combs. One of the dead women laughed at something.
Then the east door slid back a hand's width, and a clanswoman leaned out to retrieve the lacquer tray she had set down on the hall floor on her way in.

The retrieval did not go well. She got the tray. She also got the whole of her lord, lit brazier-orange from collarbone to thigh and entirely unbothered about it, and her hand missed the door track twice on the way back in.
*Clack.*
"Eyes," the veteran said from inside, without heat.
"...Yes, Captain."
The door shut.

Snow ticked against the doors, the brazier drew long shadows up the weapon racks, and the most feared man on the continent stood naked in the heart of a conquered duchy twirling a wooden sword by its balance point, without a shred of impatience, because the thing at the end of this wait was a sight he'd been looking toward for a very, very long time.
The east door slid open.

Four clanswomen filed out first and formed a rank along the wall, and their scarred veteran came last. Before taking her place she paused and bowed, this time to Quinlan, which she had pointedly not done on arrival.
Then Ayame stepped out and Quinlan's brain stopped functioning.

They had dressed her in ritual white, layered silk bound at the waist with a pale obi knotted for ceremony. Her black hair was up off her neck, pinned with lacquered combs, and her mouth had been painted a quiet, devastating red. She crossed the floor exactly as ordered: like an heirloom, like the finest thing the clan had ever produced walking on its own two feet.

Not long ago, other hands had prepared this woman to be looked at in a slave house. Tonight every hand had been hers to command, every choice had been her own, and the audience was one man. She wore the difference more proudly than any crown.
Quinlan looked. He made no secret of it.
Ayame arrived at the middle of the floor. She took in her partner, propped against a pillar with a practice sword resting on one shoulder, and her eyebrow made the long climb.

It made the climb slowly, because it had a great deal of territory to cross on the way: the chest, the ridged stomach, the enormous slab of him standing mere days out of a continental war without a mark on it, and the part of him that had already formed a firm opinion about tonight.
Her ears went pink. Her chin did not move a millimeter.
Along the wall, five dead women were having considerable difficulty locating somewhere neutral to look.
"You've outdone yourselves." Quinlan addressed the rank without taking his eyes off their lady. "Thank you. I'll reunite you with your families in the coming days. Now leave us."

Five bows arrived in one motion, and then the clanswomen came apart into pale flame, their scarred veteran going last and unhurried about it, radiating the unmistakable intent to tell the entire army.
The hall belonged to the two of them.

"Unbelievable." The composure held for precisely as long as it took her to say the word. "The most sacred hall of my clan, and its guest of honor is loitering in it without a stitch on, like this is a tavern brawl."
"You wanted naked."
"I said it a long time ago. Once. While half-dying of embarrassment. You shouldn't even remember it... For me, only mere months passed, but for you-"
"Naked. Trainer swords. The loser submits to the winner." He recited it like scripture, tapping the ironwood flat against his own collarbone.
Her grin returned in full force. "Of course you would remember... You'd remember it till the end of time."
"Yep."

"..." She stood a moment longer, and the amusement went warm at its edges, because he had stripped bare in her ancestors' hall on the strength of one flustered sentence she had barely survived saying, and in all the time since, he had never once made her feel foolish for it.
Quinlan pushed off the pillar, and the practice blade spun once around his grip, lazy as a coin trick, before it settled.
"Enough ceremony. Bratty women need to be taught a lesson. And my dearest Ayame, you've been one hell of a brat recently."
The taunt landed square where her pride lived, and Ayame's chin came up.
"Excuse me?" Her eyes had gone bright with it, already sorting through which of her recent crimes he could possibly have in mind.
"Don't think you got away with your crime. You extracted my seed without me knowing about it."
The brightness came off her face and took several other expressions with it.

"...The hot spring." It arrived a full register above the voice she dueled in. Then she recalculated, landed on the only possible source, and looked briefly murderous about it. "Daddy's Little Bitch snitched on me..."
"That's one slight more on your tab, bratty woman of mine," Quinlan sighed, theatrically disappointed. "Don't badmouth your sister-wives."
Then he smirked. "But yes, Aurora was very proud of you. She said you were professional about it."

"I was professional about it!" The second-in-command of the most dangerous family on the continent delivered this at a volume her ancestors had never once been subjected to inside that hall. "It was a sample. For research. You were busy staring at my sister's chest, I saw an opening, and I took it."
"You put it in a vial."
"Where else was I supposed to put it?!"
"Your belly? Where I intended to store it?"
Her hands went to her obi, and her mouth sharpened into the smile she saved for worthy enemies.
"Alright, let's settle this."
She untied it without hurry, eyes never leaving his, and let silk and ceremony slide off her together, pooling around her ankles like a surrendered banner.
"I once gave you a beating, draped in nothing but bandages."
Then Ayame stood naked on her ancestors' floor and let him look his fill.
"Now, draped in nothing but moonlight..."

He took in the small waist, the perky tits rising with a breath she took her sweet time over, the flat stomach with the crimson bloodfather mark riding low on it like a signature, the thighs a lifetime of stances had built.
The brazier turned the whole warm length of her gold down one side, and the moon coming off the snow garden did the other in silver.
Her chin was up, and her mouth was painted for exactly this.
The practice blade rose into both her hands.
"...I'll teach you the same thing all over again, since you don't seem very receptive to my teachings, first student of mine. This time I'll beat some humility into you properly!"
The pride of the Fujimori grinned at her lover across the floor of her ancestors, all teeth and not one scrap of mercy.
"Come, my arrogant primordial!"
